Their roles fit into a broader sequence: incoming signals reach receiving surfaces, are integrated, and can lead to an outgoing axonal action potential. The soma also supplies metabolic and synthetic support.

By contrast, the origin of neural cells concerns differentiation into cell classes, and convergence concerns the pattern of connections between cells. These are related but distinct levels of analysis. A neuron can have the same named anatomical parts as another neuron while receiving different inputs and projecting to different targets. The answer is strongest when each structural label is tied to its immediate functional role.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-mc40.title: Question 40 — Integration: Dendrites and soma
l02-mc40.markdown:
The focus here is how receiving surfaces participate in a network. Dendrites and the soma possess receptors for signals from other neurons, and many inputs can converge on one cell. Their combined effects influence whether the cell reaches the threshold for an outgoing action potential.

The keyed option therefore goes beyond naming anatomical parts: it explains reception and integration. Divergence describes the opposite organizational direction, one cell influencing several targets, often through axonal branches. Keep input number separate from input effect. Many inputs can include both excitation and inhibition, so more synapses do not automatically imply more firing. The receptor actions and their timing must also be considered.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — The cell body (soma)
l02-sa01.markdown:
The soma supports the neuron's metabolic and synthetic needs and contains the nucleus. Within the nucleus, genes provide information used to produce proteins. Transcription factors influence which genes are transcribed and at what rate. During transcription, a complementary RNA message is produced; during translation, ribosomes use that message to assemble a protein.

Connect this to neuronal function by giving examples of protein products: receptors influence responsiveness, enzymes support transmitter synthesis and metabolism, and channels and transporters control membrane processes. Proteins needed at distant terminals can then be delivered through axoplasmic transport. Thus, the soma's role is not separate from signaling; it supplies much of the machinery that makes signaling possible. A good answer distinguishes the location of transcription from the location of translation and explains how changes in expression can alter later neural responses without requiring an immediate change in the DNA sequence.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — The squid giant axon
l02-sa02.markdown:
The squid giant axon is used in the source material as an accessible preparation for studying the electrical properties of a neuron. The key measurement compares voltage inside the axon with an external reference. An electrode outside compared with another outside does not measure the transmembrane difference; placing one electrode inside allows that difference to be recorded.

Connect the preparation to resting potential by explaining why the interior is negative relative to the exterior under resting conditions. Unequal ion distributions, selective membrane permeability, and maintenance of gradients are central. Then connect it to excitability: changing membrane conductances can produce local voltage changes and, at threshold, an action potential. The question does not require biographical detail about the researchers or unsupported historical claims. It requires an explanation of how a physical preparation makes a cellular electrical phenomenon measurable. The existing answer is a topic placeholder rather than a model response.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Characteristics of the postsynaptic potential
l02-sa03.markdown:
Postsynaptic potentials are graded: stronger synaptic input can produce a larger local voltage change. They decay with time and distance and can summate. Inputs close together in time support temporal summation; inputs arriving from different locations support spatial summation. Excitatory and inhibitory changes jointly influence the membrane near the action-potential initiation region.

The connection to firing is a threshold transition. If the combined depolarization reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels generate an all-or-none spike. A local potential need not produce a spike, and a larger local potential does not simply become a proportionally larger spike. Instead, the pattern of input can change whether and how frequently spikes occur. Explain this sequence explicitly: **synaptic input → local conductance change → graded potential → integration → threshold or no threshold**. This is also why a drug acting at a synapse can alter firing indirectly without itself being a voltage-gated sodium-channel blocker.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Glia – Schwann Cells and Oligodendrocytes Cell Function
l02-sa04.markdown:
Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes both form myelin, but in different divisions of the nervous system. Schwann cells serve peripheral axons, whereas oligodendrocytes form myelin around central axons. The lecture also contrasts their relationships to regeneration after injury. Myelin supports rapid conduction by allowing action potentials to be regenerated at nodes rather than continuously along the entire axon.

Relate this to sodium-channel-blocking drugs by distinguishing two ways conduction can fail. Myelin disruption impairs the structural conditions for efficient propagation, whereas a channel blocker prevents or modifies the ionic events needed to regenerate an action potential. Both can interfere with transmission, but their immediate mechanisms differ. A complete answer should therefore name the cell type and location, explain the role of myelin and nodes, and then compare structural insulation with channel availability. Neither explanation requires assuming that the drug directly destroys the myelin sheath.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — Organization of the Nervous System
l02-sa05.markdown:
Begin with the central nervous system, consisting of brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system, which connects central circuits with the rest of the body. Within the peripheral system, distinguish somatic pathways associated with sensory input and skeletal-muscle control from autonomic pathways regulating organs and glands.

Spinal nerves illustrate how these divisions communicate. Sensory afferents carry information toward the spinal cord, while motor efferents carry output away toward muscles. Because a spinal nerve contains both, it is a mixed nerve. Their cell bodies and entry or exit relationships are not identical: the lecture identifies dorsal root ganglia for sensory neurons and the ventral horn for somatic motor neurons. Connect the organizational diagram to a functional sequence of sensing, central processing, and responding. Avoid equating peripheral with unimportant or assuming that every cranial nerve contains the same mixture of fibers as a spinal nerve.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 26. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa06.title: Short Essay 6 — Developmental origins of the CNS The CNS Has Distinct Regions Reflecting Embryological
l02-sa06.markdown:
The neural tube develops into the spinal cord and major brain divisions. Use the developmental map to organize adult structures: forebrain divisions include telencephalon and diencephalon, the midbrain is the mesencephalon, and hindbrain divisions include metencephalon and myelencephalon. Within these regions, nuclei are clusters of cell bodies and tracts are bundles of axons.

The functional connection is hierarchical but overlapping organization. Later or more elaborated regions do not eliminate the functions of other levels; they participate in more complex regulation and behavioral control. For example, cortical planning still depends on pathways connecting to motor and brainstem systems. The prompt repeats the developmental-origin topic rather than specifying a separate comparison, so the clearest response links the embryological scheme to recognizable adult structures and communication pathways. Do not turn the map into a rigid claim that each psychological function belongs exclusively to one developmental compartment.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 31. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa07.title: Short Essay 7 — Metencephalon
l02-sa07.markdown:
The metencephalon includes the pons and cerebellum. The cerebellum combines sensory information, including body position and balance, with motor-related information, helping coordinate movement. Its connections with the pons and other regions make it part of a broader sensorimotor network rather than an isolated source of muscle commands.

The tectum belongs to the mesencephalon and contains the superior and inferior colliculi. The lecture emphasizes visual orienting for the superior colliculi and auditory-related orientation for the inferior colliculi. Their connection is functional rather than anatomical identity: sensory events can guide orientation, while cerebellar processing helps coordinate the resulting behavior. A strong comparison identifies the correct division, the named structures, and their differing contributions. Avoid treating both regions simply as “movement centers”; explain the kind of information each emphasizes and how sensory input can be linked to organized motor output.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 36. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa08.title: Short Essay 8 — Diencephalon Hypothalamus:
l02-sa08.markdown:
The hypothalamus belongs to the diencephalon and integrates neural regulation with endocrine function through its relationship with the pituitary. The lecture associates its many nuclei with functions such as feeding, sleep–wake regulation, sexual behavior, and aggression. These examples link internal physiological conditions with motivated behavior.

The telencephalon includes the cortex and underlying structures involved in memory, emotion, movement, and motivation. Its connection to hypothalamic functions is through interacting systems: behavior depends on both internal-state regulation and the processing of environmental information, memories, and possible actions. Do not describe the hypothalamus as the whole endocrine system or the telencephalon as only the cortical surface. The answer should distinguish their anatomical membership and main functional emphases, then explain why neither acts alone in producing organized behavior. The broad course framing supports an integration argument, not a one-region explanation of every motivated act.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 41. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa09.title: Short Essay 9 — Human vs. rat brains
l02-sa09.markdown:
The lecture supports comparison through shared organization and differences in relative development. Human and rat brains contain the same major mammalian subdivisions, which makes comparisons of some circuits and drug mechanisms possible. However, the proportions of those subdivisions differ. The source emphasizes relatively prominent olfactory structures in rats and larger, more folded cerebral hemispheres in humans.

Interpret the final slogan in that context: it encourages recognition of conserved biological organization, not a literal claim that humans descend from living rats. The practical connection is to animal models. A conserved receptor or circuit can support useful investigation, but similarity does not establish identical behavior, dosing, or clinical response across species. A good answer explains both why comparison is informative and why extrapolation has limits. Simply saying that one species has a larger brain misses the more important issue of how different components are organized and proportioned.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 46. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l02-sa10.title: Short Essay 10 — Integration: Origin of the cells of the nervous system and Anatomy a neuron
l02-sa10.markdown:
Cell origin and neuronal anatomy describe different stages of explanation. Origin concerns how embryonic cells differentiate into specialized neurons and glia. Anatomy concerns the structures through which a differentiated neuron receives information, maintains itself, and sends signals: dendrites, soma, axon, and terminals.

Connect the two by showing how specialization produces a functional arrangement. Dendrites provide receiving surfaces, the soma supplies metabolic and protein-synthesis machinery, and the axon communicates with distant targets. Glial specialization contributes support and, in some cell types, myelination that improves conduction. The relationship is therefore **development of specialized cell types → organization of cellular structures → neural function**. Avoid implying that all nervous-system cells are neurons or that every neuron has exactly the same shape. Shared structural principles can support different roles depending on a cell's connections and specialized properties.

**Source:** Lecture 2 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 2.

**Review:** [Lecture 2 study guide](../study-guides/lecture02.qmd).

l03-mc01.title: Question 1 — Discovery of a Neurotransmitter
l03-mc01.markdown:
The historical example concerns evidence that a nerve can influence another tissue through a released chemical. In the textbook's account of the heart experiment, stimulation of the vagus nerve slowed the heart, and fluid from that preparation transferred the effect to another heart. The transferable effect supported a chemical mediator rather than only direct electrical continuity.

The lecture calls the substance “vagustoff” and identifies it as acetylcholine. The key names the investigator and substance but omits the experimental logic. The important connection is **nerve stimulation → release of a substance → altered target activity**. This provides a foundation for the later distinction between electrical signaling along an axon and chemical signaling across a synapse.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc02.title: Question 2 — General Concepts
l03-mc02.markdown:
At a typical chemical synapse, the presynaptic terminal releases neurotransmitter into a gap, and the transmitter binds receptors on the receiving cell. The releasing and receiving machinery occupy different locations, explaining the usual direction of communication from presynaptic to postsynaptic cell.

The key summarizes this standard arrangement. It should not be generalized to every form of neural communication: the lecture explicitly mentions exceptions, including electrical synapses, and later introduces retrograde signals. Also distinguish crossing the synaptic cleft from crossing the postsynaptic membrane. A transmitter can activate a membrane receptor without entering the receiving cell. Receptors transmit information about binding, not necessarily the transmitter molecule itself.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc03.title: Question 3 — Types of Synapses
l03-mc03.markdown:
Synapses can be classified by the cellular structures that meet. An axon may contact a dendrite, a soma, or another axon. These arrangements place a signal at different points in the receiving neuron's processing machinery. The textbook also distinguishes chemical communication from electrical connections.

The functional question is therefore not just where two cells touch, but what that location permits the signal to influence. A contact on an axon terminal can regulate release, whereas a contact on a dendrite can contribute to the inputs being integrated by the receiving neuron. The existing key merely names “types of synapses.” A substantive answer should identify the arrangement and connect it to its possible signaling role.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc04.title: Question 4 — Astrocytes regulate synapses TRIPARTITE SYNAPSE
l03-mc04.markdown:
A tripartite synapse includes the presynaptic element, the postsynaptic element, and associated astrocytic processes. The concept expands the usual two-neuron picture by recognizing that the surrounding glial cell helps regulate the chemical environment and the handling of released transmitter.

For example, astrocytic uptake can limit extracellular transmitter and participate in recycling precursor material. This can influence how long a signal lasts and how surrounding cells are exposed. The key's short label should therefore be unpacked into a functional explanation, not memorized as a three-part slogan. Astrocytes are not simply an extra neuron transmitting the same action potential; they contribute through their own regulatory processes.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc05.title: Question 5 — Neurotransmitters Encompass Several Different Kinds of Chemical Substances
l03-mc05.markdown:
Neurotransmitters are chemically diverse. The lecture distinguishes amino acids such as glutamate and GABA, monoamines such as dopamine and serotonin, acetylcholine, purines, peptides, lipids, and gases. Classification matters because these substances do not necessarily share the same synthesis, storage, release, or inactivation mechanisms.

The keyed option correctly identifies amino-acid and monoamine examples, but it is not an exhaustive list. Nor does membership in a chemical class specify a single behavioral effect. The receptor subtype, location, and circuit remain important. Some neurons can produce more than one transmitter, so identifying a neuron by its principal transmitter is useful shorthand rather than a claim that it contains only one signaling substance.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc06.title: Question 6 — Neuropeptides are synthesized differently
l03-mc06.markdown:
Small-molecule transmitters are generally synthesized using enzymes available in axon terminals. Neuropeptides instead begin as larger precursor proteins produced through the cell's protein-synthesis machinery, chiefly in the soma, and are processed and transported toward terminals. Their supply therefore depends on a longer production-and-delivery sequence.

This explains the lecture's point that peptide replenishment is slower. Releasing a peptide-containing vesicle cannot simply be followed by immediate local synthesis of an entirely new precursor protein in the same way as replenishing many small-molecule transmitters. The key concerns **where and how the signal is made**, not whether peptides can influence neural activity. Both categories can be effective signals despite using different supply pathways.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc07.title: Question 7 — Neuromodulators Are Chemicals That Do Not Act Like Typical Neurotransmitters
l03-mc07.markdown:
Volume transmission allows a released chemical to influence cells beyond a narrowly defined synaptic contact. A neuromodulator can change the responsiveness of a region or alter how other transmitter signals operate. The lecture contrasts this with the more spatially focused “wiring” picture of one release site aligned with a particular receiving site.

The distinction is about signaling arrangement and action, not an absolute list of chemicals. The same substance can participate in more than one mode depending on where and how it is released. Varicosities help illustrate release along neuronal processes. The key therefore should not be interpreted as saying that neuromodulators never bind receptors or that they always generate a completely separate kind of biochemical response.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc08.title: Question 8 — Neutrotransmitter Release Involves Exocytosis and Recycling of Synaptic Vesicles
l03-mc08.markdown:
An arriving action potential depolarizes the terminal membrane and opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Calcium entry triggers the machinery that allows a docked vesicle to fuse with the membrane and release its contents. This is exocytosis, concentrated at specialized release regions called active zones.

The key correctly identifies calcium as the link between electrical activity and vesicular transmitter release. Calcium is not simply another name for the transmitter, and sodium influx producing an axonal spike is not the same event as calcium-triggered fusion at the terminal. After release, membrane can be retrieved by endocytosis and reused. A complete explanation follows the sequence from depolarization to calcium entry to fusion, rather than skipping directly from spike to receptor binding.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc09.title: Question 9 — Lipid and Gaseous Transmitters Are Not Released from Synaptic Vesicles
l03-mc09.markdown:
The lecture uses lipid and gaseous signals to show that the vesicle-release model has exceptions. These signals can be synthesized when needed rather than stored in conventional synaptic vesicles. Some are produced postsynaptically and travel back to influence the presynaptic cell, making them retrograde messengers.

The direction of signaling is therefore different from the standard presynaptic-release sequence. Endocannabinoids and nitric oxide illustrate this broader range of mechanisms in the source material. The key does not mean that all signaling molecules diffuse in the same way or have identical targets. Identify the relevant contrast: on-demand synthesis and nonvesicular signaling versus storage in vesicles followed by calcium-triggered exocytosis.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc10.title: Question 10 — Release Involves Exocytosis and Recycling of Synaptic Vesicles
l03-mc10.markdown:
Exocytosis adds vesicle membrane to the cell surface, so continued release requires membrane retrieval and rebuilding of release-ready vesicles. The lecture distinguishes clathrin-mediated endocytosis, ultrafast retrieval involving endosomal processing, and kiss-and-run release, in which a vesicle does not fully collapse into the surface membrane.

These models differ in timing and membrane handling, but all address the problem of sustaining repeated secretion. During strong activity, bulk endocytosis can retrieve larger amounts of membrane. The keyed option names one retrieval mechanism; it does not establish that every vesicle follows that route. Keep **endocytosis**, which retrieves membrane, separate from **exocytosis**, which releases transmitter.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc11.title: Question 11 — Autoreceptors control the rate of neurotransmitter release
l03-mc11.markdown:
Autoreceptors respond to the same transmitter released by the neuron that bears them. In the inhibitory feedback examples taught here, terminal autoreceptors reduce further release, while somatodendritic autoreceptors reduce the neuron's firing rate. Both can limit transmitter output, but at different points in the sequence.

This explains why stimulating an autoreceptor can reduce overall transmission even though the drug is a receptor agonist. Agonism describes what happens at a receptor; it does not guarantee greater output from the whole pathway. Heteroreceptors instead respond to a different transmitter and can enhance or suppress release. The key distinguishes the location and immediate consequence of autoreceptor feedback.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc12.title: Question 12 — Mechanisms of Neurotransmitter Inactivation
l03-mc12.markdown:
A synaptic signal needs a way to end. The lecture describes enzymatic breakdown, transporter-mediated reuptake into the presynaptic terminal, and uptake into other cells, including glia. These mechanisms reduce the amount of transmitter available to continue activating receptors.

Reuptake and degradation are not identical: a transporter moves a molecule, whereas an enzyme chemically transforms it. This distinction explains different drug targets. Blocking reuptake can prolong extracellular transmitter action without directly stimulating the postsynaptic receptor. Blocking degradation changes a different part of the same cycle. The keyed option names two major inactivation routes; a full explanation connects removal to the duration and spread of the signal.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc13.title: Question 13 — Neurotransmitter Receptor Families
l03-mc13.markdown:
A transmitter produces an effect only where an appropriate receptor and response mechanism are present. Different receptor subtypes for the same transmitter can engage different channels or intracellular pathways. As a result, one transmitter can produce different effects in different cells or circuits.

The keyed option correctly treats a receptor as a signaling protein rather than as a transporter that carries transmitter across the membrane. Binding changes the receiving cell's activity through the receptor's mechanism. This is why the transmitter name alone does not establish whether a particular response is excitatory or inhibitory. Specify the receptor subtype, cellular location, and downstream action before predicting the functional outcome.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc14.title: Question 14 — Ionotropic Receptors Consist of Multiple Subunits That Together Form an Ion Channel
l03-mc14.markdown:
An ionotropic receptor contains an ion channel as part of its receptor complex. Transmitter binding changes the receptor's state and permits selected ions to move through the channel. This provides a relatively direct route from chemical binding to a change in membrane conductance and potential.

The key captures the simple closed–open–closed sequence. However, prolonged exposure can also produce desensitization, in which responsiveness falls despite the continued presence of ligand. The effect depends on which ions the channel conducts and their driving forces, not merely on the fact that a channel opens. This differs from a metabotropic receptor, which initiates signaling through G proteins rather than being the conducting pore itself.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc15.title: Question 15 — Metabotropic Receptors Consist of a Single Subunit That Works by Activating G Proteins
l03-mc15.markdown:
A metabotropic receptor communicates through an associated G protein. After ligand binding, the G protein can influence an ion channel or regulate an effector enzyme involved in producing or removing intracellular second messengers. The receptor therefore initiates a chain of events rather than directly opening a pore within its own structure.

This helps explain the lecture's contrast between slower onset and longer-lasting effects relative to many ionotropic responses. The key should not be read as saying every metabotropic response must alter gene expression or that every G-protein pathway uses the same messenger. The pathway can branch and act at several levels. Follow receptor activation to its specific effector before predicting the cell's response.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc16.title: Question 16 — Allosteric modulation
l03-mc16.markdown:
An allosteric site is distinct from the principal agonist-binding site. A modulator binding there can change how the receptor responds to an agonist. A positive modulator increases the response under the relevant conditions, while a negative modulator reduces it.

The key therefore describes modification of another ligand's action, not simply replacement of that ligand at its binding site. This distinction becomes important in the GABA lecture, where drug effects depend on receptor modulation. Do not assume that a positive modulator directly produces the same action as an agonist in the absence of transmitter. The course emphasizes changing receptor responsiveness through a separate binding location.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc17.title: Question 17 — Tyrosine Kinase Receptors
l03-mc17.markdown:
Tyrosine kinase receptors provide a route by which neurotrophic signals influence cellular growth, survival, and longer-term functioning. Binding initiates intracellular signaling that can change protein activity and gene expression. Their significance extends beyond generating an immediate excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic potential.

The keyed option identifies the relationship with neurotrophic factors. This distinguishes them from ionotropic receptor channels and from the G-protein-coupled class discussed immediately before. All transmit information across the cell boundary, but they do so through different molecular machinery. An explanation should connect the receptor class to its signaling function rather than treating “growth factor” as simply another transmitter stored in every synaptic vesicle.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc18.title: Question 18 — Drugs can alter all aspects of synaptic transmission
l03-mc18.markdown:
A drug can alter transmission at several steps: precursor supply or synthesis, vesicular storage, release, receptor activation, reuptake, or enzymatic breakdown. The same overall increase in transmitter influence can therefore arise from different mechanisms. A reuptake inhibitor, for example, prolongs availability without necessarily acting as a direct receptor agonist.

Conversely, reducing synthesis and blocking postsynaptic receptors both weaken signaling but act at different locations. The lecture's overview should be read as a sequence of possible intervention points. For any example, identify **the immediate target, the change in transmitter availability or receptor function, and the predicted downstream effect**. The existing keyed statement names the overview without supplying these causal steps.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc19.title: Question 19 — Neuroendocrinology is extremely interesting Take Behavioural Endocrinology (PSYC 383) next term!
l03-mc19.markdown:
The final slide is an invitation to another course, not a substantive scientific claim. Its wording cannot establish a correct mechanism or distinguish scientifically valid alternatives. The only defensible interpretation of the existing key is recognition of the slide's closing message.

For scientific review, the supplied textbook separately discusses endocrine communication: hormones enter the circulation and influence cells with appropriate receptors, whereas conventional synaptic signaling operates across a much more localized junction. That comparison is textbook context, not content stated on this promotional slide. This item should not be used to judge understanding of neuroendocrinology until it is rewritten with an actual conceptual question and answer.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-mc20.title: Question 20 — Integration: Discovery of a Neurotransmitter
l03-mc20.markdown:
The discovery example asks how chemical communication was demonstrated. The transferable effect in the heart preparation supported the presence of a released substance, later identified as acetylcholine. That is an inference from an experimental manipulation and an observed effect, not merely the naming of a neurotransmitter.

General synaptic concepts describe the broader mechanism illustrated by the experiment: a releasing cell communicates chemically with a receptive target. The keyed historical names point to the demonstration, while the neighboring topic supplies the general model. Explain the link by distinguishing **evidence for a chemical mediator** from **the standard organization of chemical transmission**. Remember that the lecture later includes exceptions to the simplest one-way vesicular model.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — The variety of neurotransmitters is vast Over 100 chemicals have been
l03-sa01.markdown:
Organize the diversity into chemical groups rather than trying to memorize an isolated total. The lecture includes amino acids, monoamines, acetylcholine, purines, peptides, lipids, and gases. Give representative examples and then explain why the classification matters: it predicts differences in synthesis, storage, release, and removal.

For instance, peptide signaling depends on precursor-protein synthesis and transport, while many small-molecule transmitters can be replenished at terminals. Some lipid and gaseous signals are synthesized on demand rather than released from conventional vesicles. Receptor diversity adds a second level of complexity: one transmitter can act on several receptor subtypes, and some neurons release more than one signaling substance. The connection to psychopharmacology is that there is no single universal “neurotransmitter mechanism” for every drug to modify. A useful answer moves from chemical diversity to mechanistic diversity and then to the need to identify a specific drug target.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Mechanism of exocytosis
l03-sa02.markdown:
Trace exocytosis from the arrival of a depolarizing signal. Voltage-gated calcium channels open, calcium enters the terminal, and calcium-sensitive machinery promotes fusion of a prepared vesicle with the presynaptic membrane. The contents are released into the cleft, after which membrane retrieval supports further rounds of secretion.

The slide's protein list is abbreviated. Chapter 3 distinguishes the calcium-sensing role of synaptotagmin from the fusion machinery involving SNARE proteins, including synaptobrevin. This distinction explains why both calcium detection and membrane interaction are needed. Then contrast the pathway with lipid and gaseous signals: these are not packaged and released through the same vesicular cycle and can be synthesized on demand, including in the postsynaptic cell. Some act retrogradely on the presynaptic element. The answer should therefore compare **stored, vesicular release** with **on-demand, nonvesicular signaling**, rather than assuming that every transmitter uses exocytosis.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Neurotransmitters in the periphery
l03-sa03.markdown:
The same signaling chemical can participate in central and peripheral functions because suitable receptors occur in multiple tissues. A transmitter acting in an autonomic pathway or at a peripheral target does not need a different name simply because the target is outside the brain. Its effect depends on receptor subtype, cellular machinery, and the organ or circuit involved.

This connects directly to receptor families. A drug can affect the intended central pathway while also acting on peripheral receptors, producing additional effects. The lecture's opioid example illustrates why gastrointestinal actions can accompany central actions. The gut–brain discussion adds bidirectional communication and possible microbiome-related influences. Do not infer from that discussion that every neurotransmitter made in the gut directly enters the brain; the source describes a communication system, not a universal transport route. A strong response identifies the shared chemical, distinguishes target locations, and explains how receptor distribution creates multiple physiological consequences.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Second Messenger Systems
l03-sa04.markdown:
A first messenger, such as a transmitter, binds a receptor outside the cell. Receptor-linked machinery then changes an intracellular second messenger. Second messengers can activate protein kinases, which add phosphate groups to target proteins and change their functioning. Depending on the target, this can alter channels, enzymes, or longer-term cellular responses.

The textbook examples include cAMP, cGMP, calcium-related signaling, and phosphoinositide pathways. Phosphodiesterases help terminate cyclic-nucleotide signals, so inhibiting these enzymes can prolong the intracellular message. Connect this to tyrosine kinase receptors by identifying a shared purpose—transmitting an extracellular signal into intracellular regulation—without collapsing distinct receptor mechanisms into one. Tyrosine kinase receptors are not simply another name for G-protein-coupled receptors. The lecture's typed “gAMP” should be read against the textbook's cGMP terminology, and the explanation should distinguish the messenger molecule from the kinase that acts downstream.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l03-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — Integration: Discovery of a Neurotransmitter and General Concepts
l03-sa05.markdown:
The discovery example supplies experimental evidence for a chemical mediator, while the general-concepts slide presents a model of how chemical communication usually operates. In the heart experiment described by the textbook, a transferable substance reproduced an effect of nerve stimulation. That supported chemical mediation and led to the identification associated with vagal signaling.

Connect this to a typical synapse: a presynaptic element releases transmitter, the transmitter crosses a gap, and a receiving cell responds through appropriate receptors. Electrical activity within the releasing neuron and chemical signaling to the target are therefore linked but distinct. The general model is not an absolute rule for all communication; the lecture mentions electrical synapses and later discusses retrograde signals. A strong answer explains what the experiment established and then shows how the synaptic model extends that insight, rather than treating a scientist's name and a list of synaptic parts as separate facts.

**Source:** Lecture 3 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 3.

**Review:** [Lecture 3 study guide](../study-guides/lecture03.qmd).

l04-mc01.title: Question 1 — Behavioral Pharmacology
l04-mc01.markdown:
Behavioral pharmacology connects drug administration to a measurable change in behavior. The scientific aim is not simply to observe that an animal moves differently, but to use controlled comparisons to investigate the relationship between a drug, nervous-system processes, and behavioral outcomes.

The lecture identifies applications in understanding mechanisms, developing models, and screening candidate compounds. A behavioral change does not by itself identify a specific receptor or establish clinical benefit. Those interpretations require additional evidence. The keyed option states the field's purpose; the methods introduced later specify how that purpose is pursued. Keep the research question, the experimental manipulation, and the measured outcome distinct.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc02.title: Question 2 — Animals are necessary for behavioural pharmacology
l04-mc02.markdown:
Animal studies can permit close control of living conditions, prior experience, and genetic background. They can also support measurements or interventions that would not be appropriate in human participants. These features help researchers isolate possible causes of a behavioral effect.

The key identifies one advantage, but control does not automatically make an animal model an exact copy of a human disorder. The lecture's generalization argument depends on meaningful similarities alongside awareness of differences. It also emphasizes animal-care requirements and the three Rs. A good explanation therefore combines experimental value with limits and ethical obligations, rather than interpreting the title as a claim that every psychopharmacological question must be studied in animals.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc03.title: Question 3 — Controls in animal behavioural pharmacology
l04-mc03.markdown:
A vehicle control receives the preparation used to deliver the drug without the active test compound. It helps distinguish effects of the compound from effects of injection, handling, or the vehicle itself. A positive control receives a treatment with a well-characterized effect in the assay.

The controls answer different questions. The vehicle establishes a comparison without the test drug, while the positive control checks that the procedure can detect the expected kind of effect. If a candidate appears ineffective and the positive control also fails, the assay may be the problem. The keyed option correctly separates these functions; neither control alone establishes every aspect of specificity, validity, or safety.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc04.title: Question 4 — You can just watch them and see what they do!
l04-mc04.markdown:
Direct observation can identify changes such as tremor, salivation, immobility, or altered activity. Quantifying these behaviors helps describe a drug's effect and can reveal whether a compound is sedating or stimulating. The important step is turning observation into a defined, consistently measured outcome.

A change in movement does not automatically identify a change in mood, anxiety, or motivation. For example, a drug that impairs movement could alter performance in a test whose intended interpretation concerns something else. The key therefore describes useful initial measurements, not a complete diagnosis of an internal state. Later behavioral assays need to be interpreted in light of such basic motor and physiological effects.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc05.title: Question 5 — Does the drug alter affective states?
l04-mc05.markdown:
The lecture presents fear-conditioning and forced-swim procedures as examples of assays aimed at aspects of affect-related behavior. In fear conditioning, an initially neutral cue can acquire significance through pairing with an aversive event. A subsequent response to the cue is a learned behavioral measure.

The crucial qualification is **fear-related or depressive-like behavior**, not direct access to an animal's complete subjective experience or a clinical diagnosis. Drug effects on movement, learning, or perception can influence the measured response. The keyed option identifies the relevant tests, but explanation requires naming what is observed and distinguishing it from the broader state being inferred. One assay result should not be treated as proof of an entire disorder.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc06.title: Question 6 — Does the drug alter the stress response?
l04-mc06.markdown:
Chronic-stress paradigms examine consequences of repeated or prolonged adverse conditions rather than a single immediate response. The lecture lists unpredictable mild stress, social defeat, and maternal separation as different experimental approaches. Their procedures and the questions they address are not interchangeable.

Sucrose preference is introduced as a measure related to anhedonia, the reduced responsiveness to normally rewarding experiences. Interpreting a change requires considering what the animal can perceive, consume, and physically do. The keyed option gives one stress paradigm, not the full definition of stress. A complete explanation connects the exposure manipulation to the subsequent behavioral measure and avoids equating the procedure's name with an observed outcome.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc07.title: Question 7 — Does the drug alter reward and reinforcement?
l04-mc07.markdown:
Reward and reinforcement are related but distinct experimental concepts. A reinforcer is identified by its effect on behavior: obtaining it increases or maintains the response that produces it. In drug self-administration, the animal performs an action to obtain the drug, allowing researchers to examine its reinforcing properties.

The lecture also includes intracranial self-stimulation, progressive-ratio breakpoint, and conditioned place preference. These measure different aspects of the relationship between an event and behavior. A high response rate is not a direct reading of pleasure, because motor capacity and the response requirement also matter. The key identifies a relevant method; the explanation should specify what the animal does and what consequence follows.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc08.title: Question 8 — Conditioned place preference
l04-mc08.markdown:
Conditioned place preference uses an association between an environment and an experience. One setting is paired with a drug or other event, and later preference for that setting is assessed. The environment can acquire motivational significance even when the drug is not being delivered during the preference test.

This is principally a Pavlovian arrangement: the context predicts the event. It differs from self-administration, in which an action produces the drug. The key therefore identifies learned place preference as evidence about rewarding associations, not as a direct measure of every aspect of addiction. Initial preferences, learning, and the ability to explore are relevant to interpreting the observed choice.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc09.title: Question 9 — Emerging technologies in ethology
l04-mc09.markdown:
Computer vision can convert video into quantified descriptions of behavior, such as movement patterns or the occurrence of defined actions. The lecture emphasizes the possibility of collecting richer observations in habitat-based environments and extends the idea to wearable sensors in humans.

Automation changes how behavior is measured; it does not remove the need to define the behavior or interpret it appropriately. An algorithm's label is not, by itself, proof of anxiety, pleasure, or a specific neural mechanism. The keyed option concerns measurement technology rather than a new neurotransmitter assay. Connect the data to the scientific question, and distinguish a detected movement pattern from the psychological construct it may be used to investigate.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc10.title: Question 10 — Stereotaxic Surgery
l04-mc10.markdown:
Stereotaxic methods use an anatomical coordinate system to position an implant or intervention relative to a targeted brain location. A brain atlas and reference landmarks help translate a desired region into a reproducible placement. This is important when a research question concerns a particular circuit or nucleus.

The key identifies precise placement as the contribution of the method. Stereotaxic surgery does not itself measure transmitter concentration, identify a protein, or establish a behavioral effect; it enables other tools to be placed appropriately. Anatomical verification remains important because a result depends on where the intervention actually occurred. Distinguish the positioning procedure from the recording, sampling, or manipulation that follows it.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc11.title: Question 11 — Invasive measurement of neurotransmitters
l04-mc11.markdown:
Microdialysis and fast-scan cyclic voltammetry both provide information about extracellular neurochemistry, but they use different measurement principles. Microdialysis samples substances across a probe membrane for analysis. Voltammetry uses electrochemical changes at an electrode to detect suitable electroactive chemicals and can follow relatively rapid fluctuations.

The key groups them as invasive neurochemical methods because the sensing device is placed in the relevant tissue. Neither is identical to recording action potentials, and neither measurement alone establishes how much transmitter activated a particular postsynaptic receptor. Link the observed chemical signal to its sampling location and timing. Behavioral and neurochemical data can complement one another without becoming interchangeable measurements.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc12.title: Question 12 — Invasive measurement of electrical activity
l04-mc12.markdown:
Electrical recording asks about neural voltage changes or firing activity, rather than directly measuring the concentration of a transmitter. An electrode positioned in or near the relevant tissue can detect electrical events, with the interpretation depending on placement and recording arrangement.

The distinction from the preceding slide is the quantity measured: microdialysis and voltammetry investigate neurochemistry, while electrophysiological recording investigates electrical activity. A change in firing may accompany a change in transmitter release, but one cannot simply substitute for the other. The keyed option is a topic placeholder. A meaningful answer needs to name the measurement and explain how it relates to the neural process of interest without claiming that all electrical recordings reveal the same level of activity.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc13.title: Question 13 — enkephalin
l04-mc13.markdown:
The enkephalin example illustrates **in situ hybridization**, which locates a specified RNA sequence in tissue. Detecting messenger RNA provides evidence about expression of the corresponding gene in particular cells or regions. It does not directly measure the amount of translated protein present at that moment.

This is why the slide emphasizes that mRNA does not always equal protein. Translation, processing, transport, and degradation separate transcript abundance from the final protein signal. Immunohistochemistry addresses protein localization through a different assay. The key's important content is this measurement distinction; “enkephalin” is the example being examined, not the name of the technique or a reason to equate the two readouts.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc14.title: Question 14 — DREADDs
l04-mc14.markdown:
DREADDs are engineered receptors used to change cellular activity through administration of a suitable activating ligand. The name emphasizes their experimental design: receptor expression and drug administration are combined to manipulate a selected cell population rather than merely observe it.

This makes the method different from staining tissue or measuring naturally occurring transmitter concentrations. The causal question is whether changing the activity of the targeted cells changes an outcome. Appropriate comparisons must separate effects of receptor expression, ligand administration, and their combination. The lecture supplies the acronym rather than a full protocol, so the explanation should remain at the level of experimental logic and not assume that every receptor–ligand system has identical effects or perfect specificity.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc15.title: Question 15 — Positron emission tomography (PET)
l04-mc15.markdown:
PET detects signals from an administered radioactive tracer. What the image means depends on the tracer: a glucose-related tracer can inform metabolic activity, while an appropriate receptor-binding tracer can inform receptor availability or related pharmacological processes. The scanner does not directly photograph neurotransmitter molecules firing between cells.

The keyed option correctly connects PET with radioactivity and several possible applications. Those applications should not be collapsed into one universal readout. A change in tracer signal must be interpreted in relation to the tracer's binding, uptake, and distribution. The lecture's FDG example therefore differs from a radioligand selected to investigate a particular drug target.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-mc16.title: Question 16 — Integration: Behavioral Pharmacology
l04-mc16.markdown:
Behavioral pharmacology is defined by its scientific question: how drugs alter behavior and what those alterations reveal about underlying mechanisms. Animal research is one experimental setting in which that question can be investigated under controlled conditions. The two are connected, but they are not equivalent definitions.

The keyed option describes the purpose of the field, whereas statements about controlled housing or known histories describe practical features of an animal study. To reason beyond the labels, specify the drug manipulation and the behavioral outcome, then ask what the comparison can establish. A controlled behavioral effect can support further mechanistic investigation without automatically identifying the responsible receptor or proving relevance to every human condition.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Is the drug a good anxiolytic?
l04-sa01.markdown:
An anxiolytic assay needs a defined behavioral measure linked to anxiety-like responses. The lecture includes open-field, elevated plus-maze, and defensive-burying procedures. Explain what changes in approach, avoidance, or defensive behavior are being interpreted, rather than assuming that the animal's subjective anxiety has been directly measured.

The connection to other affect-related tests is the distinction between an observable response and the broader construct inferred from it. Fear conditioning and forced-swim behavior measure different aspects of performance and should not be treated as interchangeable diagnoses. A drug that changes locomotion, sensation, learning, or coordination can also change performance. Appropriate vehicle and positive controls, together with basic activity measures, help interpret the result. A strong response therefore describes the assay, predicts the behavioral change of interest, and explains at least one alternative explanation that must be considered before calling the compound anxiolytic.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Rat in Operant Chamber (“Skinner Box”)
l04-sa02.markdown:
In an operant chamber, an animal learns that a response produces a consequence. A lever press followed by access to a reinforcer is different from a cue merely predicting an event. The schedule determines the response requirement: a fixed-ratio schedule requires a specified number of responses, while a progressive-ratio schedule raises that requirement and permits measurement of the breakpoint.

The key connection is between a controlled contingency and quantified behavior. Emerging video-analysis methods can add detailed descriptions of movement or action patterns, but observing behavior does not itself create an operant contingency. An automated system may measure the behavior in a chamber or a more naturalistic environment; the researcher still needs to specify which actions have which consequences. Distinguish reinforcement, defined by its effect on responding, from an unsupported claim about subjective pleasure. Also consider whether a drug changes the ability to perform the response rather than only the value of its consequence.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Immunohistochemistry (immunocytochemistry) Hypocretin (orexin)
l04-sa03.markdown:
Immunohistochemistry uses recognition of a protein to reveal its distribution in prepared tissue. The orexin example therefore concerns a protein-related signal. In situ hybridization instead detects a complementary RNA sequence, with the enkephalin example illustrating the location of a particular transcript.

The connection is that both provide spatial information about a biological target, but at different stages of expression. RNA must be translated and the resulting protein may be processed, transported, or degraded, so the signals need not match exactly. A high transcript signal does not automatically prove a high concentration of functional protein at the same location. A strong answer identifies the target measured by each technique, explains the gene-expression relationship between them, and states what cannot be concluded from either assay alone. Neither tissue-localization method directly records moment-to-moment firing or behavioral reinforcement.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l04-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Integration: Behavioral Pharmacology and Animals are necessary for behavioural pharmacology
l04-sa04.markdown:
Behavioral pharmacology defines the research aim: understanding drug-induced changes in behavior and their mechanisms. Animal studies provide particular ways to pursue that aim, including control of environment and prior experience, defined manipulations, and access to measurements not appropriate in humans. These advantages can help test causal explanations rather than relying only on correlations.

The connection is methodological, not an identity between the field and one species or assay. The value of a model depends on how the measured behavior and underlying mechanism relate to the human question. Shared mammalian organization can support comparison, while species differences and the limits of the assay constrain generalization. The lecture also emphasizes animal-care standards and the three Rs. A complete response should therefore explain a controlled drug–behavior comparison, describe what animal work makes possible, and acknowledge why a successful animal result is not automatically a successful clinical treatment.

**Source:** Lecture 4 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 4.

**Review:** [Lecture 4 study guide](../study-guides/lecture04.qmd).

l05-mc01.title: Question 1 — What is a catecholamine?
l05-mc01.markdown:
Catecholamines share a chemical structural feature: a catechol group together with an amine-containing component. The lecture includes dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine in this group. Their related structures are reflected in a linked biosynthetic pathway, but the three are not interchangeable in their distribution or functions.

The keyed option identifies chemical classification rather than a receptor type or an effect such as arousal. “Dopaminergic” describes a dopamine-related cell, pathway, or process; “noradrenergic” refers to norepinephrine. Distinguish these adjectives from the receptor families and transporters introduced later. A molecule's chemical family helps organize its metabolism and synthesis, while its functional effects require information about its targets and circuitry.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc02.title: Question 2 — The biosynthetic pathway for catecholamines
l05-mc02.markdown:
The catecholamine pathway begins with tyrosine. Tyrosine hydroxylase converts it to L-DOPA and is emphasized as the rate-limiting enzyme; subsequent enzymatic steps produce dopamine and, in appropriate cells, norepinephrine and epinephrine. The enzymes expressed by a cell therefore help determine which final transmitter it can synthesize.

This explains why blocking tyrosine hydroxylase reduces synthesis and why supplying L-DOPA can bypass that particular step. Feedback from catecholamine availability and changes associated with cell firing regulate pathway activity. The key concerns synthesis, not vesicular packaging or reuptake. A transporter inhibitor can change extracellular dopamine without being an inhibitor of the enzyme that initially produces it.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc03.title: Question 3 — Vesicular packaging of dopamine in the axon terminal
l05-mc03.markdown:
Synthesis in the terminal cytoplasm is not sufficient for normal vesicular release. VMAT transports monoamines into synaptic vesicles, where they are available for later exocytosis and are protected from some cytoplasmic metabolic processes. Blocking this packaging step can progressively reduce the vesicular supply.

Reserpine is the lecture's example of a VMAT inhibitor. Its effect should not be confused with blocking DAT at the cell surface: DAT clears extracellular dopamine into the cell, whereas VMAT loads intracellular vesicles. Blocking these two transporters can therefore have very different consequences. The key correctly identifies the packaging mechanism; the behavioral effects follow from changing transmitter availability rather than directly antagonizing every dopamine receptor.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc04.title: Question 4 — Psychostimulants increase dopamine release
l05-mc04.markdown:
Amphetamine-type stimulants can increase extracellular catecholamine availability through mechanisms that differ from ordinary action-potential-triggered vesicular release. The lecture emphasizes that release can occur without the usual firing-dependent sequence. The textbook relates this to transmitter redistribution and transporter-mediated outward movement.

The key then links increased catecholamine signaling to changes in activity. At higher exposure, repetitive stereotyped actions can replace more general locomotion, so greater stimulation does not always appear as more distance traveled. This also distinguishes a drug's immediate molecular action from its behavioral endpoint. Increased release is not the same mechanism as directly stimulating a dopamine receptor, even though both can enhance some dopamine-related effects.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc05.title: Question 5 — Catecholamine synapses are not “normal”
l05-mc05.markdown:
Catecholamine axons can have repeated swellings, or varicosities, along their length rather than only one terminal at an endpoint. These en passant arrangements support a broader distribution of potential signaling sites and fit the lecture's discussion of modulatory transmission.

However, the source explicitly cautions that not every dopamine varicosity is a demonstrated release site. A visible swelling containing relevant material is therefore not sufficient evidence for identical functional release at every location. The key identifies the anatomical arrangement, not a proof that all catecholamine communication is diffuse or nonsynaptic. Connect structure to possible signaling opportunities while retaining the lecture's uncertainty about the function of every varicosity.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc06.title: Question 6 — Reuptake of catecholamines
l05-mc06.markdown:
After release, dopamine and norepinephrine can be removed from the extracellular space by membrane transporters. Reuptake returns transmitter to a releasing cell, where it can be metabolized or repackaged. Uptake by other cells supplies additional clearance routes.

Blocking a transporter can increase the amount of transmitter remaining available outside the cell and prolong receptor exposure. This is an indirect enhancement of signaling, not necessarily direct receptor agonism or increased synthesis. Keep DAT and NET at the plasma membrane distinct from VMAT on vesicles. The sequence is **release → extracellular action → clearance → reuse or metabolism**, and the transporter acts at the clearance step.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc07.title: Question 7 — Enzymatic degradation of catecholamines
l05-mc07.markdown:
MAO and COMT chemically transform catecholamines. Their actions differ from reuptake, which moves transmitter without necessarily destroying it. Inhibiting a metabolic enzyme can increase the availability or persistence of its substrates, but the consequences depend on which enzyme form and tissues are affected.

The lecture contrasts nonselective and selective MAO inhibitors and gives therapeutic examples. The main reasoning point is selectivity: the same enzyme family participates in more than one physiological setting, so changing metabolism can create effects beyond the intended neural target. Do not interpret “breakdown enzyme” as implying that inhibition automatically improves every function. Identify the affected substrate, location, and pathway before predicting the outcome.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc08.title: Question 8 — Byproducts of catecholamine metabolism
l05-mc08.markdown:
Metabolism produces identifiable breakdown products. The lecture associates dopamine with homovanillic acid, while norepinephrine metabolism is discussed through MHPG and VMA in different settings. These compounds can provide indirect information about catecholamine handling.

A metabolite measurement is not the same as a direct measurement of moment-to-moment receptor activation. Its concentration reflects production, metabolism, transport, and elimination over the sampled setting and interval. The key's reference to COMT identifies one contributing enzyme, but the fuller answer must name the relevant metabolite and explain what the measurement can and cannot indicate. Avoid substituting a dopamine metabolite for a norepinephrine metabolite simply because both parent substances are catecholamines.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc09.title: Question 9 — How to kill a dopamine neuron
l05-mc09.markdown:
The lecture uses loss of nigrostriatal dopamine function to investigate the contribution of that pathway to movement. Dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra project to the dorsal striatum; their degeneration in Parkinson's disease and experimental disruption in animal models support a role in motor function.

The key concerns the relationship between pathway integrity and behavior, not a practical method for producing neuronal injury. A lesion experiment asks how behavior changes when a defined system is disrupted, but interpretation must consider the location and specificity of the manipulation. Distinguish loss of dopamine synthesis or signaling from physical loss of the neuron itself; those interventions can produce related deficits without being biologically identical.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc10.title: Question 10 — Cool little spinning trick
l05-mc10.markdown:
A unilateral dopamine-system lesion creates an imbalance between the two sides. Amphetamine depends on available presynaptic dopamine mechanisms, so its effect is greater on the relatively intact side. Apomorphine acts directly at dopamine receptors and can reveal altered postsynaptic sensitivity on the denervated side.

The resulting rotation is therefore a behavioral readout of asymmetry, not proof that all dopamine-enhancing drugs act identically. The relevant contrast is **enhancing transmitter output** versus **direct receptor stimulation**. To interpret the experiment, identify which side retains functioning terminals and which receptors may have adapted after loss of input. The abbreviated key names the drugs, but the mechanistic explanation is what accounts for their differing effects.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc11.title: Question 11 — Ascending dopamine pathways have been implicated in several important behavioral functions
l05-mc11.markdown:
The dopamine-deficient mouse separates a transmitter's function from destruction of the whole neuron. The animals show severe reductions in feeding, drinking, and activity, and L-DOPA restores these behaviors by bypassing the missing synthesis step. This supports a role for dopamine in activating and organizing behavior, not simply in the physical ability to swallow or grasp food.

The existing key oversimplifies the genetic design. **Chapter 5 specifies that tyrosine hydroxylase is knocked out and then restored in DBH-expressing noradrenergic cells**, preserving norepinephrine synthesis. Merely leaving the DBH gene intact would not explain preserved synthesis upstream of its substrate. This source clarification is essential to understanding what the model selectively tests.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc12.title: Question 12 — Heterogenous behavioural functionality of dopamine neurons
l05-mc12.markdown:
Dopamine's effects depend on the neurons and targets involved. The lecture links mesolimbic projections with arousal, locomotion, and responses to rewarding or aversive events, while mesocortical projections support prefrontal functions such as attention and working memory. This is why dopamine should not be reduced to a single “pleasure chemical.”

The key identifies functional diversity across pathways. The COMT example further shows that transmitter handling in a particular region can influence cognition. A change in dopamine is therefore incomplete information unless its location, timing, and target receptors are specified. The same transmitter can participate in different computations because it acts within differently organized circuits.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc13.title: Question 13 — The fascinating pharmacodynamics of dopamine
l05-mc13.markdown:
The lecture presents an affinity-based hypothesis linking firing pattern to receptor recruitment. Relatively low tonic dopamine can engage higher-affinity D2 receptors, while larger phasic increases can additionally recruit lower-affinity D1 receptors. The proposed consequence depends on both concentration and receptor properties.

This is explicitly a model in the source, not a rule that every tonic event affects only D2 receptors and every burst only D1 receptors. D2 receptors also provide inhibitory autoreceptor feedback at terminals and somatodendritic sites. Distinguish affinity from efficacy, and distinguish a receptor's location from its molecular family. These distinctions explain how the same dopamine increase can have different effects across cells and stages of signaling.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc14.title: Question 14 — Behavioural outcome of DAT knockout
l05-mc14.markdown:
DAT normally contributes to clearing extracellular dopamine. Removing DAT disrupts that clearance, allowing altered and prolonged dopamine exposure. The lecture connects this manipulation with hyperactivity, impulsivity, and cognitive changes in the animal model.

The reasoning runs from transporter function to extracellular signaling and then to behavior.
