It does not follow that the mouse is a complete model of every aspect of ADHD, or that matching one behavioral feature proves an identical human cause. Genetic deletion can also produce adaptations over development. The key therefore supports a role for dopamine clearance in behavioral regulation, while the clinical comparison remains a comparison of selected features rather than a diagnosis.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc15.title: Question 15 — Behavioural outcome of D1 knockout
l05-mc15.markdown:
A drug can elevate extracellular dopamine without producing its usual behavioral effect if a necessary receptor-mediated step is missing. The receptor-knockout examples therefore help test the contribution of D1- and D2-related signaling to stimulant-induced locomotion.

The lecture also contrasts transporter overexpression and amphetamine responsiveness, reinforcing that both the presynaptic transporter and postsynaptic receptor machinery matter. These are different experimental manipulations, not interchangeable ways of “removing dopamine.” The key's generalization should be read in the context of the reported locomotor endpoint. Failure of that response does not establish that every effect of the drug, every dopamine function, or every compensatory mechanism has disappeared.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc16.title: Question 16 — Intrastriatal shifts arising from protracted drug seeking (Porrino et al, 2007)
l05-mc16.markdown:
The lecture describes progressive recruitment of dorsolateral striatal circuitry during extended drug seeking. Its diagram links ventral and dorsal striatal systems through interacting dopamine-related loops. This provides a circuit-level account of a shift in the control of behavior over time.

The source then proposes altered DAT as a possible molecular contributor, while explicitly stating that the precise mechanism is unresolved. Do not turn that proposal into an established explanation. A change in regional activity, a change in transporter expression, and a causal role for a particular cell type are separate claims requiring different evidence. The later experiments are introduced to investigate this gap, not to show that the question was already settled.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc17.title: Question 17 — DAT protein DAT mRNA Effectof heroin exposureon striatalDATproteinandmRNA
l05-mc17.markdown:
The reported result is a mismatch between two measurements: striatal DAT protein changes little, whereas measured DAT mRNA is markedly reduced after heroin self-administration. Protein abundance and transcript abundance are not interchangeable, so this is not automatically a contradiction.

The lecture uses the mismatch to motivate questions about cellular origin and anatomical location. Protein in an axon terminal can originate from synthesis in a cell body elsewhere, while locally measured RNA may belong to another cell population. The key should therefore be interpreted as the specific result presented in the lecture, not a universal finding for every heroin exposure. The next step is to identify which cells contribute to each measurement.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc18.title: Question 18 — Why thelargediscordancebetweenDATRNA and protein? Ventral Midbrain
l05-mc18.markdown:
The lecture's proposed explanation depends on anatomy. Dopamine-neuron cell bodies lie in the ventral midbrain, while their axons carry DAT protein into striatal tissue. A striatal protein measurement can therefore include material from neurons whose cell bodies and principal RNA-synthesis machinery are elsewhere.

The source asks which locally situated cells account for the striatal DAT transcript signal and proposes astrocytes as a candidate. “We bet on astrocytes” is a hypothesis leading to a cell-localization test, not evidence by itself. Distinguish the location of a protein, the origin of its cell, and the identity of a locally detected transcript. The explanation should preserve the hypothesis-to-test sequence rather than assuming the answer from the initial bulk assay.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc19.title: Question 19 — Effectof heroin exposureon astrocyticDATinsitu RNAScope insituhybridizationrevealedthatheroin
l05-mc19.markdown:
The lecture reports that RNAscope in situ hybridization localized a reduction in DAT mRNA to striatal astrocytes after heroin self-administration. This adds cell-related spatial information that a bulk protein or transcript assay alone cannot provide.

The result concerns **RNA expression in the reported cells and condition**. It does not by itself demonstrate the amount of functional DAT protein at the membrane or quantify how much dopamine clearance those cells perform. Those are later functional questions. The key should therefore be connected to the previous hypothesis: localization supplies evidence about the source of the transcript change, while selective manipulation is needed to investigate its physiological contribution.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc20.title: Question 20 — FiberPhotometry &Optogenetics
l05-mc20.markdown:
Fiber photometry records fluorescence from a population expressing a sensor such as GCaMP. The signal provides an indirect indicator related to cellular activity while behavior is occurring. It does not ordinarily resolve the independent spike train of every neuron contributing to the collected light.

Optogenetics, shown alongside it in the lecture, serves a different purpose: light-sensitive proteins allow activity to be manipulated. The distinction is **recording a signal** versus **causally perturbing a system**. The key describes photometry, not the entire combined slide. A complete interpretation identifies what the sensor reports, which population expresses it, and how a recorded association differs from a manipulation that tests contribution to behavior.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 25. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc21.title: Question 21 — CONTROL DAT KO CONTROL DAT KO
l05-mc21.markdown:
The proof-of-principle slide compares control and DAT-knockout conditions in targeted cell populations. Its purpose is to establish that the intended manipulation can be achieved in the relevant neuronal or astrocytic preparation before interpreting downstream effects on dopamine handling.

Demonstrating a change in a molecular marker is an important validation step, but it is not yet the same as demonstrating a change in clearance or behavior. The key names the manipulation and cell groups rather than stating the full result. Follow the evidential order: **targeted intervention → confirmation of the intended cellular change → functional measurement → behavioral interpretation**. Skipping the validation step makes a negative or positive functional outcome difficult to explain.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 27. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc22.title: Question 22 — Control DAT KO Effectof CRISPR/Cas9 neuronalDATdeletiononDA reuptake
l05-mc22.markdown:
The source reports that DAT deletion in VTA neurons only partially reproduces the effect of an organism-wide DAT knockout on dopamine reuptake. This comparison motivates a question about the remaining clearance capacity and whether astrocytic DAT contributes to it.

It does not prove that all residual uptake is astrocytic. Incomplete deletion, other cell populations, or other clearance processes would also require consideration. The lecture itself ends with a question rather than a definitive causal attribution. A careful explanation separates the observed partial effect from the proposed source of the remainder. The next informative experiment would selectively test the candidate contribution while verifying the specificity and effectiveness of the manipulation.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 28. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc23.title: Question 23 — Integration: What is a catecholamine?
l05-mc23.markdown:
Chemical classification identifies dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine as catecholamines because of their shared structural features. The biosynthetic pathway explains how cells make these related chemicals from tyrosine through successive enzymatic steps. The first statement is about **what belongs to the family**; the second is about **how family members are produced**.

The keyed option gives the classification. It should not be replaced by a statement about TH, VMAT, or DAT, because those identify an enzyme or a transporter rather than the chemical group itself. Connecting classification to synthesis is useful, but the two are not identical definitions. A catecholamine can share a precursor pathway with another while acting in different neural systems.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-mc24.title: Question 24 — Integration: The biosynthetic pathway for catecholamines
l05-mc24.markdown:
The pathway question asks about conversion of a precursor into transmitter. Tyrosine hydroxylase acts at the rate-limiting step from tyrosine toward L-DOPA, after which additional enzymes produce dopamine and, in appropriate cells, further catecholamines. This is why enzyme expression constrains the products a cell can make.

Chemical classification instead identifies the shared structure of catecholamines. Vesicular transport and plasma-membrane reuptake occur after transmitter has been synthesized and should not be substituted for its biosynthesis. The key correctly emphasizes precursor and enzyme. A useful check is to ask whether the proposed mechanism changes the molecule chemically, packages it inside a vesicle, or moves it back across the cell surface.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Dopamine neuron membrane dynamics influence dopamine release
l05-sa01.markdown:
Dopamine output depends on both firing and feedback. Tonic single-spike activity produces a different pattern of release from a burst of closely spaced spikes. During a burst, release can temporarily exceed clearance and produce a larger extracellular change. Terminal autoreceptors reduce release, while somatodendritic autoreceptors can reduce firing; the lecture connects these effects to calcium- and potassium-channel regulation.

Relate this to catecholamine axonal anatomy. Varicosities distribute possible release sites along a fiber, and released dopamine can influence targets beyond a simple one-terminal/one-receptor picture. However, the lecture cautions that not every varicosity has demonstrated dopamine release machinery. Thus, the amount and distribution of signaling depend on **where release can occur, the firing pattern, autoreceptor feedback, and the rate of removal**. The response should explain these interacting controls rather than assuming that every action potential produces a fixed, identical dopamine concentration at every nearby receptor.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Anatomical heterogeneity of dopaminergic projections The nigrostriatal pathway originates in the substantia
l05-sa02.markdown:
Identify the origin and target of each major pathway. The nigrostriatal projection runs from substantia nigra to dorsal striatum and is emphasized for movement. The mesolimbic projection originates in the VTA and reaches limbic-related targets, including nucleus accumbens. Mesocortical projections also originate in the VTA but reach cortex, including prefrontal regions involved in cognition.

The lesion example connects this anatomical map to function. Disrupting the nigrostriatal system can produce motor deficits, while changing another projection may affect a different combination of motivational or cognitive processes. This is why “dopamine loss” is an incomplete explanation without a location. Also distinguish a neuron that cannot synthesize dopamine from a neuron that has been physically destroyed. Both alter signaling, but they leave different cellular structures and possible compensations. The intended lesson is selective pathway analysis, not a practical procedure for damaging neurons.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — There are five main subtypes of dopamine receptors organized into
l05-sa03.markdown:
All five dopamine receptor subtypes discussed in the textbook are metabotropic, grouped into D1-like and D2-like families. In the lecture's central contrast, D1 activation promotes adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP production, while D2 activation reduces that pathway and can regulate potassium conductance. Receptor family therefore predicts a signaling tendency, not a single behavior.

Connect this to the affinity hypothesis: tonic and phasic dopamine concentrations may recruit receptor populations differently because D2 receptors have higher affinity in the course's account. Then add location. D2 receptors on dopamine neurons can function as autoreceptors and reduce further output, while receptors on target cells participate in postsynaptic responses. A complete explanation therefore combines **family, affinity, signaling mechanism, and cellular location**. Avoid assuming that all D2 activation means less movement or that all D1 activation has the same effect regardless of the circuit.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — WesternBlot&qPCR
l05-sa04.markdown:
Western blotting measures a protein-related signal after separation and antibody detection, while quantitative PCR measures amplification of a selected nucleic-acid sequence. When studying mRNA expression, the RNA is first represented through a complementary-DNA preparation; the amplification signal is then used to compare abundance. This additional step clarifies the lecture's compressed description of qPCR and gene expression.

The heroin example illustrates why the two readouts need not agree: striatal DAT protein changes little while DAT mRNA decreases. Protein stability, translation, cellular composition, and the origin of axons can separate a tissue's transcript and protein signals. The lecture particularly pursues the anatomical possibility that transported neuronal DAT protein and locally expressed transcripts come from different cellular sources. A strong answer identifies the target measured by each assay and explains the mismatch as a research question requiring localization and functional tests, not as proof that either assay must be wrong.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — Moving forward:manipulations ofastrocyticorneuronalDAT Question: Can we utilize a CRISPR/Cas9
l05-sa05.markdown:
The proposed experiment asks whether DAT in different cell populations contributes differently to dopamine handling. Selective CRISPR/Cas9-based deletion is intended to distinguish neuronal from astrocytic contributions rather than eliminating the transporter throughout the whole organism. The targeting strategy is therefore part of the causal question.

The proof-of-principle images address whether the desired manipulation was achieved. A subsequent reuptake measurement asks whether that manipulation changes function. These stages must remain separate: successful targeting does not automatically establish a large physiological role, and a functional result is hard to interpret without confirming targeting. The source then compares neuronal deletion with the more extensive effect of organism-wide deletion and raises, but does not settle, the possibility of an astrocytic contribution. A strong response follows the experimental sequence and identifies the need for matched controls, evidence of cell specificity, and an appropriate functional outcome without presenting the proposed mechanism as an established conclusion.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 26. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l05-sa06.title: Short Essay 6 — Integration: What is a catecholamine? and The biosynthetic pathway for catecholamines
l05-sa06.markdown:
A catecholamine is identified by its chemical structure, while its biosynthetic pathway explains how that structure is produced and modified in a cell. The lecture includes dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine and traces their common origin to tyrosine. Tyrosine hydroxylase controls the rate-limiting step toward L-DOPA, and additional enzymes determine the later products.

The connection is that a shared pathway creates a family of related transmitters, but not every cell expresses every enzyme needed for every family member. This helps explain why dopamine and norepinephrine neurons can share packaging and metabolic features while remaining distinct signaling systems. Include one pharmacological implication: inhibiting a synthesis enzyme changes transmitter production, whereas blocking reuptake changes the persistence of transmitter already released. A complete comparison therefore links chemical identity, enzyme availability, and possible intervention points rather than treating “catecholamine” as another name for dopamine alone.

**Source:** Lecture 5 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 5 study guide](../study-guides/lecture05.qmd).

l06-mc01.title: Question 1 — Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system
l06-mc01.markdown:
Noradrenergic cell bodies are concentrated in brainstem groups, especially the locus coeruleus, but their projections reach many distant regions. The enzyme dopamine beta-hydroxylase is important because it converts dopamine toward norepinephrine synthesis and helps identify the noradrenergic phenotype.

The key concerns anatomical origin and transmitter identity. It does not imply that norepinephrine acts only in the locus coeruleus. Extensive projections allow this relatively localized system to influence arousal, sensory processing, and cognition across the forebrain and other targets. The lecture also connects it to familiar catecholamine mechanisms—vesicular storage, reuptake, metabolism, and tonic or phasic activity—so anatomy and transmitter handling should be understood together.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc02.title: Question 2 — Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR
l06-mc02.markdown:
Adrenergic receptors include several subtypes with different signaling functions. The lecture highlights the inhibitory autoreceptor role of alpha-2 receptors: when activated on a norepinephrine neuron, they can reduce further transmitter output through effects on firing or release.

This is negative feedback, not a statement that every adrenergic receptor suppresses activity. Alpha-2 receptors can also occur at other locations, where their functional consequences depend on the receiving cell. The existing key names “the autoreceptor” but does not identify the mechanism. The useful distinction is between a receptor detecting the neuron's own transmitter to regulate output and a receptor on a different target cell mediating that cell's response.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc03.title: Question 3 — What is impulsivity
l06-mc03.markdown:
The lecture separates **impulsive action** from **impulsive choice**. Motor impulsivity concerns difficulty withholding or stopping a response, such as acting before the appropriate cue. Cognitive impulsivity concerns choices favoring an immediate outcome over a delayed one, with insufficient forethought about later consequences.

The keyed option defines the motor component. It should not be taken as a complete definition of every form of impulsivity. The source also distinguishes impulsivity from broader problems learning rules, evaluating risk, or using probabilities. Someone can perform poorly on one kind of task without necessarily failing on another. The measurement must match the specific component being discussed.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc04.title: Question 4 — Measuringimpulsivityinthelab-humans
l06-mc04.markdown:
Questionnaires and performance tasks measure different aspects of impulsivity. The Barratt scale collects reports across attentional, motor, and nonplanning dimensions. Stop-signal and go/no-go tasks examine response inhibition, whereas delay-discounting tasks examine how delay changes the value assigned to an outcome.

The key names the questionnaire approach, but a full explanation should connect each measure to the intended construct. A questionnaire score is not identical to the latency of stopping a response, and neither directly measures every aspect of everyday decision-making. The lecture's range of methods reinforces that impulsivity is multidimensional. Choosing an assay requires first specifying whether the concern is action, choice, attention, or planning.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc05.title: Question 5 — Prefrontal brain regions involved in impulse control Prefrontalbrainregionsinvolvedin impulsecontrol
l06-mc05.markdown:
The lecture associates medial and dorsolateral/dorsomedial prefrontal systems with attention, planning, executive control, and the inhibition of actions. Orbitofrontal systems are emphasized for action–outcome relationships, reward value, and updating choices when circumstances change.

The keyed option identifies the first grouping. The distinction helps explain why response inhibition and delay-related choice are not necessarily the same deficit. These functions still depend on interactions with striatum and other regions; the slide is not a claim that one prefrontal area works alone. Interpret the anatomical labels as components of control networks, and match the behavioral task to the particular operation being tested.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc06.title: Question 6 — Subcortical brain regions involved in impulse control Subcorticalbrainregionsinvolvedinimpulsecontrol
l06-mc06.markdown:
Subcortical systems contribute to selecting, initiating, inhibiting, and valuing actions. The lecture connects dorsal striatum with action control, nucleus accumbens with motivational influences, and amygdala with learned value and the significance of cues. Brainstem and midbrain catecholamine systems modulate these interactions.

The key therefore identifies striatum as relevant to both choice and motor impulsivity. It does not support a simple contrast in which cortex supplies control and all subcortical activity supplies impulsivity. Organized behavior depends on communication among these systems. The source's emphasis on interactions is essential: a change in one node can alter the function of the network without that node containing the entire psychological process.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc07.title: Question 7 — Circuits involved in impulse control Circuitsinvolvedin
l06-mc07.markdown:
The circuit diagram integrates the preceding lists of brain regions. Impulse control requires information about goals, current stimuli, expected outcomes, motivational state, and whether an action should be performed or stopped. These functions are distributed across interacting prefrontal and subcortical systems.

The key's phrase “interactions between many regions” is correct but needs this functional interpretation. A connection diagram does not by itself prove that every link is equally important for every task. Impulsive action and impulsive choice can place different demands on the network. Use the diagram to explain how information is coordinated, rather than treating it as a list of independent locations with one-to-one labels for behavior.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc08.title: Question 8 — Neurochemicalregulationof impulsivity
l06-mc08.markdown:
An inverted-U relationship means that increasing catecholamine signaling is helpful only within part of the range. At a low level, prefrontal functioning may be under-supported; at an intermediate level, performance is better; at an excessive level, such as under stress, performance can deteriorate again.

The key names the shape, but the mechanism-relevant point is **dependence on the starting state**. The same direction of drug-induced change can move one system toward the optimum and another beyond it. This explains why “more dopamine” or “more norepinephrine” is not a universal prescription for improved cognition. The source uses the model to frame prefrontal control and stimulant effects, not to provide an individual dosing rule.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc09.title: Question 9 — Attention-deficit hyperactive disorder (ADHD) Attention-deficit hyperactivedisorder (ADHD)
l06-mc09.markdown:
The lecture presents ADHD as a neurodevelopmental disorder involving patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity–impulsivity. It distinguishes inattentive, hyperactive, and combined presentations. These categories emphasize that the disorder is not equivalent to a single episode of distractibility or one impulsive choice.

The numerical diagnostic and prevalence statements in the key are part of the supplied lecture and should not be treated as a current clinical assessment guide. The conceptual point is the organization of persistent behavioral difficulties and their developmental context. Later slides explore possible neural mechanisms, but a group-level imaging finding is not interchangeable with a diagnosis. This question is for understanding course framing, not diagnosing oneself or another person.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc10.title: Question 10 — Neurobiology of ADHD – seminal PET studies Neurobiologyof ADHD–seminalPETstudies
l06-mc10.markdown:
The early PET examples use a dopamine precursor tracer to investigate aspects of dopamine synthesis or handling in specified regions. The lecture relates these findings to a hypothesis of reduced prefrontal dopaminergic functioning in ADHD. The interpretation depends on what the tracer signal represents and which comparison region is used.

This is different from directly counting receptors or measuring all dopamine activity with one universal scan. The lecture later introduces findings that complicate a single-deficit account, including receptor-availability comparisons and performance-related variation. The key should therefore be read as the reported interpretation of particular studies, not proof that every person with ADHD has the same measurable prefrontal dopamine abnormality.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc11.title: Question 11 — Neurobiologyof ADHD–animalstudies
l06-mc11.markdown:
The animal-study comparison emphasizes regional selectivity. In the presented results, methylphenidate increases catecholamine measures in prefrontal and striatal regions, whereas atomoxetine's reported dopamine and norepinephrine increases are concentrated in prefrontal cortex. Their transporter actions therefore do not translate into an identical regional pattern.

A NET inhibitor can affect dopamine in prefrontal cortex because local clearance mechanisms differ from those in dopamine-rich striatal systems. The key concerns the specific study comparison, not an absolute statement about every dose, species, or brain region. Connect transporter target, regional anatomy, and measured extracellular transmitter before predicting behavior. Similar clinical aims do not mean that two drugs have the same pharmacological mechanism.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc12.title: Question 12 — Neurobiologyof ADHD–PETstudies
l06-mc12.markdown:
The lecture combines structural and molecular imaging findings, which must be kept separate. Reduced gray-matter volume is a structural MRI result, whereas a PET radioligand can provide information about receptor availability. Equivalent receptor availability does not imply identical structure, transmitter release, or task performance.

The presented studies also relate striatal dopamine measures to attentional performance across diagnostic groups. This complicates the idea that every observed difference is unique to ADHD. The key identifies only part of the evidence. A careful interpretation specifies the modality and measured quantity for each result, then distinguishes a group comparison from a performance association and from the effect of methylphenidate.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc13.title: Question 13 — Methylphenidate (Ritalin)
l06-mc13.markdown:
Methylphenidate is presented as blocking dopamine and norepinephrine transporters, reducing reuptake and prolonging extracellular transmitter availability. Amphetamine has a different mechanism that includes transporter-mediated outward movement and increased catecholamine release. Both can enhance signaling, but they act differently on transmitter handling.

The slide uses the phrase “inverse DAT/NET agonist” for amphetamine. Its intended point here is **reverse transport**, not the receptor-pharmacology definition of inverse agonism involving constitutive receptor activity. DAT and NET are transporters, not dopamine or adrenergic receptors. Keeping these categories separate prevents a common error: interpreting a transporter blocker as necessarily blocking the postsynaptic effects of the transmitter.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc14.title: Question 14 — Sideeffectsof stimulant medications
l06-mc14.markdown:
Stimulant effects are not confined to the cognitive process being targeted. The lecture includes insomnia, appetite reduction, anxiety, nausea, and cardiovascular effects among possible unwanted outcomes. These illustrate the broader distribution and functions of catecholamine systems.

The source also links ventral striatal dopamine effects to concerns about reinforcement and misuse. That is a mechanism-based reason for distinguishing compounds and delivery patterns, not a conclusion that every prescribed exposure inevitably produces addiction. The keyed list should be understood as possible effects rather than a prediction for every person. This is course-level pharmacology, not advice to start, stop, or alter medication.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc15.title: Question 15 — ADHDpharmacology–noradrenaline Guanfacine (Intuniv)
l06-mc15.markdown:
Guanfacine acts at alpha-2A adrenergic receptors, while atomoxetine acts primarily by blocking NET. One therefore changes receptor signaling and the other changes transmitter clearance. The lecture connects guanfacine with prefrontal functioning and signal-to-noise regulation.

The key labels alpha-2A as an autoreceptor, but receptor location matters. **Chapter 5 discusses alpha-2-mediated facilitation of prefrontal cognition as well as inhibitory autoreceptor effects elsewhere.** It would be misleading to explain every cognitive benefit solely as suppressing norepinephrine release. Identify the receptor subtype and relevant circuit before interpreting the outcome. This distinction is the reason a receptor agonist and a reuptake inhibitor need separate mechanistic explanations.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-mc16.title: Question 16 — Integration: Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system
l06-mc16.markdown:
The central noradrenergic system is an anatomical projection system, whereas an adrenergic autoreceptor is one molecular feedback mechanism within it. The locus coeruleus and related brainstem groups provide norepinephrine-containing projections to many targets. DBH expression supports the transmitter identity of those neurons.

An autoreceptor detects the neuron's own released transmitter and can regulate further firing or release. The keyed option describes the origin and chemical identity of the system, not the complete receptor mechanism. The connection is that broad projection systems still require local regulation. A change in autoreceptor signaling can alter output from a neuron whose axons influence many distant regions.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Measuring impulsivity in the lab - rodents Measuringimpulsivityinthelab-rodents
l06-sa01.markdown:
Match each rodent task to the component it measures. Delay discounting examines choices between outcomes differing in timing and value, making it relevant to cognitive impulsivity. Stop-signal procedures examine stopping an initiated action. In the five-choice serial reaction-time task, premature responding before the appropriate cue provides a measure relevant to motor impulsivity, while other performance measures concern attention.

Connect these tasks to the lecture's prefrontal distinctions. Medial and related prefrontal systems contribute to top-down control and response inhibition, while orbitofrontal functions include updating values and action–outcome relationships. These are network contributions, not exclusive locations for entire behaviors. A strong answer also notes that a drug can change sensory detection, movement, motivation, or learning and thereby affect task performance. Explain what the animal does, which response is scored, and why that score supports a particular interpretation rather than simply naming a task and a brain region.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Impulsivityandpsychiatricdisorders
l06-sa02.markdown:
The lecture places several disorders within a discussion of impaired control, including substance-use, gambling, binge-eating, obsessive-compulsive, and attention-related disorders. This grouping highlights overlapping behavioral dimensions; it does not mean the conditions are identical or arise from one uniform mechanism.

ADHD is introduced as neurodevelopmental and can involve inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity in different combinations. Relate it to the broader discussion by distinguishing failure to inhibit an action from preference for an immediate outcome and from persistent repetitive behavior. A person can show different profiles across these dimensions. Neural explanations therefore need to connect a specified task or symptom to a relevant circuit and transmitter mechanism. A strong answer describes the overlap while preserving diagnostic and mechanistic differences. The course examples are not sufficient for diagnosing an individual or interpreting every impulsive act as evidence of psychiatric disorder.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Attention-deficit hyperactivedisorder (ADHD)
l06-sa03.markdown:
The lecture uses an inverted-U model to explain why increasing catecholamine signaling can sometimes improve control rather than simply produce more overt activity. When prefrontal function is on the low side of the proposed optimum, an appropriate increase in dopamine or norepinephrine signaling may improve attention and executive performance. Excessive signaling can instead impair it.

Methylphenidate changes transmitter handling by blocking DAT and NET. Its mechanism is therefore not a direct instruction to “calm” a neuron; behavioral improvement is an outcome of altered signaling in relevant circuits. The lecture's imaging examples also complicate a universal low-prefrontal-dopamine account, showing the need to distinguish structure, synthesis-related signals, receptor availability, and performance. A complete explanation presents the model as a course framework, links the drug to its immediate target, and avoids concluding that every individual has the same deficit or will respond identically.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l06-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Integration: Organization and function of the central noradrenergic system and Adrenergic receptors THE AUTORECEPTOR
l06-sa04.markdown:
The noradrenergic system describes where norepinephrine neurons originate, where they project, and which functions they influence. The locus coeruleus is a prominent source of extensive projections, allowing a relatively localized cell group to modulate many regions. Adrenergic receptors describe how cells respond to the transmitter.

An autoreceptor is a particular functional placement: the receptor is on a norepinephrine neuron and responds to its own transmitter. In the inhibitory alpha-2 feedback mechanism emphasized here, activation reduces further output by changing firing or release. This connects a local molecular event to a widely distributed projection system. However, the same receptor family can also occur on other cells, so receptor subtype alone does not determine whether it is acting as an autoreceptor. A strong comparison distinguishes anatomy, receptor identity, cellular location, and downstream function before predicting a drug effect.

**Source:** Lecture 6 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 5.

**Review:** [Lecture 6 study guide](../study-guides/lecture06.qmd).

l07-mc01.title: Question 1 — A point of clarity
l07-mc01.markdown:
The important detail is the **selective restoration of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)**, not simply the presence of the dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH) gene. TH performs the first step in the catecholamine synthesis pathway. Removing TH would otherwise prevent the production of dopamine and the norepinephrine made from it. Placing a functional TH sequence under DBH regulatory control restores synthesis in cells that normally make norepinephrine.

Dopaminergic cells do not receive this restoration, so they remain dopamine deficient. The opening slide clarifies the model from the preceding lecture. The key's first sentence is incomplete without its second sentence: an intact DBH gene alone cannot compensate for a missing upstream precursor. This is a genetic manipulation of synthesis, not blockade of a dopamine receptor.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc02.title: Question 2 — Serotonin synthesis is regulated by enzymatic
l07-mc02.markdown:
Serotonin, **5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT**, is an indoleamine rather than a catecholamine. Its precursor is tryptophan. Tryptophan hydroxylase first converts tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP); aromatic amino acid decarboxylase then converts 5-HTP to serotonin. The hydroxylation step is the rate-limiting step emphasized in the lecture.

The keyed option correctly identifies the transmitter and its chemical class, but a fuller understanding also requires this two-step sequence. Enzyme activity and the availability of tryptophan jointly influence how much serotonin can be synthesized. Do not substitute tyrosine hydroxylase merely because its name sounds similar: that enzyme belongs to the catecholamine pathway, whereas tryptophan hydroxylase belongs to the serotonin pathway.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc03.title: Question 3 — Tryptophan hydroxylase
l07-mc03.markdown:
The original keyed option is a **topic placeholder**, not a substantive statement about the enzyme. The figure on this slide distinguishes TPH2, associated with serotonergic neurons, from TPH1 in non-neuronal cells, including cells of the gut and pineal gland. Both concern serotonin synthesis, but their tissue locations matter when interpreting a drug's effects.

The slide's telotristat example illustrates this distinction. It describes inhibition of peripheral serotonin synthesis without entry across the blood–brain barrier, linking drug distribution to the tissues in which enzyme inhibition occurs. Thus, inhibiting a serotonin-synthesis enzyme does not automatically mean lowering brain serotonin. This explanation supplies the missing concept; the existing choices should not be treated as a well-formed, uniquely discriminating MCQ.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc04.title: Question 4 — Uptake of dietary tryptophan
l07-mc04.markdown:
The relevant quantity is not simply how much tryptophan a meal contains, but **tryptophan relative to the other large neutral amino acids competing for transport into the brain**. More circulating tryptophan may not increase brain entry if competing amino acids increase at the same time. Brain entry affects the precursor available to tryptophan hydroxylase and therefore can influence serotonin synthesis.

The lecture uses a low-protein, high-carbohydrate meal to illustrate this ratio. In its account, insulin promotes uptake of competing amino acids into peripheral tissues, increasing tryptophan's relative access to transport. The point is a transport-and-synthesis mechanism, not a guarantee that a particular meal will produce a predictable mood change in every individual.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc05.title: Question 5 — Elevating tryptophan to asses its role in behaviour
l07-mc05.markdown:
Tryptophan loading increases the availability of the **precursor** used to synthesize serotonin. The lecture contrasts direct administration of tryptophan with dietary approaches, including tryptophan-rich proteins and changes in the balance between carbohydrate and protein. These approaches seek to alter precursor availability rather than directly activate a serotonin receptor.

Their interpretation depends on the preceding transport principle: tryptophan competes with other large neutral amino acids for brain entry. An increase in total dietary protein is therefore not equivalent to an increase in the tryptophan-to-competitor ratio. The answer panel's unfinished “Dietary” phrase should be read using the complete slide, not as a complete explanation. These are research examples, not instructions for self-treatment.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc06.title: Question 6 — Serotonin depletion effects psychological processing
l07-mc06.markdown:
Acute tryptophan depletion reduces the precursor available for brain serotonin synthesis. The lecture reports **selective effects**, including poorer consolidation of verbal information, negative cognitive bias, and reduced sleep duration or quality. It also notes relatively little effect on working memory or attention in the studies discussed.

This pattern matters because “serotonin affects cognition” is much broader than the evidence presented. Consolidating information into memory is not identical to briefly holding and manipulating information in working memory. Likewise, a negative processing bias is not itself a diagnosis of depression. A good interpretation names the manipulation, identifies the particular measured outcome, and avoids concluding that lowering serotonin uniformly impairs every cognitive function or necessarily causes a psychiatric disorder.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc07.title: Question 7 — Most dietary tryptophan never becomes serotonin
l07-mc07.markdown:
Tryptophan has metabolic destinations other than serotonin. The lecture emphasizes the **kynurenine pathway**, reporting that most ingested tryptophan is metabolized through that route rather than converted to 5-HT. This explains why dietary tryptophan intake cannot be equated directly with serotonin production.

Stress and inflammation can influence enzymes involved in this alternative pathway. Consequently, changing tryptophan metabolism may affect both the substrate available for serotonin synthesis and the production of kynurenine metabolites. The lecture links these metabolites to several psychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions, but involvement is not the same as a complete causal explanation of those diseases. The percentage in the key is the course's stated estimate, not a fixed conversion rule for every individual and physiological condition.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc08.title: Question 8 — Synaptic pharmacodynamics similar to catecholamines
l07-mc08.markdown:
VMAT2 moves serotonin from the cytoplasm into **synaptic vesicles**, where it is stored for release. This is different from SERT, which returns released serotonin across the neuron's plasma membrane. Blocking VMAT with reserpine interferes with storage, leaving transmitter vulnerable to intracellular metabolism and eventually reducing vesicular serotonin available for release.

The lecture also distinguishes two feedback locations. Terminal autoreceptors inhibit release locally, whereas somatodendritic autoreceptors can reduce release indirectly by slowing neuronal firing. These mechanisms resemble the catecholamine systems because all are monoaminergic systems, but their transmitter-specific plasma-membrane transporters and receptors differ. Identify which step is affected—storage, firing, release, or reuptake—rather than treating all transporter blockers as equivalent.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc09.title: Question 9 — Anatomical organization of serotonin projections
l07-mc09.markdown:
Serotonergic cell bodies are concentrated in brainstem groups associated with the **raphe nuclei**, while their axons reach much more widely. The dorsal and median raphe groups highlighted in the lecture provide most serotonergic fibers to the forebrain. A small set of source regions can therefore influence many anatomically separated target areas.

Distinguish a neuron's cell-body location from the location of its terminals. Finding serotonergic fibers in the hippocampus or cortex does not mean that all of their parent cell bodies are located there. This source-to-target organization helps explain serotonin's involvement in multiple functions, while also warning against treating the entire serotonergic system as one uniform circuit with one behavioral effect.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc10.title: Question 10 — Immunohistochemistry of TPH2 & SERT
l07-mc10.markdown:
The images use **different molecular markers to visualize different parts of the serotonergic system**. TPH2 is an enzyme involved in neuronal serotonin synthesis; its staining in the dorsal raphe helps identify serotonergic cells. SERT is the serotonin transporter, and staining in the hippocampus reveals serotonergic innervation in a target region.

The contrast connects anatomy to molecular function: a transmitter-synthesis marker can identify a source population, while a transporter marker can reveal fibers extending through other tissue. Immunohistochemistry indicates where the recognized protein is detected; it does not by itself measure moment-to-moment serotonin release or neuronal firing. The very short answer label therefore needs this interpretation, rather than just memorization of two region names.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc11.title: Question 11 — Electrophysiological properties of serotonin neurons
l07-mc11.markdown:
The lecture presents observations from different preparations rather than one simple rule that “serotonin causes wakefulness.” Earlier cat recordings associated regular firing with waking, more irregular activity with slow-wave sleep, and cessation during REM sleep. The later mouse work described on the slide distinguishes slow tonic activity from bursts, with different consequences for sleep and waking.

The central lesson is that **firing pattern, cell population, and experimental method matter**. Observing activity during a behavioral state is not the same as manipulating that activity and demonstrating an effect on the state. Preserve those distinctions when comparing the findings; they should not be collapsed into a claim that every increase in serotonergic activity necessarily has the same effect on sleep.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc12.title: Question 12 — There are LOTS of different serotonin receptors
l07-mc12.markdown:
Serotonin's effects depend on which receptor subtype it activates. The lecture's 5-HT1A example links receptor activation to **reduced adenylyl cyclase activity, less cAMP, and increased potassium-channel opening**. These changes can hyperpolarize the membrane and reduce the likelihood of firing.

Location adds another layer. A 5-HT1A receptor on a serotonergic neuron can function as an autoreceptor, reducing that neuron's activity; the same subtype on another neuron acts postsynaptically. Therefore, an inhibitory cellular effect does not translate automatically into one predictable behavioral effect throughout the brain. The listed brain regions help identify possible sites of action, but identifying the region and receptor location requires additional evidence beyond a systemic drug response.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc13.title: Question 13 — Deeper look at the IP3 signaling pathway
l07-mc13.markdown:
The pathway begins with ligand binding to a G-protein-coupled receptor and proceeds to **phospholipase C (PLC)**. PLC cleaves PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ moves through the cytosol to receptors on the endoplasmic reticulum, where it triggers calcium release into the cytosol. DAG and calcium then support activation of protein kinase C.

Follow the sequence rather than memorizing disconnected abbreviations. The receptor detects the extracellular signal; the intracellular messengers distribute it; calcium and kinase activity help generate the cellular response. The calcium increase described here comes from an intracellular store, not necessarily from calcium entering through the receptor itself. That distinction separates this metabotropic pathway from direct opening of an ionotropic receptor channel.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc14.title: Question 14 — 5-HT2A is implicated in hallucinations
l07-mc14.markdown:
The question concerns a **receptor-level link to hallucinogenic effects**, not simply the amount of serotonin present in the brain. The lecture associates DOI and the effects of LSD with stimulation of 5-HT2A receptors, which are abundant in the cortex and signal through intracellular pathways.

This is different from blocking serotonin reuptake or reducing its synthesis. Those manipulations change transmitter availability across multiple receptor populations rather than selectively reproducing one receptor's signaling. The lecture also contrasts stimulation with inverse agonist actions at relevant serotonin receptors in some antipsychotic drugs. Keep its cautious wording: a receptor contribution to hallucinations does not make every serotonergic drug hallucinogenic, nor does it provide a complete explanation of schizophrenia or psychedelic experience.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc15.title: Question 15 — 5-HT3A is ionotropic
l07-mc15.markdown:
The 5-HT3 receptor is the important **ionotropic exception** among the serotonin receptor families discussed. Ligand binding opens a cation channel directly, allowing the ion movements described on the slide and producing rapid excitation. This differs from 5-HT1A or 5-HT2A signaling through G proteins and intracellular pathways.

The lecture places 5-HT3 receptors both in the CNS and on vagal terminals associated with the gut. Its ondansetron example links receptor blockade to suppression of nausea and vomiting signals. The drug is not described as removing all serotonin or blocking every serotonin receptor. The explanatory chain is receptor subtype → channel function → anatomical pathway → physiological effect, rather than “serotonin is always excitatory.”

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc16.title: Question 16 — There are heaps of serotonin receptors
l07-mc16.markdown:
The receptor-family diagram organizes the many serotonin receptors into groups. Its main contrast is **5-HT3 as a ligand-gated ion channel versus the other depicted families as G-protein-coupled receptors**. Subtypes within those families differ in signaling, distribution, and function, so naming the transmitter alone does not specify the response.

The original answer is only a statement that the topic is important; it supplies no receptor distinction and is not an adequate substantive answer. For revision, be able to contrast 5-HT1A inhibition of cAMP signaling, 5-HT2A phosphoinositide signaling, and rapid 5-HT3 channel-mediated excitation. The current MCQ should be improved before formal grading rather than treating its placeholder as proof of mastery.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc17.title: Question 17 — Serotonin in anxiety
l07-mc17.markdown:
The lecture brings together pharmacological and genetic evidence for serotonin's involvement in anxiety. It describes anxiolytic effects of 5-HT1A agonists in experimental animals and increased anxiety-like behavior in 5-HT1A-knockout mice. These observations support a role for the receptor, but do not by themselves identify the responsible brain region or receptor location.

That limitation is central to the answer. A systemically administered agonist can act at both autoreceptors and postsynaptic receptors, and a whole-animal knockout has broad consequences. It would therefore be premature to conclude that one particular serotonergic projection mediates the effect. The following lecture example narrows the question by manipulating nerve terminals and examining behavior in a defined circuit.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc18.title: Question 18 — Identifying the precise anxiety-modulating mechanism
l07-mc18.markdown:
The experiment narrows the anxiety question by manipulating **serotonergic nerve terminals**, rather than simply administering a drug throughout the body. In the lecture's account, terminal excitation increases serotonin release and increases open-arm time in the elevated plus-maze; terminal inhibition produces the opposite, anxiety-like pattern.

The lecture interprets this evidence as supporting a contribution from postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors in the studied circuit. The logic is that increasing transmitter delivery to target cells reduces the measured anxiety-like behavior, rather than reducing transmitter output through autoreceptor inhibition. Keep the scope specific: open-arm time is a behavioral index, not a direct report of subjective anxiety, and the finding does not establish that every serotonergic projection has the same function.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc19.title: Question 19 — Serotonin in hunger and eating
l07-mc19.markdown:
The feeding example distinguishes **appetite-suppressing and appetite-promoting signals** within hypothalamic circuitry. The lecture describes arcuate-nucleus neurons associated with α-MSH and others associated with NPY and AgRP. Their projections reach the paraventricular nucleus, where melanocortin signaling contributes to the regulation of feeding.

α-MSH activates MC3/4 receptors and favors appetite suppression; AgRP antagonizes those receptors and favors feeding. This receptor opposition explains more than saying that serotonin “controls hunger.” Serotonin can influence the balance within the circuit, but the downstream peptides and receptors determine how that influence is expressed. The lorcaserin example belongs to the course's historical pharmacology discussion; it should not be interpreted here as a current prescribing recommendation.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-mc20.title: Question 20 — Integration: A point of clarity
l07-mc20.markdown:
This integration item revisits the dopamine-deficient mouse to reinforce **cell-type-selective synthesis**. TH is needed upstream of both dopamine and norepinephrine. Restoring functional TH under DBH regulatory control enables norepinephrine-producing cells to recover their pathway while dopamine-producing cells remain deficient.

The useful connection to this lecture is that transmitter availability depends on particular enzymes in particular cells. In the serotonergic system, tryptophan hydroxylase and precursor availability supply a different synthesis pathway. Neither case is equivalent to a receptor antagonist: reducing synthesis changes the supply of transmitter, whereas antagonism changes how a target cell responds to transmitter already present. Read the full restoration detail, not the misleading shorthand that an intact DBH gene alone preserves norepinephrine synthesis.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Depleting 5-HT to assess its role in behavior
l07-sa01.markdown:
A developed response should distinguish **enzyme inhibition from precursor depletion**. PCPA inhibits tryptophan hydroxylase, interrupting the rate-limiting synthesis step even when precursor is available. Acute tryptophan depletion instead reduces tryptophan availability relative to the competing amino acids used for brain transport. Both approaches can reduce serotonin synthesis, but they act at different points in the causal chain.

Connect these approaches to tryptophan loading by explaining the opposite manipulation: increasing accessible precursor can increase the opportunity for serotonin synthesis when the relevant enzymes and transport conditions permit it. Then interpret the evidence carefully. A behavioral change after depletion supports a contribution from the manipulated serotonergic processes; it does not demonstrate that serotonin alone controls the behavior or that all brain regions are affected identically. The lecture's memory, cognitive-bias, and sleep findings illustrate distinct outcomes that should be named separately. These are research manipulations, not personal medication or dietary advice.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — The serotonin transporter (SERT)
l07-sa02.markdown:
SERT is the **plasma-membrane transporter that retrieves released serotonin**, helping terminate its extracellular action. It is not VMAT2, which loads transmitter into intracellular vesicles, and it is not MAO-A, which participates in metabolic breakdown. Blocking SERT with an SSRI changes serotonin's availability outside cells rather than directly activating a serotonin receptor.

The anatomical connection is that raphe neurons send projections to widespread forebrain targets, including cortex and hippocampus. SERT at their terminals therefore influences signaling in the regions those projections reach. The effect in a given target depends on its receptor populations, local circuitry, and feedback regulation; a common transporter target does not imply an identical response everywhere. A strong answer traces release → extracellular receptor exposure → reuptake, then connects terminal location to the raphe-to-forebrain organization. The lecture's knockout observations additionally remind us that lifelong removal of a transporter is not necessarily equivalent to acute pharmacological inhibition.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — 5-HT2A
l07-sa03.markdown:
5-HT2A is a **metabotropic serotonin receptor**. In the pathway emphasized by the lecture, receptor activation engages phospholipase C, which splits PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ acts at endoplasmic-reticulum receptors to release stored calcium into the cytosol; calcium together with DAG promotes PKC activation. The kinase then changes the activity of cellular targets.

Explain how each stage passes information onward. Serotonin is the extracellular signal; IP₃ and DAG carry the signal within the cell; calcium and PKC translate it into a cellular response. This is not a channel through which serotonin itself enters the neuron. Contrast it with 5-HT1A signaling, which reduces cAMP and can increase potassium conductance, or with the ionotropic 5-HT3 receptor. The comparison shows why two drugs acting on different serotonin receptor subtypes can have different physiological and behavioral effects despite being described broadly as serotonergic.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Behavioral effects of serotonin
l07-sa04.markdown:
The lecture associates serotonergic manipulations with changes in eating, anxiety, pain sensitivity, learning, memory, and aggression. To explain this rather than merely list functions, connect the widespread projections of raphe neurons to the diversity of receptor subtypes in their target circuits. Changing serotonin availability can therefore affect several processes, with effects that depend on where and how the manipulation is made.

Use the anxiety examples to illustrate the evidence hierarchy. Systemic 5-HT1A agonists and knockout findings implicate the receptor but leave its relevant location unresolved; targeted terminal manipulations provide more circuit-specific evidence. Lesion and neurotoxin studies are another approach, but the slide's grouping of substances should not be interpreted as proving identical toxicity or selective neuronal killing under every exposure condition. Chapter 6 treats MDMA-related findings with greater qualification. A strong response separates the manipulation, measured behavior, and inference, rather than concluding that serotonin is a single-purpose “mood chemical.”

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l07-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — Integration: A point of clarity and Serotonin synthesis is regulated by enzymatic
l07-sa05.markdown:
These topics concern different transmitter systems but share the principle that **neurotransmission depends on selective biochemical synthesis**. In the dopamine-deficient model, TH is removed and selectively restored in DBH-expressing cells, preserving norepinephrine synthesis while leaving dopaminergic cells deficient. Simply leaving DBH intact would not supply the missing upstream precursor.

Serotonin synthesis instead begins with tryptophan. Tryptophan hydroxylase produces 5-HTP, and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase converts 5-HTP to serotonin. The rate-limiting enzyme and precursor availability influence the supply of transmitter. The connection is experimental: manipulating enzymes or their expression can change transmitter availability and allow researchers to test contributions to behavior. The distinction is equally important: TH and TPH belong to different pathways, and a result obtained from a dopamine-deficient animal cannot be assumed to describe serotonin function. Explain the shared logic without merging the two pathways or treating synthesis deficits as receptor blockade.

**Source:** Lecture 7 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 6.

**Review:** [Lecture 7 study guide](../study-guides/lecture07.qmd).

l08-mc01.title: Question 1 — Acetylcholine biosynthesis
l08-mc01.markdown:
Acetylcholine synthesis joins **choline and an acetyl group supplied by acetyl-CoA**, using choline acetyltransferase (ChAT). The product is acetylcholine, and neurons using it are described as cholinergic. ChAT therefore identifies a synthetic function, rather than a receptor or a transporter.

The lecture emphasizes precursor availability and neuronal activity as influences on synthesis. Distinguish ChAT from acetylcholinesterase (AChE): the former makes ACh, whereas the latter breaks released ACh down. Also distinguish synthesis from vesicular loading, which uses VAChT. Following these separate steps prevents the common mistake of assuming that any drug reducing cholinergic transmission must directly inhibit ChAT; the course's examples often act instead on uptake, storage, or release.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc02.title: Question 2 — Compounds affecting acetylcholine storage and release
l08-mc02.markdown:
VAChT packages acetylcholine into **synaptic vesicles**, making it available for regulated release when the terminal is activated. Vesamicol blocks this packaging step, so less transmitter can be released even if ACh synthesis and the arrival of an action potential still occur.

The lecture contrasts storage blockade with toxins affecting release itself. Botulinum toxin prevents vesicle fusion, while black widow spider venom is described as promoting massive peripheral ACh release. These are different interventions in the same signaling sequence. Identify whether the change concerns transmitter production, vesicle filling, or fusion with the terminal membrane. The keyed option concerns filling vesicles, not receptor antagonism or enzymatic breakdown of ACh after it reaches the synaptic cleft.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc03.title: Question 3 — The cholinergic pharmacology of Botox
l08-mc03.markdown:
The essential mechanism is **presynaptic inhibition of acetylcholine release**. Botulinum toxin enters peripheral cholinergic terminals and disrupts the machinery needed for synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane. At a neuromuscular junction, reduced ACh release means less stimulation of the muscle's nicotinic receptors, producing weakness or paralysis.

This explains why a toxin can also have carefully controlled therapeutic uses in conditions involving excessive muscle contraction. The molecular action is not the same as blocking the muscle receptor directly or inhibiting ACh breakdown. The answer's bacterial origin and uptake description identify the substance, but the release-to-muscle-response chain explains the effect. The course examples describe pharmacological principles, not instructions for handling or administering the toxin.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc04.title: Question 4 — Acetylcholine is broken down by acetylcholinesterase
l08-mc04.markdown:
Acetylcholinesterase terminates cholinergic signaling by **hydrolyzing ACh to choline and acetic acid**, as described in the lecture. Rapid removal matters at neuromuscular junctions because continuing receptor stimulation would interfere with the separation of successive contractions and relaxation.

The slide distinguishes soluble and membrane-associated enzyme arrangements, including the specialized form at the neuromuscular junction. Their positioning helps bring enzyme and released transmitter together efficiently. Reversible AChE inhibitors have the opposite effect from blocking ACh release: they prolong the availability of transmitter that has already been released. The dementia examples illustrate that mechanism in the course; they do not mean that these drugs restore lost neurons or reverse every cause of cognitive impairment.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc05.title: Question 5 — What happens to the byproducts of ACh catabolism
l08-mc05.markdown:
The recycled molecule is **choline**, not intact acetylcholine. AChE first breaks released ACh down in the extracellular space. Choline transporters then return choline to the terminal, where ChAT can use it with acetyl-CoA to synthesize new transmitter.

Blocking choline uptake with hemicholinium-3 reduces precursor availability and therefore reduces subsequent ACh production. This differs from the monoamine examples in which the transmitter itself is taken back up by a transporter such as SERT or DAT. It also differs from inhibiting AChE, which slows transmitter breakdown rather than limiting precursor recycling. A complete explanation follows the cycle from release to hydrolysis, precursor uptake, and resynthesis instead of calling every transport process “ACh reuptake.”

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc06.title: Question 6 — Acetylcholine in the autonomic nervous system
l08-mc06.markdown:
Both autonomic branches use **ACh at the preganglionic-to-ganglionic synapse**. In the simplified organization emphasized by the lecture, parasympathetic postganglionic neurons also release ACh at their targets, whereas sympathetic postganglionic neurons generally release norepinephrine. The position of the synapse matters as much as the branch name.

Thus, “sympathetic means norepinephrine” is incomplete: it overlooks the cholinergic first synapse. Likewise, identifying a neuron as cholinergic does not by itself tell you whether it is sympathetic or parasympathetic. Trace CNS → autonomic ganglion → target organ, and label the transmitter at each connection. The key summarizes the course's general arrangement; it should not be used as an exceptionless inventory of every peripheral autonomic pathway.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc07.title: Question 7 — Acetylcholine in the somatic nervous system
l08-mc07.markdown:
A neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a **somatic motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber**. The motor terminal releases ACh, which activates nicotinic ACh receptors on the muscle membrane. Channel opening depolarizes that membrane and links the nervous system's signal to muscle activation.

The short keyed phrase names the junction but does not explain why it belongs to this topic. The important distinction is from an autonomic pathway, which uses a ganglionic relay to regulate organs and glands. It is also distinct from an ACh synapse between two neurons within the brain. Keep the transmitter, receptor class, and target cell together: ACh is the signal, the nicotinic receptor is the detector, and skeletal muscle is the target.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc08.title: Question 8 — Cholinergic projections in the NS
l08-mc08.markdown:
The lecture distinguishes **long-range cholinergic projection systems** from local interneurons. Basal forebrain neurons provide cholinergic input to cortex, hippocampus, and other limbic structures. Cholinergic cells in the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei project to regions including the thalamus and basal ganglia.

The origin of a projection is not the same as its target. A cholinergic terminal in the cortex can belong to a neuron whose cell body lies in the basal forebrain. This organization helps explain how a relatively localized population can influence widespread neural processing. By contrast, the striatal interneurons discussed later act within a local circuit. The key is the source-to-target arrangement, not an assumption that ACh has one function in every destination.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc09.title: Question 9 — Acetylcholine receptor subtypes
l08-mc09.markdown:
