The two receptor families are distinguished by their responses to characteristic agonists: **nicotinic receptors respond to nicotine, and muscarinic receptors respond to muscarine**. Both are receptors for the endogenous transmitter acetylcholine; their names do not mean nicotine or muscarine is normally required for cholinergic signaling.

The functional distinction is even more useful. Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that can produce rapid excitation. Muscarinic receptors couple to G proteins and influence intracellular signaling or ion channels indirectly. A drug acting at one family therefore need not reproduce all the effects of ACh. Do not confuse these receptor names with the enzymes ChAT and AChE, which respectively synthesize and break down the transmitter.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc10.title: Question 10 — Nicotinic receptors
l08-mc10.markdown:
A nicotinic ACh receptor is an **ionotropic receptor**: its protein complex includes the channel through which cations move after agonist binding. The lecture emphasizes inward positive charge and depolarization, explaining the rapid excitatory response in neural and muscle targets.

The receptor is assembled from five subunits, but Chapter 7 distinguishes different combinations in muscle and neuronal receptors. The slide's list of subunit names should not be interpreted as saying every receptor contains one of each listed type. Subunit composition matters because it changes receptor properties and drug sensitivity. The central contrast is with muscarinic signaling, which uses G proteins rather than making the receptor itself the directly gated ion channel.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc11.title: Question 11 — Muscarinic receptors
l08-mc11.markdown:
Muscarinic receptors act through **G-protein-linked signaling**, rather than forming the fast cation channel characteristic of nicotinic receptors. The lecture groups M1, M3, and M5 with phosphoinositide signaling, and M2 and M4 with inhibition of cAMP production, increased potassium conductance, and reduced terminal calcium-channel opening.

These mechanisms explain why ACh does not have one fixed effect wherever it is released. Opening potassium channels can reduce excitability, while reducing presynaptic calcium entry can reduce transmitter release. Other muscarinic pathways produce different cellular changes. Start with the receptor subtype and its location, then infer the likely cellular consequence. The broad “excitatory” and “inhibitory” labels summarize the course examples rather than replace that mechanistic reasoning.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc12.title: Question 12 — Distribution of AChRs in the brain Let’s focus on the striatum
l08-mc12.markdown:
The figure shows **regional differences in nicotinic receptor subunit combinations**, including receptors in the caudate-putamen, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and cerebellum. It then directs attention to the striatum, where the following slide examines local cholinergic regulation of dopamine terminals.

This connects anatomy to pharmacology: a receptor's location and composition help determine which circuit a drug can influence. Detecting receptors in a region does not mean every cell there synthesizes ACh. The original keyed option merely repeats the slide heading, so it does not actually identify a distribution or mechanism. Use the figure and subsequent striatal circuit to learn the concept, but treat this item as needing substantive answer choices before formal assessment.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc13.title: Question 13 — Pavlovian to instrumental transfer
l08-mc13.markdown:
Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer occurs when a **reward-predicting cue changes the performance of an independently learned action**. Pavlovian learning establishes the cue–outcome relationship; instrumental learning establishes that an action produces an outcome. During transfer, presentation of the cue can invigorate the action.

The lecture's drug-cue example illustrates how an object associated with prior reward can acquire motivational significance. Merely recognizing the object is not the full phenomenon: the important result is a change in goal-directed effort or responding. Likewise, performing a previously rewarded action without a cue is instrumental behavior but not, by itself, evidence of transfer. The distinction lies in the interaction between the two forms of learning.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc14.title: Question 14 — Pavlovian to instrumental transfer in the rat
l08-mc14.markdown:
The slide's diagram separates three stages. First, a neutral cue is paired with reward. Second, an action such as lever pressing is trained to obtain reward. Finally, the cue is presented while the action is available, allowing comparison of **responding during the cue with responding without it**. Increased responding during the reward-predicting cue is the transfer effect illustrated.

Testing without normal reward delivery helps distinguish the cue's motivational influence from new reinforcement during the test. The keyed option in this MCQ is only a topic placeholder and does not describe these stages. The diagram provides the substantive answer; a valid assessment should ask about the separate learning histories, test comparison, or interpretation instead of rewarding recognition of the heading alone.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc15.title: Question 15 — Striatal dopamine in response to CS presentation in PIT Aitken et al., 2014
l08-mc15.markdown:
The plotted trace aligns dopamine measurements with **conditioned-stimulus presentation**. The lecture labels the response as phasic and identifies fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) as the recording method. The important observation is a temporally associated dopamine increase when the reward-predicting cue appears during the transfer test.

This is more specific than saying dopamine is present in the striatum, but it remains a measurement of a relationship between cue presentation and neurochemical activity. The trace alone does not establish that the measured rise is sufficient or necessary for increased lever pressing. That stronger causal question motivates the later manipulation of cholinergic interneurons and nicotinic receptors. Keep the observed signal separate from the causal interpretation being tested.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-mc16.title: Question 16 — Dopamine spikes in response to CS presentation in PIT Collins et al., 2019
l08-mc16.markdown:
The lecture describes a counterintuitive result: **stimulating striatal cholinergic interneurons suppresses PIT**, while blocking β2-containing nicotinic receptors with DHβE restores it in that condition. The comparison implicates nicotinic signaling in how the manipulation changes cue-driven responding.

This does not justify the conclusion that dopamine is irrelevant to PIT. The lecture instead raises a tonic-versus-phasic hypothesis: changing ongoing cholinergic control of dopamine terminals may alter how cue-related dopamine signals are expressed. That remains a proposed interpretation in the supplied slide, not a fully established mechanism to be asserted as fact. Distinguish the observed stimulation/blockade results from the hypothesis offered to explain why “more activation” need not produce more motivated responding.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — AChE is an enzyme that catalyzes a catabolic reaction
l08-sa01.markdown:
AChE is the **enzyme**, ACh is its **substrate**, and hydrolysis is the catalyzed reaction. The reaction is catabolic because it breaks ACh into smaller products, described in the lecture as choline and acetic acid. The enzyme accelerates this process rather than becoming the signal or being consumed each time a transmitter molecule is broken down.

Connect breakdown to both termination and recycling. Removing ACh from the cleft limits receptor stimulation, helping separate successive signals. Choline is then taken back into the terminal and used by ChAT with acetyl-CoA to make new ACh. Thus, breakdown and synthesis are opposite chemical directions but complementary stages of the transmitter cycle. The original answer panel lists terms without developing this relationship; a complete response must supply it. Predicting drug effects further demonstrates understanding: AChE inhibition prolongs released ACh action, whereas inhibition of choline uptake limits precursor recycling and can reduce subsequent synthesis.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Acetylcholine microcircuits in the central nervous system
l08-sa02.markdown:
Striatal cholinergic interneurons provide **local regulation**, unlike the long-range basal-forebrain projections described earlier. Their activity interacts with dopamine signaling in circuits involved in movement and motivated behavior. The lecture uses reduced dopamine in Parkinson's disease to illustrate how changing one transmitter can disturb the balance of a circuit rather than simply turning the entire circuit off.

Receptor identity explains the possible interactions. Nicotinic receptors are fast ligand-gated channels, including β2-containing receptors on dopamine terminals in the later example; muscarinic receptors use slower G-protein-linked mechanisms. ACh can therefore alter transmitter release and the activity of different cells through different receptor pathways. A strong answer connects local cell type → receptor location → cellular effect → circuit consequence. The course's anticholinergic treatment example illustrates this balance concept; it does not imply that blocking all cholinergic signaling is beneficial or that one transmitter's concentration alone determines every motor symptom.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Cholinergic interneurons of the striatum
l08-sa03.markdown:
The local circuit contains **cholinergic interneurons and dopamine terminals bearing β2-containing nicotinic receptors**. ACh can activate these receptors, promote calcium entry and influence vesicular dopamine release. The lecture proposes a role in maintaining tonic dopamine availability, which should be distinguished from brief, cue-related phasic responses.

Connect the circuit to PIT by following the experiments: a reward-predicting cue can increase instrumental responding, and dopamine transients accompany cue presentation. However, optogenetic stimulation of cholinergic interneurons suppresses PIT in the reported experiment, while nicotinic blockade restores the effect under stimulation. This means that describing the circuit as simply “ACh increases dopamine, so behavior must increase” is inadequate. The slide suggests tonic-versus-phasic regulation as an explanation, but leaves the mechanism open. A developed response reports the observed comparisons accurately and labels that mechanistic account as a hypothesis rather than presenting an unresolved interpretation as the experiment's direct measurement.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l08-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Integration: Acetylcholine biosynthesis and Compounds affecting acetylcholine storage and release
l08-sa04.markdown:
Synthesis and storage are **successive but distinct requirements** for cholinergic transmission. ChAT makes ACh from choline and acetyl-CoA in the terminal. VAChT then transports ACh into synaptic vesicles. When the release machinery is activated, filled vesicles can fuse with the membrane and release their contents.

The distinction explains why normal synthesis does not guarantee normal transmission. Blocking VAChT with vesamicol reduces vesicular filling even if ACh continues to be produced; blocking fusion with botulinum toxin prevents release even if transmitter is present in vesicles. Conversely, limiting choline uptake can reduce the precursor supply for synthesis. These interventions affect different links in the same chain and should not all be described as receptor antagonists. A strong comparison identifies the enzyme versus transporter, the chemical production versus packaging step, and the shared consequence that disruption can reduce the ACh delivered to receptors when a neuron fires.

**Source:** Lecture 8 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 7.

**Review:** [Lecture 8 study guide](../study-guides/lecture08.qmd).

l09-mc01.title: Question 1 — Glutamate biosynthesis
l09-mc01.markdown:
Glutaminase converts **glutamine to glutamate**, supplying part of the transmitter pool used by glutamatergic neurons. Glutamate is also an amino acid with metabolic roles in many kinds of cells, so its mere presence in a cell does not establish that the cell releases it as a neurotransmitter.

The lecture distinguishes the specialized transmitter pool from these other biochemical functions. Glutamatergic neurons must also package glutamate into vesicles and release it at appropriate terminals. Do not confuse glutaminase with glutamine synthetase: the latter converts glutamate into glutamine in astrocytes, helping recycle material back to neurons. The two enzymes support opposite steps in a shared neuron–glia cycle rather than performing the same reaction.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc02.title: Question 2 — Vesicular packaging of glutamate
l09-mc02.markdown:
VGLUT proteins transport glutamate into **synaptic vesicles**. They are therefore markers of the capacity for vesicular glutamate signaling, not enzymes that synthesize glutamate or transporters that remove it from the extracellular space. EAATs perform the latter uptake function.

The co-transmission examples qualify an overly rigid “one neuron, one transmitter” rule. A cell identified by dopamine, serotonin, ACh, or GABA markers may also express a VGLUT and release glutamate. In the VTA example, the lecture describes dopamine and glutamate release from separate vesicles at different terminal types. Thus, co-expression does not imply that the two chemicals necessarily occupy the same vesicle or are released identically at every synapse of that neuron.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc03.title: Question 3 — Glutamate reuptake
l09-mc03.markdown:
EAATs remove glutamate from the **extracellular space**, limiting the duration and spread of excitation. Astrocytic EAAT2 has a particularly prominent role in the lecture's account, illustrating that transmitter inactivation is not exclusively a job for the presynaptic neuron.

This uptake has two linked consequences: it helps end a signal and prevents excessive extracellular glutamate from stimulating receptors continuously. Glutamate taken into astrocytes can subsequently enter the glutamate–glutamine recycling pathway. The approximate uptake percentage in the key expresses the course's emphasis on astrocytes; the mechanistic distinction is more important than treating that number as universal. VGLUT fills vesicles, EAAT removes extracellular transmitter, and glutamine synthetase performs an intracellular chemical conversion.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc04.title: Question 4 — EAAT knockout
l09-mc04.markdown:
Removing EAAT2 compromises a major route for **clearing extracellular glutamate**. The lecture reports seizures and shortened survival in knockout mice, linking disrupted clearance to excessive excitation. The result demonstrates why a normally useful excitatory transmitter must be tightly regulated outside cells.

The manipulation is not equivalent to eliminating glutamate synthesis or blocking all glutamate receptors. Transmitter can still be released, but its removal is impaired. This makes the experiment informative about transport and extracellular regulation. However, a constitutive knockout affects an animal over development as well as during testing, so its full phenotype should not be reduced to the effect of one brief drug exposure. The evidence supports the importance of uptake, not an unrestricted claim that glutamate is inherently harmful.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc05.title: Question 5 — Astrocytic metabolism of glutamate
l09-mc05.markdown:
The recycling sequence is **uptake into astrocytes → conversion to glutamine → transport to neurons → reconversion to glutamate**. Glutamine synthetase catalyzes the astrocytic conversion; glutaminase catalyzes the neuronal conversion. This couples removal of released transmitter to replenishment of the supply used for later signaling.

There is a wording problem in the original key: transporters do not themselves convert glutamate into glutamine. The lecture's shorthand should be distinguished from the clearer account in Chapter 8, which assigns transport to EAATs and conversion to the enzyme glutamine synthetase. Keeping movement and chemical transformation separate makes the cycle intelligible and explains how astrocytes support both signal termination and continued neurotransmission.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc06.title: Question 6 — Anatomical organization of the glutamate system
l09-mc06.markdown:
Glutamate supports **widely distributed fast excitatory transmission**, including cortical pyramidal-cell projections and excitatory hippocampal pathways. This broad anatomical presence is why the lecture calls it a “workhorse” rather than assigning it one narrow psychological function.

Its contribution depends on the circuit and receptor involved. In one setting glutamate carries an immediate signal; in another, receptor activation contributes to plasticity and longer-lasting changes in synaptic strength. The unfinished list in the answer panel is not a complete account of the pathway anatomy. Also note a source discrepancy: the slide says “parallel fibers of the cerebrum,” whereas the assigned chapter describes cerebellar parallel fibers. That wording should be checked rather than memorized uncritically.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc07.title: Question 7 — Ionotropic glutamate receptors
l09-mc07.markdown:
AMPA, kainate, and NMDA receptors are **ionotropic glutamate receptors**, named after agonists used to distinguish their pharmacology. Activation opens a channel directly, rather than beginning the G-protein signaling sequence characteristic of metabotropic glutamate receptors.

The lecture emphasizes AMPA receptors as major mediators of fast excitatory responses. NMDA receptors add special requirements and a calcium-permeable component that links activity to intracellular signaling and plasticity. Receptor names identify pharmacological categories, not the transmitter normally released at each synapse: endogenous glutamate can act at these receptor families. The key begins with AMPA and kainate, but understanding the topic requires recognizing NMDA as the third ionotropic family in the lecture's comparison.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc08.title: Question 8 — NMDA receptors are very interesting
l09-mc08.markdown:
NMDA channel opening requires more than glutamate alone. A **co-agonist, glycine or D-serine, must also occupy its site**, and sufficient depolarization must relieve the magnesium block within the channel. Once those conditions are met, sodium and calcium can pass, linking excitation to intracellular signaling.

This combination explains the receptor's coincidence-detection role: transmitter arrival must coincide with a sufficiently depolarized postsynaptic cell. A source qualification matters here. The slide associates the co-agonists with astrocytic release, but Chapter 8 explicitly discusses evidence for primarily neuronal D-serine formation. The sources should not be collapsed into a claim that astrocytes are the exclusive origin. The shared, well-supported point is the co-agonist requirement and voltage-dependent magnesium block.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc09.title: Question 9 — Metabotropic glutamate receptors
l09-mc09.markdown:
Metabotropic glutamate receptors signal through **G proteins and intracellular effectors**, rather than directly forming the ion channel of an AMPA or NMDA receptor. The lecture groups mGluR1 and mGluR5 with postsynaptic phosphoinositide signaling, and Groups II and III mainly with mechanisms that reduce transmitter release through inhibitory signaling.

This shows why an excitatory transmitter can also recruit feedback that limits further transmission. The relevant question is which receptor is activated and where it is located, not simply whether glutamate is present. The lecture marks mGluR6 as an exception in its grouping, so the broad presynaptic description should not be treated as an exceptionless location rule for every metabotropic subtype.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc10.title: Question 10 — AMPA and NMDA receptors in learning and memory
l09-mc10.markdown:
A positive allosteric modulator **enhances the response to glutamate already present**, rather than acting as a direct substitute at the transmitter's binding site. This offers a way to modify ongoing signaling while retaining some dependence on the timing and location of endogenous glutamate release.

The lecture reports learning or memory enhancement in experimental animals but not the same success in the clinical trials it discusses. That contrast is an important limitation, not a detail to omit. Its question about direct agonists connects to the later excitotoxicity discussion: indiscriminate enhancement of excitation can be hazardous. A plausible receptor mechanism and encouraging animal performance are not enough to establish safe, effective cognitive enhancement in humans.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc11.title: Question 11 — A mechanism for glutamate in memory formation
l09-mc11.markdown:
The NMDA receptor can detect the conjunction of **presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic depolarization**. In the lecture's Pavlovian-learning example, a conditioned-stimulus input releases glutamate while another input helps depolarize the postsynaptic cell. With co-agonist binding and relief of the magnesium block, calcium can enter through NMDA receptors and initiate strengthening processes.

This provides a cellular model for why appropriately paired inputs may become more effective together. The phrase “fire together, wire together” is a summary, not a substitute for explaining the receptor requirements. It is also not proof that every form of learning uses precisely this mechanism. The lecture presents LTP as a mechanistic connection between patterned activity and lasting changes in synaptic effectiveness.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc12.title: Question 12 — Long-term potentiation
l09-mc12.markdown:
Long-term potentiation is a **lasting increase in synaptic effectiveness**, commonly evaluated as a larger EPSP evoked by a comparable input after an induction event. A larger EPSP brings the postsynaptic membrane closer to firing threshold, but it is not itself the same thing as an action potential.

The lecture lists several routes to a stronger response: increased presynaptic transmitter release, more postsynaptic receptors, changes in receptor function, and structural changes. These possibilities distinguish an observed physiological effect from its underlying mechanism. To demonstrate potentiation, compare the response to an equivalent test input before and after induction; merely increasing the stimulus strength during testing would not establish that the synapse itself had strengthened.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc13.title: Question 13 — Measuring LTP in the laboratory Stim
l09-mc13.markdown:
The figure separates **stimulation of an input pathway from recording the postsynaptic response**. Its hippocampal example shows stimulation of Schaffer-collateral input and recording in the CA1 region. The accompanying traces illustrate a larger postsynaptic EPSP after LTP induction than before, following a comparable presynaptic event.

This comparison tests a change in communication between cells, not simply the existence of electrical activity. A bigger response is meaningful only relative to the baseline and the controlled test input. The original keyed phrase, “Stim Record,” labels the apparatus but does not explain the measurement. A substantive answer should identify where stimulation and recording occur and what before-versus-after change would count as evidence of potentiation.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc14.title: Question 14 — AMPAand NMDA receptors ✤ AMPAand NMDA receptorsmediate
l09-mc14.markdown:
AMPA-mediated excitation can depolarize a postsynaptic neuron sufficiently to **relieve the NMDA channel's magnesium block**. With glutamate and the required co-agonist present, the unblocked NMDA channel can then carry calcium as well as sodium. Calcium supplies the intracellular signal that links this brief electrical event to subsequent plasticity mechanisms.

Do not interpret the slide's shorthand as saying glutamate cannot bind an NMDA receptor at resting voltage. The assigned chapter distinguishes ligand binding from ion flow: magnesium can block the channel even when the required ligands are bound. Nor must AMPA be the only possible source of depolarization. It is the source emphasized in this example of cooperation between two glutamate receptor classes.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc15.title: Question 15 — Calcium triggers a cascade of events ✤ Ca2+entersthecell through the NMDA receptor and
l09-mc15.markdown:
Calcium entering through activated NMDA receptors can engage **protein kinases and signaling pathways that strengthen transmission**. The lecture links CaMKII to additional AMPA receptors in the membrane and associates CaMKII and PKC with increased AMPA-receptor conductance. These changes can make the same future input produce a larger response.

The keyed sentence selects the lecture's retrograde-messenger branch: a signal originating postsynaptically, described as nitric oxide, can influence the presynaptic terminal and increase glutamate release. That direction is the reverse of the usual transmitter handoff. Read it as part of the lecture's schematic account, not as the sole necessary pathway for all LTP. The slide also includes transcription and protein synthesis associated with longer-lasting structural changes.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc16.title: Question 16 — Calcium triggers a cascade of events ✤ Ca2+entersthecell and activatesprotein
l09-mc16.markdown:
This slide distinguishes **early changes in synaptic function from later changes supported by gene expression and structure**. AMPA-receptor trafficking and altered conductance can strengthen the postsynaptic response, while CREB-related transcription and protein synthesis provide a route to longer-lasting modifications of dendrites and synapses.

The original key repeats the nitric-oxide example from the previous question, but that is only one branch of the slide. A complete explanation follows calcium entry through NMDA receptors into kinase activity, receptor regulation, and longer-term cellular changes. “Retrograde” refers specifically to a signal traveling from the postsynaptic cell toward the presynaptic terminal; it does not mean that all transmitter release runs backward or that every strengthening mechanism is presynaptic.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc17.title: Question 17 — Multiple ways to die
l09-mc17.markdown:
The substantive distinction is between **lytic cell injury and programmed cell-death mechanisms**. Necrosis can involve osmotic swelling, membrane rupture, and release of cellular contents. Programmed death involves regulated biochemical processes; apoptosis includes removal of cellular material without the same pattern of lytic spillage.

The original keyed timing statement should not be treated as settled. Lecture slide 22 describes necrosis as slow and apoptosis as fast, whereas Chapter 8 describes relatively rapid necrosis under intense exposure and delayed programmed death. The chapter also distinguishes adult programmed necrosis from apoptosis and assigns different roles to synaptic GluN2A and extrasynaptic GluN2B receptors. These are explicit source discrepancies requiring instructor review; they cannot support a unique timing-based answer as currently written.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc18.title: Question 18 — Stroke
l09-mc18.markdown:
A stroke is a **sudden cerebrovascular event**. The lecture distinguishes hemorrhage, involving bleeding, from ischemia, involving inadequate blood supply. It identifies an infarct as an area of dead or dying tissue and the surrounding penumbra as important to the discussion of further injury.

The point of introducing these terms is to connect a vascular problem to cellular consequences. Reduced blood supply can disrupt the energy-dependent processes that normally maintain ion gradients and regulate neurotransmitter availability. Subsequent excitotoxic signaling is one proposed contributor to damage, not the definition of stroke itself. The answer's two short labels therefore need the vascular distinction and tissue context; neither “infarct” nor “glutamate toxicity” alone describes every aspect of the event.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc19.title: Question 19 — Glutamate toxicity in stroke
l09-mc19.markdown:
The lecture connects ischemia to **excessive extracellular glutamate and injury to nearby neurons**. Loss of adequate blood supply compromises normal cellular function, and disrupted glutamate regulation can lead to prolonged activation of excitatory receptors. The preceding receptor discussion explains why sustained ion entry, especially calcium signaling under pathological conditions, can become damaging.

This mechanism motivates efforts to protect tissue around an infarct. It does not mean glutamate is the initial vascular blockage or the only pathway of ischemic damage. The clinical-treatment question is separate: even if excitotoxicity contributes to injury, blocking one receptor class must still be shown to improve outcomes safely under actual treatment conditions. That is why the next slide discusses unsuccessful NMDA-blocker trials.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-mc20.title: Question 20 — NMDA receptor blockers in stroke
l09-mc20.markdown:
The lecture contrasts a **plausible neuroprotective mechanism with disappointing clinical trial results**. NMDA receptors participate in excitotoxic processes, so blocking them seemed a reasonable strategy for limiting ischemic injury. However, the historical trials cited on the slide did not establish the hoped-for clinical benefit.

This does not prove that NMDA receptors play no role in the injury mechanism. It shows that mechanistic involvement is not sufficient to demonstrate that a particular treatment improves patient outcomes. The supplied slide does not give enough information to attribute failure to one specific cause, such as dose, timing, or adverse effects, so those explanations should not be invented. Interpret “they don't seem to work” within the trials and course context, not as a current universal treatment guideline.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 25. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — The diversity of EAATs
l09-sa01.markdown:
EAATs are **plasma-membrane transporters that remove extracellular glutamate**, with subtype distributions that differ across cells and regions. The lecture emphasizes astrocytic EAAT2, EAAT1 in cerebellar astrocytes, neuronal EAAT3, EAAT4 in Purkinje cells, and EAAT5 in retinal bipolar cells. This distribution illustrates division of labor rather than five interchangeable labels for a single presynaptic mechanism.

Connect uptake to recycling by following astrocytic glutamate into glutamine synthetase, which converts it to glutamine. Glutamine can then return to neurons and be converted back to glutamate by glutaminase. Uptake both limits receptor exposure and supports continued transmitter supply. Keep the molecular roles separate: EAATs move the molecule across a membrane; enzymes change its chemical identity; VGLUT later packages neuronal glutamate into vesicles. The EAAT2-knockout seizure example further shows why the uptake step matters for network stability, not merely for conserving precursor material.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Another binding site directly inside the channel
l09-sa02.markdown:
The NMDA channel contains a site at which the lecture's named drugs can **block ion flow without competing for glutamate's binding site**. The lecture calls these uncompetitive antagonists because channel activation is required before they gain access to their relevant blocking site. Thus, receptor activation can enable the blocker to exert its inhibitory action.

This differs from an ordinary competitive antagonist that prevents an agonist from occupying its own site. It also differs from metabotropic glutamate receptors: those receptors engage G proteins and intracellular pathways rather than supplying the NMDA ion-channel pore. A strong response identifies the location of action, the dependence on channel activation, and the consequence—reduced ion flow through the activated receptor. PCP, ketamine, MK-801, and memantine illustrate the category in the lecture, but sharing a broad channel-blocking mechanism does not make their clinical effects, risks, or uses interchangeable.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — ✤ Withslice electrophysiology,we can induce LTPin cells and record thechange in EPSP 1.Establish a baseline: stimulatepresynapticaxons @low
l09-sa03.markdown:
The experimental logic has **baseline, induction, and post-induction testing**. A low-frequency test input first establishes the size of the evoked postsynaptic response. A stronger patterned input is then used to induce plasticity. Finally, the original test conditions are reinstated so that any persistent increase can be attributed to altered synaptic responsiveness rather than simply continued stronger stimulation.

The lecture uses EPSPs and the possibility of reaching action-potential threshold to illustrate the change. A larger EPSP to the same input is the central measure; generating an action potential is not required in every demonstration of LTP. Connect the procedure to NMDA-dependent plasticity by explaining that sufficient depolarization and glutamate signaling during induction permit calcium entry and subsequent strengthening processes. The diagram's separate stimulation and recording locations make this an assessment of transmission between cells. A complete answer must compare responses before and after induction, not just state that high-frequency stimulation makes neurons fire.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — High levels of glutamate is toxic
l09-sa04.markdown:
Excitotoxicity is injury caused by **excessive or prolonged excitatory receptor activation**, not the ordinary presence of glutamate in neural tissue. Normally, release and EAAT-mediated uptake keep signaling spatially and temporally regulated. When that regulation fails, sustained ion entry and associated intracellular processes can overwhelm cells and activate damaging pathways.

The supplied sources disagree on some details of cell death, so identify that explicitly. Chapter 8 describes rapid lytic necrosis under severe exposure, delayed programmed death under other conditions, and a distinction between apoptosis and programmed necrosis. The lecture reverses some timing labels and includes broader “good/bad” and cancer statements that are not established by the assigned chapter's explanation. A strong answer should describe swelling, membrane rupture, programmed biochemical changes, and receptor context without treating apoptosis as always beneficial or claiming excitotoxic necrosis automatically causes cancer. The reliable connection is between dysregulated excitation and cell injury, with the disputed details reserved for instructor clarification.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l09-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — What about MSG
l09-sa05.markdown:
The key distinction is **where the glutamate is and how tissue is exposed to it**. Glutamate has normal metabolic and neurotransmitter functions and also occurs in food, contributing to umami taste. Excitotoxicity refers to excessive receptor exposure in neural tissue; it does not follow merely from identifying glutamate in something eaten.

The lecture explains its MSG example through the blood–brain barrier and the separation between dietary intake and extracellular brain concentrations. Connect this to synthesis and recycling: neurons and astrocytes regulate the brain's transmitter pool through their own transport and metabolic processes. The original answer ends with a rhetorical question, so it needs this compartment-based reasoning. Claims about particular sensitivity symptoms, regulatory status, or the design of the cited feeding study should be interpreted as course statements, not expanded into universal safety guarantees. The scientific lesson is to distinguish substance identity from dose, route, tissue distribution, and the exposure required to produce a specific effect.

**Source:** Lecture 9 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 26. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 9 study guide](../study-guides/lecture09.qmd).

l10-mc01.title: Question 1 — Biosynthesis of GABA
l10-mc01.markdown:
Glutamic acid decarboxylase (**GAD**) converts glutamate to GABA. This is a synthesis reaction, distinct from moving GABA into vesicles or removing it after release. The fact that a major excitatory transmitter is the precursor of a major inhibitory transmitter is a useful reminder that function depends on the molecule's receptors and circuit context, not simply its biochemical ancestry.

The lecture links reduced GABA synthesis to increased susceptibility to excessive excitation and convulsions. This explains GABA's role in regulating network excitability, rather than merely labeling it “inhibitory.” Its synthesis-inhibitor examples are experimental pharmacology, not substances to use for self-experimentation. A correct explanation identifies the precursor, enzyme, product, and consequence of disrupting the pathway.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc02.title: Question 2 — GABA transport
l10-mc02.markdown:
VGAT and GAT transporters act at **different membranes and stages**. VGAT loads GABA into intracellular synaptic vesicles, whereas GAT proteins remove released GABA from the extracellular space into neurons or astrocytes. Confusing these steps reverses the predicted effect of transporter inhibition.

The lecture's tiagabine example inhibits GAT-1, reducing uptake and increasing extracellular GABA availability. It does not directly fill vesicles or activate GABA receptors as an agonist. The subsequent receptor response still depends on the GABA present and the receptors available. This is the same reasoning used earlier to distinguish vesicular monoamine transporters from DAT or SERT: “transport blocker” is incomplete unless the transporter and direction of transport are specified.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc03.title: Question 3 — Astrocytes are important with GABA too
l10-mc03.markdown:
Astrocytes contribute to **GABA metabolism and precursor recycling**, as they do for glutamate. Chapter 8 explains that GABA breakdown begins with GABA aminotransferase and proceeds through multiple steps toward succinate, with glutamate generated in the pathway. Astrocytic glutamate can then be converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase.

Glutamine can return to neurons, be converted back to glutamate, and supply GABA resynthesis through GAD. The original key compresses this into a single sentence; it should not be read as a complete one-step chemical equation. The important connection is that transmitter removal does not merely dispose of material: metabolic cooperation between neurons and glia also helps maintain the substrate needed for later signaling.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc04.title: Question 4 — Co-release of GABA is common
l10-mc04.markdown:
The co-release examples challenge a strict **one-neuron/one-transmitter rule**. The lecture describes GABA release from neurons also associated with glycine, ACh, dopamine, or glutamate. In some cases multiple vesicular transport systems coexist; in others, packaging involves transport machinery ordinarily associated with another transmitter.

Co-release does not make the two transmitters functionally identical. Simultaneous glutamate and GABA signaling can have different effects on the target cell because their receptors and conductances differ. This allows finer control than labeling a whole neuron simply “excitatory” or “inhibitory.” The evidence to look for concerns transmitter handling and release, not merely whether a molecule can be detected somewhere inside the cell for metabolic reasons.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc05.title: Question 5 — GABAergic projections: direct and indirect pathway Direct
l10-mc05.markdown:
The direct and indirect basal-ganglia diagrams illustrate **inhibition and disinhibition across a chain of connections**. In the simplified direct pathway, striatal inhibition of an inhibitory output region can reduce its inhibition of the thalamus, facilitating motor-related signaling. The indirect pathway involves additional connections that can increase inhibitory output and restrain that signaling.

The key “Thalamus Thalamus” is a figure-label extraction error, not a meaningful answer. A useful explanation must trace the sign of each connection rather than assume that activating any GABAergic neuron suppresses every downstream region. The Parkinson's comparison then shows how altered dopamine input changes the balance of these pathways. This item needs substantive choices before it can validly assess the circuit concept.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc06.title: Question 6 — GABAergic interneurons
l10-mc06.markdown:
The slide illustrates **disinhibition of a VTA dopamine neuron**. At baseline, a GABA interneuron inhibits the dopamine cell. Activation of the μ-opioid receptor on the inhibitory neuron reduces its activity and GABA release. With less inhibitory input, the dopamine neuron can increase firing.

The critical reasoning involves two inhibitory steps: inhibiting an inhibitor can increase activity downstream. It would therefore be wrong to infer that an inhibitory cellular drug action must always reduce activity throughout the entire circuit. The original keyed option is a topic placeholder and omits the illustrated mechanism. The figure supplies the actual teaching point; it should be used to understand disinhibition, while the MCQ's answer choices remain a revision issue.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc07.title: Question 7 — GABAA receptors are most common The actions of GABA are primarily
l10-mc07.markdown:
GABAA receptors are **ligand-gated ion channels**, commonly assembled from five subunits. In the adult-neuron example used by the lecture, opening the channel permits chloride conductance that inhibits the postsynaptic cell. GABAB receptors, by contrast, work through G proteins and indirect effects on channels and signaling pathways.

The common two-α, two-β, one-γ arrangement is a useful example, not the composition of every GABAA receptor. Differences in subunits help explain why receptor populations respond differently to modulators such as benzodiazepines, anesthetics, and neurosteroids. The central distinction is receptor mechanism: rapid channel-mediated inhibition versus metabotropic inhibition. Do not mistake the receptor family name for the enzyme GAD or the uptake transporters GATs.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc08.title: Question 8 — Modulation of the GABAA receptor
l10-mc08.markdown:
Muscimol is an **orthosteric GABAA agonist**, acting at the transmitter-recognition site to activate the receptor. Bicuculline is a competitive antagonist that prevents GABA from acting at that site. Picrotoxin and the other channel-modulating examples illustrate inhibition at sites different from the GABA-binding pocket.

These distinctions explain why reduced GABAA function can increase network excitability and provoke convulsions: the intervention removes part of the system's inhibitory restraint. The lecture notes additional complexity in PTZ's interaction, so “different binding site” should not be turned into an oversimplified claim about every dose–response relationship. Identify the drug's site and functional effect first, then distinguish direct agonism, competitive antagonism, and channel/allosteric inhibition.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc09.title: Question 9 — Allosteric modulation of the GABAA receptor
l10-mc09.markdown:
The decisive comparison is **a modulator with GABA present versus the same modulator without GABA**. In the lecture's diazepam example, the drug enhances the receptor's response to GABA but does not activate the channel alone. That supports classification as a positive allosteric modulator rather than an orthosteric agonist.

The slide contrasts this with sufficiently high concentrations of certain barbiturates, anesthetics, or neurosteroids, which can directly gate channels. It also describes inverse effects at the benzodiazepine site that reduce GABA's effectiveness. These distinctions concern receptor pharmacology, not an assurance that a GABA-dependent drug is harmless. The course's broad ethanol statement belongs to this simplified comparison and should not be extended to explain every action of alcohol in the brain.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc10.title: Question 10 — Organization and Function of the GABAergic System (6 of 9)
l10-mc10.markdown:
The table links anesthetic effects to **patterns of receptor modulation**, especially enhancement of GABAA-mediated inhibition. The lecture also shows that different agents have effects at other receptor classes and that receptor subunit composition can influence sensitivity.

This helps explain why sharing an anesthetic effect does not imply identical molecular actions or identical side effects. In the figure, the principal GABAA effect is distinguished from additional actions labeled as high-dose or antiemetic effects. The mixed phrases in the original answer are extracted labels, not a coherent causal explanation. Read the table by comparing a drug across receptor columns and distinguishing its primary inhibitory action from additional receptor effects, rather than treating every listed effect as equally strong or universal.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc11.title: Question 11 — Seizure frequency correlates with hormonal load Many females suffer from
l10-mc11.markdown:
The lecture describes **catamenial epilepsy**, in which seizure occurrence varies with the menstrual cycle in some people with epilepsy. Its explanation contrasts the relatively proconvulsant influence attributed to estrogen with inhibitory effects associated with progesterone and its neuroactive metabolites.

The important mechanism is a change in the balance of excitation and inhibition over time, not simply a high absolute level of one hormone. The estrogen-to-progesterone relationship and changes around particular cycle phases are presented as relevant to seizure likelihood. These are population and mechanistic observations, not a prediction that every individual has the same pattern. The following neurosteroid example connects hormonal metabolism more specifically to allosteric regulation of GABAA receptors.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc12.title: Question 12 — Seizure frequency correlates with hormonal load Neurosteroids: synthesized in the
l10-mc12.markdown:
Progesterone can be converted to **allopregnanolone**, a neuroactive steroid that positively modulates GABAA receptors. Chapter 8 explains that neurosteroids can enhance inhibition, including at extrasynaptic δ-containing receptors that differ from the usual benzodiazepine-sensitive receptor population.

The lecture's phrase “binds delta subunit” is stronger than the chapter's explanation of activity at δ-containing receptors; receptor composition and the exact binding site should not be treated as the same claim. The experimental graph illustrates increased resistance to PTZ-induced seizures under the reported conditions, not a universal clinical outcome. The mechanistic connection is steroid metabolism → receptor modulation → altered inhibitory restraint. The key's spelling “allopregnalone” is retained in the answer panel but clarified here as allopregnanolone.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc13.title: Question 13 — The baclofen muscimol cocktail
l10-mc13.markdown:
The combination pairs **GABAB agonism by baclofen with GABAA agonism by muscimol**. These receptor classes inhibit neural activity through different mechanisms: muscimol acts at a ligand-gated channel, while baclofen engages metabotropic signaling that can reduce firing or transmitter release.

The lecture uses the combination as an example of reversible experimental inhibition of a brain region. Reversibility distinguishes it from destroying tissue with a permanent lesion. However, changing behavior after regional inhibition does not automatically identify one cell type or prove that the region works independently of connected areas. The effect depends on the cells and receptors reached. The teaching objective is the logic of temporary functional manipulation, not a protocol for preparing or administering the drugs.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc14.title: Question 14 — Exam Information
l10-mc14.markdown:
This item reproduces **administrative information from the original lecture**, not a scientific concept about GABA. The slide specifies 70 multiple-choice questions and 50 minutes for the instructor's exam described there. It also labels that exam non-cumulative and based on lecture material.

Those historical course instructions must be distinguished from the practice exams on this website, which were deliberately requested as 45 MCQs in 50 minutes for Part II. The answer to this source-recognition item does not change the website's practice-exam format. Because it tests an announcement rather than psychopharmacological understanding, it should not contribute to a concept-mastery score without explicit instructor intent. The existing key is preserved, but its limited purpose is made clear.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc15.title: Question 15 — Syllabus update
l10-mc15.markdown:
The syllabus update explains the **transition from transmitter systems to addiction and drug classes**. An asynchronous lecture is introduced as an addiction primer, after which individual psychoactive drugs are considered in that context and beyond it.

This organizational link is useful: synthesis, transport, receptor signaling, and circuit principles provide tools for explaining the effects of the later drug classes. However, the original question asks students to recognize an announcement, not apply one of those mechanisms. It should therefore be distinguished from substantive examination coverage. The current answer remains unchanged, but a future assessment revision should replace this administrative item with a scientific question that actually tests the connection between a neurotransmitter mechanism and a drug's effects.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-mc16.title: Question 16 — Integration: Biosynthesis of GABA
l10-mc16.markdown:
The integration point is that **GABA synthesis helps establish the inhibitory capacity of a circuit**. GAD converts glutamate to GABA, after which vesicular transport, release, and receptor activation are still needed for an inhibitory signal to occur. Making the transmitter is necessary to the cycle but is not the whole process.

This connects to the lecture's transporter and receptor examples. Reducing synthesis can decrease the available inhibitory transmitter, whereas inhibiting uptake can prolong its extracellular availability. Activating a GABA receptor directly is a third intervention, acting at the receiving cell rather than at transmitter production. Distinguishing these sites explains why drugs can alter GABAergic transmission through different mechanisms even when their broad effect is described as increasing or decreasing inhibition.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Some GABAergic neurons are interneurons, while others are projection neurons
l10-sa01.markdown:
An interneuron primarily participates in a **local circuit**, whereas a projection neuron sends an axon to a more distant target. The lecture contrasts cortical and hippocampal GABAergic interneurons with striatal projection neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells. GABA is therefore not confined to short local inhibitory connections.

Connect this distinction to basal-ganglia pathways by tracing inhibition between regions. In the simplified direct pathway, inhibiting an inhibitory output can disinhibit the thalamus; in the indirect pathway, the additional connections can increase the inhibitory restraint on thalamic signaling. This explains why the net behavioral effect cannot be inferred from the word “GABAergic” alone. The target and sequence of connections matter. A strong answer gives both anatomical examples and the circuit logic, rather than saying all GABA neurons reduce movement. The Purkinje-cell degeneration example further illustrates that losing an inhibitory projection can disrupt coordination rather than simply produce uniformly greater movement.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptors The actions of GABA are primarily mediated
l10-sa02.markdown:
A positive allosteric modulator binds at a site **distinct from the transmitter's orthosteric site** and increases the response to GABA. In the lecture's benzodiazepine example, diazepam enhances inhibition when GABA is present but does not substitute for GABA as a direct channel-opening agonist. This is the central contrast with muscimol.

The source then qualifies the category by comparing drug classes and concentrations. Certain barbiturates, anesthetics, and neurosteroids can directly gate the channel at sufficiently high concentrations, while inverse actions at the benzodiazepine site reduce GABA's effectiveness. These are pharmacological distinctions, not interchangeable names for sedation. Explain the sequence from binding site to altered channel response and then to inhibition of the receiving cell. Also distinguish cellular inhibition from the net effect of a network: inhibiting an inhibitory neuron can disinhibit another cell. The answer should therefore explain receptor action first and avoid assuming identical behavioral effects across every circuit or drug.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — GABAB receptors are metabotropic
l10-sa03.markdown:
GABAB receptors are **metabotropic**, so their effects are mediated through G proteins rather than an intrinsic chloride-channel pore. Postsynaptically, the lecture emphasizes potassium-channel opening and reduced excitability. Presynaptically, inhibition of calcium-channel opening can reduce transmitter release. Reduced adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP formation provide another signaling effect.

Receptor location distinguishes autoreceptors from heteroreceptors: the former regulate a terminal using the same transmitter, while the latter regulate a terminal releasing another transmitter. Connect this to the baclofen–muscimol example by explaining that baclofen activates GABAB receptors while muscimol activates GABAA receptors. The combination recruits two different inhibitory mechanisms for reversible regional manipulation. A strong response should not say both drugs act on the same chloride channel. It should identify the receptor class, the relevant ion-channel effect, and whether the immediate consequence concerns postsynaptic firing or presynaptic transmitter release.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l10-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Integration: Biosynthesis of GABA and GABA transport
l10-sa04.markdown:
Biosynthesis changes **chemical identity**, whereas transport changes **location**. GAD converts glutamate into GABA. VGAT then moves GABA into vesicles for release. After release, GAT transporters move extracellular GABA into neurons or astrocytes, helping terminate its action and supporting subsequent metabolism and recycling.

This distinction allows a mechanistic prediction. Blocking synthesis reduces the supply available for later release; blocking vesicle filling impairs packaging; blocking uptake can increase extracellular availability and enhance receptor exposure. These interventions do not have the same effect simply because they all involve GABA. Connect the cycle to astrocytic metabolism by noting that recycled glutamine can return to neurons, become glutamate, and supply renewed GABA synthesis. A complete answer identifies GAD, VGAT, and GAT by their separate roles and follows the transmitter through the sequence, rather than treating all three as enzymes or all three as receptor targets.

**Source:** Lecture 10 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 8.

**Review:** [Lecture 10 study guide](../study-guides/lecture10.qmd).

l11-mc01.title: Question 1 — Overview
l11-mc01.markdown:
The overview establishes a **two-way relationship between circadian timing and pharmacology**. The clock can alter a drug's absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination, or target response. Conversely, a drug can influence clock timing through light-input pathways, behavior, or other clock-related mechanisms.

The initial circadian review supplies the vocabulary needed to distinguish these directions. Taking a drug at different times does not change its chemical identity, but it may change the biological conditions in which the drug acts. The original keyed option gives only part of the outline; the full slide also includes “drugs → clock.” This is an orientation question, not evidence that a student can yet explain a specific pharmacokinetic or clock-shifting mechanism.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc02.title: Question 2 — PART 1: Circadian Rhythms
l11-mc02.markdown:
This heading introduces the lecture's **foundation in circadian rhythms** before applying it to drugs. The following slides define internally generated near-24-hour rhythms, describe entrainment and phase shifts, and introduce central and peripheral clocks. Those concepts make the later examples of time-dependent drug responses interpretable.

However, the existing answer simply repeats a section title. It does not distinguish a circadian rhythm from another pattern or explain how a clock operates. The useful learning connection is that a later dosing-time effect could involve either drug handling or target sensitivity, and that a drug-induced change in activity need not itself be a phase shift. This item should be treated as an organizational prompt, not a substantive graded concept question.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc03.title: Question 3 — What Are Circadian Rhythms?
l11-mc03.markdown:
Circadian rhythms are **internally generated cycles with a period of approximately 24 hours**. Sleep–wake activity is a familiar example, but the lecture also emphasizes physiological processes throughout the body. A daily pattern alone does not prove an internal clock, because an external schedule can directly produce a repeating pattern.

The next slide provides two useful criteria: persistence under constant conditions and the capacity to be entrained by external cues. Together, these distinguish an endogenous rhythm from a response that merely follows light turning on or off. The answer's examples are therefore correct but incomplete without the endogenous and near-24-hour features. This distinction becomes essential when evaluating whether a drug changes the clock or only changes behavior temporarily.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc04.title: Question 4 — Core terminology
l11-mc04.markdown:
An **actogram** displays the timing of activity across successive days, making recurring patterns and shifts easier to see. Diurnal organisms are primarily active during the day, while nocturnal organisms are primarily active at night. Those labels describe when activity occurs, not whether the rhythm is internally generated.

To identify a circadian rhythm, the lecture also asks whether the pattern persists in constant conditions and can synchronize to an external cue. An actogram can help assess those properties, but interpretation depends on the lighting or other conditions represented. Do not confuse the graphical recording method with the underlying clock mechanism. The same type of plot can show normal entrainment, free-running activity, or a changed phase after an experimental manipulation.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc05.title: Question 5 — Evolution of Circadian Clocks Circadian clocks are present
l11-mc05.markdown:
The lecture places circadian clocks across **bacteria, plants, and animals**, emphasizing that biological timing is not unique to human sleep. The broad distribution supports the idea that anticipating regular environmental change is useful in many kinds of organisms.

The keyed option lists bacteria and plants but omits animals from the full slide. These examples do not establish that all species use an identical molecular clock, nor do they mean that every repeated behavior is circadian. The connection to pharmacology is conceptual: biological timing can be an intrinsic property of cells and tissues, rather than merely an imposed daily routine. Specific mechanisms and experimental findings still need to be interpreted in the species and tissue actually studied.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc06.title: Question 6 — Evolution of Circadian Clocks Anticipation of daily
l11-mc06.markdown:
A circadian clock can help an organism **anticipate predictable daily changes**, rather than respond only after those changes have occurred. The lecture lists light–dark transitions, social coordination, avoidance, and foraging as contexts in which appropriate timing may be advantageous.

Anticipation is the key distinction. For example, activity before a regularly scheduled event is not simply a reaction to that event happening. This connects the evolutionary discussion to food-anticipatory activity later in the lecture. The list describes possible functions of biological timing, not separate molecular mechanisms or proof that every rhythm has the same adaptive history. A developed answer explains the advantage of matching preparation and behavior to recurring environmental conditions.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc07.title: Question 7 — Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)
l11-mc07.markdown:
The **suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)** is presented as a coordinating clock that entrains to the light–dark cycle. The lesion comparison shows disruption of the normal temporal organization of sleep after SCN removal, linking this structure to the organization of daily rhythms rather than to the mere ability to sleep.

The later peripheral-clock material limits the phrase “master clock”: the SCN coordinates many rhythms but is not the sole generator of every cellular oscillation. The transplant sketch on this slide has inconsistent host/donor labels, so its details should not be used to infer precisely which graft or animal determines period without clarification. The reliable teaching point here is central coordination and light entrainment, not an unsupported reading of the mislabeled diagram.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc08.title: Question 8 — Food Anticipatory Activity (FAA)
l11-mc08.markdown:
Food-anticipatory activity is an **increase in activity before a predictable mealtime**, described in the lecture as occurring roughly one to three hours beforehand. Because the activity precedes feeding, it is not simply movement caused by eating or by the food's immediate presence.

The important experimental observation is persistence under some conditions without an intact SCN or with particular clock-gene manipulations. This challenges the idea that all timed behavior must be generated by the SCN's canonical clock mechanism. It does not establish that timing has no biological basis or that every clock-gene knockout leaves every rhythm unchanged. The result motivates consideration of food-related timing systems outside the usual SCN-centered account.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc09.title: Question 9 — Peripheral Clocks
l11-mc09.markdown:
Peripheral tissues can contain **cell-autonomous clocks**. The lecture describes the SCN as synchronizing these clocks rather than creating all of their oscillations. If central coordination is removed, individual rhythms can persist while drifting out of alignment with one another.

This distinction between generating and coordinating rhythms is crucial for pharmacology. A liver clock may influence metabolism even though the animal's overall daily organization depends on additional signals and tissues. The slide's gene-rhythmicity percentages summarize the study discussed in class; they should not be interpreted as every gene oscillating in every tissue at every moment. The central lesson is distributed rhythmicity with coordination, not a single clock issuing every molecular event directly.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc10.title: Question 10 — PART 2: How the clock changes drugs
l11-mc10.markdown:
This section changes the direction of explanation to **clock → drug response**. Circadian variation can affect the concentration of drug reaching a target or the target's sensitivity to that concentration. These are respectively pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic routes to a time-of-day effect.

A useful prediction is that an equal administered dose need not produce an equal exposure or effect at two biological times. However, this section title does not itself establish that any particular medication should be taken at night or in the morning. That requires drug-specific evidence. Because the keyed option only repeats the heading, this item is an organizational marker; it should not be counted as demonstrating understanding of the mechanisms that follow.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc11.title: Question 11 — Pharmacokinetics vs. Pharmacodynamics
l11-mc11.markdown:
**Pharmacokinetics asks what happens to the drug; pharmacodynamics asks how the drug acts on its targets.** Rhythms in gastric emptying, liver metabolism, or kidney filtration can change exposure. Rhythms in receptors or signaling can change the response even when exposure is comparable.

To interpret a time-of-day difference, first ask which quantity was measured. Different blood concentrations after the same dose point toward drug handling; different responses at comparable concentrations suggest target or signaling differences. Both processes can operate together. The lecture's distinction prevents the assumption that a stronger nighttime effect must always mean slower metabolism, or that a change in receptor expression is itself a pharmacokinetic effect.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc12.title: Question 12 — Absorption and distribution
l11-mc12.markdown:
Rhythms in **gastric emptying, intestinal blood flow, and lipid absorption** can alter how quickly an orally administered drug enters the circulation. Distribution can also vary when transport across barriers is rhythmic. The lecture's blood–brain barrier efflux example specifically comes from Drosophila.

The mechanism therefore concerns the path between administration and target exposure, not necessarily a change in receptor affinity. Faster absorption can alter the timing and height of a concentration peak, while efflux can influence access to a tissue. Preserve the experimental scope: findings in a fly barrier model do not automatically establish an identical rhythm for every human brain-active drug. Likewise, the lecture's daytime absorption statement is a course example, not a universal dosing rule.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc13.title: Question 13 — Pharmacodynamics
l11-mc13.markdown:
Pharmacodynamic rhythms concern **the biological target and its downstream response**. If receptor availability or signaling varies across the day, a given concentration of drug may have different effects at different biological times. This is distinct from having different concentrations because of absorption or clearance.

The counts of drugs with rhythmic targets are examples from the analysis cited in the lecture, not newly verified market statistics. The lecture emphasizes short-half-life drugs because a brief exposure samples a narrower time window; a sustained exposure may span more of the cycle.
