That provides a rationale for studying treatment timing, but it does not by itself show a clinical benefit for changing the timing of every drug with a rhythmic target.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc14.title: Question 14 — Chronotherapy in clinical practice
l11-mc14.markdown:
Chronotherapy examines whether **matching treatment timing to biological rhythms** improves benefit or reduces unwanted effects. The lecture uses cholesterol synthesis, nocturnal asthma symptoms, and morning stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis as examples of relevant timing relationships. Its IL-6 example links a night-associated physiological rhythm to symptoms experienced later.

The slide also gives a blood-pressure example with no difference, showing why the principle must be tested rather than assumed. These brief examples are not a complete set of prescribing instructions, and the statin statement does not distinguish every formulation or half-life. A sound answer explains the rationale and the need for drug- and outcome-specific evidence, rather than concluding that evening administration is generally superior.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc15.title: Question 15 — PART 3: How drugs change the clock
l11-mc15.markdown:
This section reverses the preceding causal direction: **drugs → clock**. A drug might alter the input that resets a clock, act on clock-related signaling, or change behavior that itself provides a timing signal. Those possibilities are different from the clock changing drug metabolism.

A central interpretive problem is distinguishing a shift in rhythmic timing from a temporary change in activity, alertness, or sleep. The later alcohol, non-photic arousal, caffeine, and melatonin examples illustrate different routes and measurements. The existing answer is only a section title, so it does not test these distinctions. Its proper role is to orient the reader; a substantive assessment should ask which mechanism or observation supports a drug-induced timing change.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc16.title: Question 16 — Photic input to the SCN
l11-mc16.markdown:
The lecture traces photic input through **intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, the retinohypothalamic tract, and the SCN**. It identifies glutamate as a transmitter in this resetting pathway and uses NMDA agonist and antagonist findings to connect synaptic signaling to phase shifts.

Blocking a receptor involved in light signaling can reduce a light-induced clock shift without necessarily abolishing every aspect of vision or every clock rhythm. The slide's “not rods and cones” phrase emphasizes the identified pathway, but the supplied lecture alone is not sufficient to establish an absolute absence of all rod/cone influence. The key mechanism to explain is retinal input → glutamatergic signaling → SCN resetting, with drug effects assessed on the resulting phase change.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc17.title: Question 17 — Non-photic arousal
l11-mc17.markdown:
A drug-associated clock change may be **mediated by the behavior the drug produces**, rather than by a direct action on the clock's molecular machinery. The lecture's non-photic-arousal example compares phase shifts under conditions in which the animal's behavioral response is allowed or constrained.

That comparison matters because observing a shift after drug administration alone leaves several causal routes open. A drug could alter arousal, movement, or other non-light signals that then influence rhythmic timing. The magnitude and direction can also depend on circadian phase. A strong interpretation therefore separates drug exposure, behavioral change, and measured phase shift, rather than treating every post-drug change in an actogram as direct binding to an SCN clock target.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc18.title: Question 18 — Non-SCN clocks in the brain
l11-mc18.markdown:
The lecture uses **rhythmic behavior surviving SCN lesions** to motivate consideration of timing systems outside the SCN. Food-anticipatory activity is associated with a food-entrainable oscillator account, while methamphetamine-associated rhythms are discussed under MASCO. It also reports persistence of MASCO under some canonical clock-gene disruptions.

The inference is that the usual SCN-centered transcriptional-clock account does not explain every observed rhythm. It is not that methamphetamine repairs the SCN or that all rhythms are independent of clock genes. The observations concern particular behaviors, interventions, and experimental preparations. Distinguish the existence of a surviving rhythm from precise knowledge of its anatomical generator or complete molecular mechanism; the slide does not establish all of those details.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc19.title: Question 19 — Stimulants
l11-mc19.markdown:
The stimulant examples connect **clock-related genes to behavioral responses to drugs**, including sensitization and conditioned place preference. Sensitization is a changed response across repeated exposures; CPP tests learned preference for a context associated with drug administration. These are related but different outcomes.

The lecture's genetic comparisons suggest that particular clock genes contribute to the responses measured in the cited experiments. They do not show that possessing a gene inevitably causes addiction or that every stimulant effect requires the same clock pathway. Nor does a changed CPP score directly measure subjective pleasure. Interpret each graph in terms of the manipulated gene, the comparison group, and the behavioral endpoint, keeping the lecture's experimental results distinct from broader claims about humans.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc20.title: Question 20 — Caffeine
l11-mc20.markdown:
The lecture's caffeine example concerns a **delay in rhythmic phase**, not merely feeling more awake after caffeine. A delay means that a recurring event in the rhythm occurs later relative to its previous timing. The actogram is used to visualize that change across successive cycles.

The approximate 40-minute value and bright-light comparison refer to the conditions of the example presented, not a fixed effect of every cup of coffee at any time. Circadian phase, exposure conditions, and the measured rhythm all matter. The key distinction is between an acute stimulant effect and a lasting shift in timing: those effects may be related, but observing one does not automatically demonstrate the other.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 25. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc21.title: Question 21 — Takeaways
l11-mc21.markdown:
The lecture's takeaways combine **distributed clocks, coordination, and two-way drug interactions**. Cellular clocks can oscillate locally, while the SCN helps synchronize the wider system. Rhythmic drug handling and target responses can then change the effect of a dose administered at different times.

Drugs can also alter timing through photic signaling or non-photic routes, including changes in behavior. The opening question about the same pill at 8 a.m. versus 8 p.m. is therefore answered at two levels: the molecule is the same, but the physiological setting may differ. The lesson is to identify the mechanism and biological time involved, not simply to add clock time as an unexplained label to a drug effect.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 27. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc22.title: Question 22 — Integration: Overview
l11-mc22.markdown:
The overview integrates **endogenous timing with drug action in both directions**. A clock-dependent change in liver metabolism is an example of timing changing drug exposure; a drug-dependent change in the response to light is an example of a drug changing clock resetting. These should not be described as the same causal process.

The circadian review supplies the distinction between phase, entrainment, and immediate behavioral output needed to interpret both examples. The existing keyed option gives a fragment of the outline, so it is not a complete mechanistic answer. Use this repeated overview item as a synthesis prompt: specify what changes first, what is measured afterward, and whether the proposed pathway involves pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, or an input to the clock.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc23.title: Question 23 — Integration: PART 1: Circadian Rhythms
l11-mc23.markdown:
The first part supplies the **criteria for recognizing an internally generated circadian rhythm**. Persistence in constant conditions distinguishes a clock-driven pattern from simple tracking of an external event, while entrainment shows that the internal timing system can synchronize with environmental cues.

Those criteria matter when a later drug experiment changes sleep or activity. A temporary increase in movement is not automatically a change in the rhythm's phase or period. The repeated section-heading answer does not test that reasoning and should not be used as a stand-alone mastery item. A useful interpretation of the integration prompt is to explain how the foundational definitions constrain claims that a drug has “changed the clock.”

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-mc24.title: Question 24 — Integration: What Are Circadian Rhythms?
l11-mc24.markdown:
Sleep–wake cycles and physiological processes illustrate that **circadian timing organizes both behavior and internal function**. The common feature emphasized by the lecture is an endogenous cycle near 24 hours, not the particular tissue or behavioral output being recorded.

This connects directly to chronopharmacology: a rhythm in sleep can be visible, while rhythms in metabolic enzymes or drug targets may be less obvious but still relevant to drug effects. The two should not be assumed to have identical timing merely because both are circadian. A good answer adds the defining criteria to the examples in the key and explains why repeated daily measurements can reveal patterns that a single measurement at one time would miss.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Core terminology continued…
l11-sa01.markdown:
A **zeitgeber** is an external timing cue that can entrain an internal rhythm. Entrainment means synchronization with that recurring cue, not destruction of the endogenous oscillator. A phase advance moves the timing of a recurring event earlier; a phase delay moves it later. A phase-response curve relates the timing of a stimulus within the internal cycle to the resulting phase shift.

The lecture's light example shows why timing matters: early subjective-night exposure is associated with delays, late subjective-night exposure with advances, and mid-subjective-day exposure with little effect in the illustrated account. The same type of cue can therefore have different consequences depending on biological phase. Connect this to the broad occurrence of clocks by explaining that internal oscillators can anticipate regular environments while still adjusting to external timing. For pharmacology, this means that a drug affecting a resetting pathway cannot be interpreted without knowing when in the internal cycle it was given.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Clock Genes Transcription-Translation Feedback Loop (TTFL)
l11-sa02.markdown:
The lecture describes a **transcription–translation feedback loop** involving CLOCK and BMAL1 followed by PER and CRY. The latter proteins accumulate, repress the processes supporting their production, and are degraded, allowing the cycle to restart. The delay among transcription, protein accumulation, inhibition, and degradation supports an oscillation rather than a permanently on or off state.

Connect the loop to peripheral clocks through the idea of cell autonomy. Many tissues can generate rhythmic activity locally; the SCN's coordinating role helps align those clocks rather than supplying every oscillation directly. When coordination is lost, rhythms may persist but drift apart. A strong answer therefore distinguishes the mechanism producing a cellular rhythm from the mechanisms synchronizing multiple tissues. The source presents the loop as approximately daily, not as a literal timer in which each isolated step takes a fixed fraction of 24 hours in every cell.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Metabolism and excretion
l11-sa03.markdown:
Rhythmic liver enzymes and kidney filtration can produce **time-dependent drug clearance**, a pharmacokinetic effect. The lecture's mouse acetaminophen example links a toxicity rhythm to the liver clock, while its barbiturate example shows that an observed duration of sleep can vary with administration time. These are examples of why equal doses do not guarantee equal concentration–time profiles or behavioral durations.

Pharmacodynamics is a separate possibility: rhythmic receptors or signaling can change the effect produced by a comparable concentration. A complete comparison therefore asks whether the clock changes exposure, response to exposure, or both. Do not infer the cause of every behavioral time-of-day difference solely from the behavior itself. The mouse liver-clock experiment supports a specific mechanism in that preparation, not a universal schedule for human medication. Explain the causal chain and preserve the species and outcome limitations of the lecture evidence.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Alcohol
l11-sa04.markdown:
The alcohol example shows a **reduction in a light-induced phase advance** under the experimental conditions illustrated. The dose comparison indicates that the magnitude of the interference varies with alcohol exposure. Importantly, blocking or reducing a response to a resetting cue is not necessarily the same as producing an equal and opposite phase shift on its own.

Connect this to non-photic arousal by distinguishing causal routes. Alcohol may alter how photic input affects clock timing in the illustrated experiment, whereas another drug's apparent clock effect may depend on the behavior or arousal it produces. To distinguish these explanations, an experiment must separate drug exposure, light conditions, behavioral opportunity, and the subsequent rhythmic phase measurement. A strong answer reports what the graph actually compares and does not claim that every sedative directly shifts the SCN. The lecture supports an experimental principle, not advice to use alcohol for sleep or circadian adjustment.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — Melatonin
l11-sa05.markdown:
A **chronobiotic** changes the timing of a biological rhythm. The lecture uses melatonin to emphasize that the time of administration relative to internal circadian phase can determine the direction and size of the shift. Its phase-response curve therefore provides more information than simply knowing a dose or whether the person becomes sleepy.

The dexamethasone comparison introduces tissue specificity: the lecture describes a shift in liver-clock timing without a corresponding SCN shift. This connects to the larger conclusion that clocks are distributed and coordinated, rather than one identical oscillator repeated everywhere. A developed response should distinguish shifting a clock from temporarily changing a physiological output and should explain why changing one tissue's rhythm need not reset all tissues equally. The figures illustrate mechanisms and timing dependence; they do not provide a personal dosing schedule, and the supplied lecture alone is not a complete clinical guide.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 26. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l11-sa06.title: Short Essay 6 — Integration: Overview and PART 1: Circadian Rhythms
l11-sa06.markdown:
The overview and the Part 1 heading are **levels of organization, not competing biological mechanisms**. The overview lays out the full lecture: circadian foundations, clock effects on drugs, and drug effects on clocks. Part 1 develops the first of those components by defining rhythms, entrainment, phase shifts, and the organization of central and peripheral clocks.

Their connection is that the foundational concepts are needed to interpret the later experiments. For example, a change in activity after a drug can only be called a phase shift if its timing relative to the ongoing rhythm is established; a different drug effect across the day can reflect rhythmic exposure or sensitivity. The original answer panel merely repeats headings and cannot serve as a full model essay. Treat this item as an organizational synthesis exercise, or revise it into a scientific comparison before formal grading. It should not be made to imply a substantive distinction that the sources do not contain.

**Source:** Lecture 11 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. No assigned textbook chapter was provided for this lecture.

**Review:** [Lecture 11 study guide](../study-guides/lecture11.qmd).

l12-mc01.title: Question 1 — Most humans are regular users
l12-mc01.markdown:
The lecture's list includes **therapeutic, recreational, and commonly consumed psychoactive substances**. A psychoactive drug affects mental processes or behavior; the term does not, by itself, specify whether use is prescribed, legal, harmful, or addictive. Caffeine is one familiar example, but the complete slide also includes several medication and recreational-drug classes.

This sets up the distinction between exposure and addiction. Regular use does not automatically demonstrate impaired control, continued use despite serious harm, or other features of a substance use disorder. The question should therefore be read as identifying the breadth of psychoactive-drug use, not as claiming that everyone using a listed substance has an addiction or that all listed substances have the same risks.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc02.title: Question 2 — Most humans use psychoactive drugs without experiencing addiction
l12-mc02.markdown:
The main point is **drug use and addiction are not equivalent categories**. The lecture's percentages illustrate that many people use psychoactive substances without developing the persistent, harmful pattern being discussed. A lower population frequency does not mean that addiction has minor consequences for those affected.

The numerical estimates belong to the lecture's source context. The slide does not provide enough information to treat them as current universal prevalence rates across all countries, age groups, or definitions of addiction. A sound explanation prioritizes the conceptual contrast and the need for a defined denominator. It should not turn the figures into either a guarantee of safety for an individual or a claim that ordinary exposure inevitably progresses to addiction.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc03.title: Question 3 — Addiction is a nuanced term surrounded by stigma
l12-mc03.markdown:
The terms in the slide describe **overlapping but nonidentical phenomena and social categories**. Physical dependence involves adaptation and possible withdrawal, while addiction concerns a broader pattern of impaired control and harmful persistence. A person can develop physical dependence during treatment without that alone establishing addiction.

The lecture also distinguishes self-stigma, social stigma, and structural stigma: negative beliefs can be internalized, expressed by others, or embedded in institutions and access to support. Person-first language helps avoid reducing someone to a diagnosis or behavior. The explanation should therefore do more than list alternative labels. It should connect precise terminology to better interpretation of evidence and less stigmatizing responses, while rejecting the simplistic claim that addiction is merely a failure of willpower.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc04.title: Question 4 — William S. Burroughs, Junky
l12-mc04.markdown:
The literary passage illustrates **an experienced transition from experimentation to a felt need for continued use**. It contributes a first-person perspective on a process that may not begin with an intention to become dependent. Its emphasis on sickness and need connects to the later discussion of withdrawal and negative reinforcement.

However, a memoir is not a controlled study or a universal biological timetable. The specific duration and frequency of use described in the passage must not be treated as a safe threshold before dependence can occur. Nor should its explanation in terms of weak competing motivations be accepted as a complete causal model of addiction. Use it as an illustration to interpret alongside the lecture's biological, psychological, and social framework, not as clinical evidence.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc05.title: Question 5 — What do we really want to know about drug addiction?
l12-mc05.markdown:
The lecture organizes addiction research around **risk, causes, and treatment**. Risk asks why some individuals or circumstances are associated with a greater probability of developing problems. Causal mechanisms ask how drug exposure, learning, adaptation, and environment help generate and maintain those problems. Treatment asks which interventions improve relevant outcomes.

These questions require different kinds of evidence. A risk factor is not necessarily a sufficient cause, and identifying a neural change does not automatically establish an effective treatment. The keyed option names only the first two questions; the full slide also asks what can be done to treat addiction. A developed response explains the relationship among these aims rather than assuming that one statistical association answers all three.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc06.title: Question 6 — Who is particularly at risk?
l12-mc06.markdown:
Risk varies with **the substance, pattern of exposure, developmental stage, health, and social environment**. The lecture discusses sex-related patterns, adolescent initiation, and co-occurring mental-health conditions, then adds genetic and environmental influences on the following slide. Its “telescoping” example concerns a potentially faster progression through stages in some groups and contexts.

None of these associations makes an individual's outcome inevitable. Higher rates in a demographic group do not establish an inherent moral or biological defect, and earlier initiation can be entangled with longer exposure and other circumstances. The key's short male/female comparison is therefore only a fragment of the lecture's risk discussion. A strong interpretation keeps the drug-specific and contextual qualifications rather than ranking whole groups as uniformly vulnerable.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc07.title: Question 7 — What causes drug addiction?
l12-mc07.markdown:
The lecture emphasizes **changes in brain function and motivation** that can increase drug seeking. Drugs act on neural systems, and repeated exposure interacts with adaptation and learning. This helps explain why stopping is not adequately described as a simple choice made in an unchanged motivational system.

The mechanism should still be placed within the broader risk discussion. Genetics, stress, adversity, and social conditions can influence exposure and responses, so a neural account need not exclude psychological or environmental causes. The presence of a brain difference also does not by itself establish whether it preceded drug use or resulted from it. The key identifies one explanatory level, not a complete claim that every case has the same cause or irreversible outcome.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc08.title: Question 8 — Features of drug addiction
l12-mc08.markdown:
The lecture lists a **pattern of interacting features**: rewarding effects, craving, tolerance, escalation, dependence, relapse, and continued use despite adverse consequences. Each term describes something different. Tolerance is a reduced response after repeated exposure; dependence concerns adaptation and withdrawal; craving is a motivational experience; relapse concerns renewed use after reduction or cessation.

No single feature on the list should be substituted automatically for the whole concept of addiction. In particular, tolerance or withdrawal can occur without the broader pattern of harmful loss of control. The answer panel's first two terms are therefore incomplete as an explanation. The important skill is to distinguish the features and show how they can contribute to a persistent cycle rather than merely memorize a list.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc09.title: Question 9 — Opponent Process Theory of Drug Addiction
l12-mc09.markdown:
Opponent-process theory explains how **compensatory responses can oppose an initial drug effect**. With repeated exposure, the opposing process can become more influential. The same dose then produces less of the original net effect, and when the drug is absent the compensatory state may remain, producing withdrawal or negative affect.

This supports the lecture's transition from taking a drug for a pleasurable effect to taking it to relieve an unpleasant state. Relief can reinforce further use even when the original pleasure has diminished. The theory is informative but not exhaustive: it does not by itself explain every initial exposure, all cue-triggered seeking, or relapse long after acute withdrawal. The lecture explicitly develops those limitations rather than treating withdrawal as the sole cause of addiction.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc10.title: Question 10 — Stages of drug addiction (a common framework) as related to opponent process theory
l12-mc10.markdown:
The three-stage framework links **binge/intoxication, withdrawal/negative affect, and preoccupation/anticipation**. Intoxication emphasizes drug effects and reinforcement; withdrawal emphasizes the negative state associated with adaptation; anticipation emphasizes craving and processes that motivate renewed seeking.

The diagram represents a recurring interaction, not a rigid sequence that every person completes in exactly the same way. Opponent processes help explain the shift in motivation between intoxication and withdrawal, while learning and cue effects contribute to anticipation. The original keyed option names only two stages, so a complete explanation must include the third. The model is useful because it organizes changing motives and neural processes without equating all drug use with the same clinical trajectory.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc11.title: Question 11 — BUT opponent processes can’t be the whole story Withdrawal
l12-mc11.markdown:
The slide challenges the idea that **relieving acute withdrawal explains all continued drug seeking**. Withdrawal has a time course, while craving, cue responses, and relapse can persist beyond the most obvious acute symptoms. The examples also show that withdrawal patterns differ across substances.

The original answer contains only a heading and figure label, so it supplies no actual explanation. The conceptual answer is that opponent processes contribute to addiction but need to be combined with mechanisms of reinforcement, associative learning, and persistent motivational change. The timelines in the figure are illustrative and should not be used to predict an individual's withdrawal course or to plan unsupervised detoxification. The lesson is a limitation of the theory, not a clinical schedule.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-mc12.title: Question 12 — Associative Learning Principles Used in Addiction Models
l12-mc12.markdown:
Operant conditioning concerns how **the consequences of an action change the likelihood of that action recurring**. A drug can positively reinforce taking behavior through its effects. Relief from an aversive state can negatively reinforce behavior; “negative” means removal of something aversive, not punishment.

Pavlovian learning supplies a complementary route: cues repeatedly associated with a drug can acquire motivational significance. Such cues may influence seeking even when no drug is immediately present. The lecture's conditioned-reinforcement and incentive-salience terms therefore should not be reduced to the pleasurable effect of a dose alone. A strong answer distinguishes the action–consequence relationship from the cue–outcome relationship and explains how both can maintain behavior.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Drugs, addiction, harm Nutt et al., 2007
l12-sa01.markdown:
The figure compares drugs along **dependence-related and physical-harm dimensions**, rather than treating “drug danger” as one self-evident quantity. A substance can occupy a different relative position depending on which outcome is measured. The accompanying ranking and legal-class colors invite comparison between a harm assessment and a regulatory category, but those categories are not the same measurement.

Connect this to the lecture's research questions by distinguishing potential harm, probability of problematic use, and consequences for a particular person or population. Dependence potential does not directly equal prevalence, and a group-level ranking does not predict the outcome of one exposure. The figure is a historical analysis attributed to Nutt and colleagues, not a newly established universal league table. A complete response should explain its axes, identify what comparison they permit, and state the limits of inference. The original answer panel only names the figure and therefore needs this substantive interpretation.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Example of tolerance: caffeine Withdrawal
l12-sa02.markdown:
The caffeine illustrations provide a **receptor-adaptation example of tolerance and withdrawal**. The lecture depicts caffeine blocking adenosine-related signaling, followed by a compensatory increase in receptor availability during repeated exposure. When caffeine is removed, the compensatory system is no longer opposed in the same way, helping explain a rebound state.

Connect that sequence to opponent-process theory: the initial drug effect is countered by an adaptation, reducing the net effect of the same exposure. In the drug's absence, the adaptation can contribute to an effect opposite to the original response. The diagram is a simplified teaching model, not a complete description of every caffeine effect or individual difference. A strong answer names the initial action, the compensatory change, the resulting tolerance, and what happens during withdrawal. Finally, distinguish this physiological adaptation from addiction: tolerance and withdrawal alone do not establish the broader harmful pattern discussed elsewhere in the lecture.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l12-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Motivation for… Brain Stimulation?
l12-sa03.markdown:
The brain-stimulation example shows that an animal can **perform an action to obtain electrical stimulation**, allowing investigators to study reinforcement without first administering a recreational drug. Repeated lever pressing demonstrates the consequence's reinforcing value in that experimental arrangement; it is not a direct verbal report of pleasure.

The lecture connects this research to dopamine projections from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens and asks whether dopamine should simply be equated with pleasure. The question mark matters: motivated responding and subjective liking are not identical observations. The broader connection to psychoactive-drug use is that drugs can interact with systems governing reinforcement and motivation, but ordinary use does not automatically become addiction. A developed response explains the action–consequence contingency, identifies the pathway discussed, and avoids the circular claim that a region is a “pleasure center” merely because an animal works to stimulate it.

**Source:** Lecture 12 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9.

**Review:** [Lecture 12 study guide](../study-guides/lecture12.qmd).

l13-mc01.title: Question 1 — Origin of The Dopamine = Pleasure Fallacy: James Old’s “Pleasure Centers in The Brain”
l13-mc01.markdown:
The self-stimulation example helped establish that **brain stimulation can reinforce an action**. An animal repeatedly performs the action that produces stimulation, making the relationship between behavior and consequence observable. The historical “pleasure center” interpretation went further by treating that responding as evidence of a particular subjective experience.

The lecture calls attention to the inferential gap: a reinforcing consequence is not automatically a direct measurement of pleasure, and electrical stimulation does not isolate dopamine as the only active mechanism. The keyed answer supplies a historical citation rather than the concept. The learning objective is to distinguish what the experiment measures—sustained responding for stimulation—from the stronger hedonic interpretation that the lecture later challenges.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc02.title: Question 2 — Renaissance of The Pleasure Fallacy: Roy Wise’s Hedonic Theory of Addiction
l13-mc02.markdown:
The hedonic account presented on this slide associates **dopamine signaling with the pleasurable effects of rewards and addictive drugs**. The drug-versus-natural-reward comparison illustrates why increased dopamine was interpreted as a common basis for reinforcing experiences.

However, the lecture presents this as an account to examine critically, not as its final conclusion. Increased dopamine does not, by itself, demonstrate increased subjective pleasure. The subsequent slides distinguish wanting, learning, and motivated responding from liking. A correct explanation therefore identifies what the historical theory proposes and why the lecture questions a simple dopamine-equals-pleasure equation. The quoted theory in the answer should not be silently converted into an endorsed, universal description of dopamine function.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc03.title: Question 3 — Do you notice a pattern?
l13-mc03.markdown:
The graphs compare **extracellular dopamine-related measurements after different drugs**, including stimulants, nicotine, morphine, and ethanol. Their shared pattern of increased dopamine in relevant reward-related regions motivates investigation of a common system even though the drugs have different primary molecular targets.

The common neurochemical response does not make the drugs pharmacologically identical or prove that dopamine concentration directly measures pleasure. The question's original answer merely asks the reader to notice a pattern and names a study; it does not state the pattern itself. A substantive response should identify the measured variable, compare the traces with baseline, and distinguish the shared downstream response from the distinct mechanisms producing it. Avoid treating an illustrative graph comparison as a complete causal theory of addiction.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc04.title: Question 4 — Drug Users as Hedonists - Social Implications
l13-mc04.markdown:
The slide examines how a **pleasure-only explanation can become a moralizing account of drug use**. If addiction is portrayed simply as choosing immediate pleasure over everything else, responses may emphasize blame or punishment while overlooking adaptation, cue-driven motivation, and circumstances that limit access to support.

The quotation in the key is the view being criticized, not a scientifically established description of people who use drugs. Nor does the slide prove that all members of a society hold the same opinion or that one belief explains every policy decision. Its purpose is to connect explanatory models with stigma and public responses. A sound answer identifies that connection without endorsing the stereotype or replacing a complex condition with a judgment about character.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc05.title: Question 5 — Contemporary psychiatry considers addiction to be a chronic, relapsing disease of the brain
l13-mc05.markdown:
The lecture emphasizes **persistent, difficult-to-control drug seeking and recurrent relapse**, rather than defining addiction solely by pleasure or acute withdrawal. This makes it possible to ask why seeking continues even when the pleasurable effect has diminished or immediate withdrawal symptoms have ended.

The brain-disease framing identifies neural mechanisms as important, but it need not exclude learning, social conditions, or recovery. Likewise, describing a disorder as often chronic or relapsing does not mean that every individual follows an inevitable lifelong course. The key contrasts explanatory emphases; it should not be read as proving that reinforcement has become irrelevant. Later cue and sensitization examples extend, rather than erase, the earlier account of how drug-taking behavior is learned and maintained.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc06.title: Question 6 — Diagnostic criteria are informed by empirical theory Positive
l13-mc06.markdown:
The diagram distinguishes **experimental theories from diagnostic criteria**. Positive reinforcement concerns obtaining rewarding consequences; negative reinforcement concerns relief from aversive states; incentive sensitization concerns increased cue-triggered wanting; habit accounts concern increasingly cue-driven patterns of seeking. These explain different aspects of behavior rather than functioning as interchangeable diagnostic labels.

The cue examples also broaden the environment: objects can act as external cues, bodily arousal as internal cues, and time of day as a temporal cue. A theory helps design a test of a proposed mechanism, while clinical criteria organize recognition of a problematic pattern. The original key combines many labels, so the task is to explain their relationships, not imply that any single cue response is sufficient to diagnose addiction.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc07.title: Question 7 — Addictive potential depends on route of administration
l13-mc07.markdown:
The diagram links **speed of drug delivery and duration of action to reinforcing potential**. A rapid rise in brain exposure can produce a more immediate consequence of taking the drug, strengthening the connection between the act and its effects. Slower, more sustained delivery can create a different exposure pattern even for a related substance.

This is a pharmacokinetic contribution to addiction risk, not a claim that route alone determines whether a person develops addiction. Dose, history, setting, and other factors also matter. The original answer is only a topic placeholder. The substantive concept is the time course connecting administration to brain effect, illustrated by the different formulations and delivery routes in the slide, not instructions for changing how a drug is used.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc08.title: Question 8 — Reward vs. reinforcement vs. relapse
l13-mc08.markdown:
A **reinforcer** is defined by its effect on behavior: its consequence increases the likelihood of the preceding action. The lecture uses “drug reward” for a positive subjective experience, such as euphoria. Those measures can be related, but one should not be substituted automatically for the other.

Reinstatement procedures model another question: after drug delivery has stopped and responding has declined, can cues, stress, or a drug exposure renew seeking? Renewed responding is an experimental outcome relevant to relapse, not an exact reproduction of every human relapse episode. The distinction helps interpret evidence: lever pressing measures behavior, self-reported pleasure measures experience, and reinstatement measures renewed seeking under specified conditions.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc09.title: Question 9 — Factors That Influence the Development and Maintenance of Drug Misuse and Addiction (8 of 18)
l13-mc09.markdown:
The proposed progression from impulsive to compulsive use involves **changes in the motivational state maintained by repeated exposure**. The lecture describes recruitment of an antireward system and a neuroadapted state in which avoiding negative affect may become increasingly important.

That account explains why continued use need not mean continued enjoyment of the original intensity. It also has limits: physical dependence does not fully explain relapse after detoxification, and cue learning, stress, and other factors can maintain seeking. The wording “may be due to” matters because this is a theoretical explanation, not an observation that directly identifies every causal step. Describe the proposed adaptation and its behavioral consequence without presenting one pathway as sufficient for all cases.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc10.title: Question 10 — A Koobian view of addiction
l13-mc10.markdown:
The three-stage account organizes addiction as a **repeating interaction of anticipation, binge/intoxication, and withdrawal-related negative effects**. The order in which a diagram begins is less important than understanding how each state can feed into renewed use. Drug effects can reinforce taking, adaptation can make absence aversive, and anticipation can organize further seeking.

The lecture also questions whether this account fully explains cue-triggered craving. Its comment that the theory “ignores craving” should not be taken literally, because preoccupation and anticipation are explicitly included. The useful critique concerns how craving is explained mechanistically, not whether the word appears in the model. A complete answer identifies all three stages and states both the model's contribution and its limits.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc11.title: Question 11 — Incentive sensitization theory of addiction
l13-mc11.markdown:
Incentive sensitization distinguishes **wanting a reward from liking its experience**. Repeated exposure can increase the motivational impact of drug-related cues even while tolerance reduces some pleasurable effects. Stronger seeking therefore need not imply a proportionately greater high.

“Incentive salience” describes the motivational significance acquired by a cue or reward, not simply conscious knowledge that it is available. This helps explain why familiar places, objects, or internal states can provoke seeking after a period without drug use. The theory does not claim that every person becomes sensitized or that pleasure never matters. Its distinctive contribution is to make dissociation between cue-driven motivation and hedonic enjoyment a central, testable possibility.
