**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc12.title: Question 12 — Dopamine and reward prediction error
l13-mc12.markdown:
The lecture's reward-prediction-error example compares **what happens with what was expected**. Initially, an unexpected reward is associated with a dopamine-neuron response. After learning, the response shifts toward a cue predicting that reward. If the expected reward is omitted, activity decreases around the time the reward should have occurred.

This pattern is not a simple meter of how much reward is being consumed. The same delivered reward can evoke different responses depending on prediction, and a cue can evoke a response before consumption. That supports a role in learning and expectation. The slide's “go silent” wording summarizes the illustrated decrease; it should not be generalized to every dopamine neuron or all activity in the entire dopamine system.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc13.title: Question 13 — Dopamine Facilitates Learning and Evokes Craving: A Role for Drug Cues in Relapse
l13-mc13.markdown:
The slide connects **learned cues, dopamine responses, and reported craving**. Its adapted prediction diagram illustrates how a response can become associated with the predictor rather than only the outcome. The accompanying human scatterplot relates cue-associated dopamine release to craving scores.

The correlation supports a relationship but does not, by itself, prove that dopamine release is the sole cause of craving or that the people with the strongest response are generally superior learners. The slide's final question about learning propensity is explicitly a hypothesis for discussion. The original answer mostly repeats figure labels, so the substantive explanation must distinguish the behavioral/neurochemical measurements from that broader interpretation. Cues can influence motivation without requiring immediate drug consumption.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc14.title: Question 14 — Pharmacokinetics of cocaine
l13-mc14.markdown:
Cocaine's route of administration influences **how rapidly exposure rises**, while metabolism and excretion help determine how it declines. The lecture contrasts rapid delivery with slower absorption and notes that the subjective effect can end well before all detectable metabolites have disappeared.

This distinction explains why detecting benzoylecgonine in urine is not equivalent to showing that someone is currently experiencing the same acute high. The slide's approximate duration is a teaching summary, not a fixed duration for all routes, doses, and individuals. It also notes cocaethylene formation when cocaine and alcohol are combined, illustrating that metabolism can create an active product rather than merely terminate drug action. These mechanisms do not imply that combining substances is safe.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc15.title: Question 15 — Pharmacodynamics of cocaine
l13-mc15.markdown:
Cocaine blocks the **plasma-membrane transporters for dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin**, reducing reuptake after release. Transmitter remains available outside cells for longer or at higher concentrations, increasing its opportunity to act on receptors. The drug is therefore not simply a direct agonist at dopamine receptors.

The lecture emphasizes dopamine-transporter inhibition in the behavioral and reinforcing effects, while other monoamines contribute to the wider profile. The phrase “increases rate of transmission” is shorthand; transporter blockade changes transmitter clearance, and the final effect depends on receptor types, feedback, and circuit location. This differs from amphetamine's prominent transporter-mediated releasing action, which is discussed later. Identify the blocked step rather than equating all stimulant mechanisms.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc16.title: Question 16 — Subjective effects of cocaine)
l13-mc16.markdown:
The lecture describes subjective effects such as **euphoria, heightened energy, and self-confidence**, with rapid delivery associated with a more abrupt “rush.” These experiences can contribute to reinforcing use, but their intensity and quality depend on exposure and circumstances.

The following qualification is important: effects described as positive at one point can become unpleasant with higher exposure or prolonged use, including anxiety, irritability, or other adverse states. A report of feeling energetic is not evidence that normal physiological limits have disappeared or that performance is safely improved. This item concerns subjective experience; the later locomotor, stereotypy, and cardiovascular examples use different outcomes and should not be treated as identical measures of the same effect.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc17.title: Question 17 — Peripheral physiological effects of cocaine
l13-mc17.markdown:
“Sympathomimetic” means that cocaine produces effects resembling **increased sympathetic activation**, including faster heart rate, vasoconstriction, elevated blood pressure, and increased temperature. Its interference with norepinephrine handling helps connect the molecular mechanism to these peripheral consequences.

The same drug also acts in the CNS, where agitation, paranoia, and other psychological effects may occur. The lecture separates these levels to show why a drug that changes mood can also pose serious cardiovascular and neurological hazards. Stronger arousal is not equivalent to healthier function. The key's physiological and behavioral lists should be organized by mechanism and target system rather than memorized as unrelated symptoms or assumed to occur identically after every exposure.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 22. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc18.title: Question 18 — Dopamine mediates the behavioural response to cocaine
l13-mc18.markdown:
The table combines **regional manipulation with different behavioral endpoints**. In its examples, nucleus-accumbens interventions affect locomotor activation and reinforcement, while dorsal-striatal interventions are associated with stereotyped behavior. Local drug effects and lesion effects provide complementary evidence about the involvement of these pathways.

The contrast matters because “dopamine mediates cocaine behavior” is too broad unless the region and behavior are specified. Increased movement, repetitive stereotypy, and working to obtain a drug are different measurements. Lesions can also influence baseline behavior and other functions, so reduced responding should not automatically be interpreted as a selective loss of pleasure. A complete reading matches each manipulation to its anatomical site and measured consequence instead of collapsing the whole table into one reward-center claim.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 23. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc19.title: Question 19 — DA receptor subtypes contribute to the effects of cocaine
l13-mc19.markdown:
Subtype-selective antagonists help test **which dopamine receptors contribute to a measured response**. However, the original key overstates the example by saying both D2 and D3 are required for locomotor stimulation. The lecture's own graph labels, consistent with Chapter 12 of the full textbook, show reduced cocaine-related locomotion after D2 blockade but increased locomotion after D3 blockade.

Those opposite directions imply different contributions, not identical requirements. The knockout comparisons concern self-administration, a separate endpoint: D1-deficient mice do not self-administer in the cited account, while D2/D3 manipulations alter rather than simply eliminate responding. This question requires instructor review because its keyed claim conflicts with the displayed evidence. The correct reasoning must preserve both receptor subtype and behavioral measure.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 24. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc20.title: Question 20 — Most people who try cocaine do not become addicted
l13-mc20.markdown:
The lecture distinguishes **trying cocaine from developing a persistent use disorder**. Initial experiences can be aversive, and cost, availability, expectations, social circumstances, and other factors can discourage repeated use. Exposure therefore does not determine one inevitable trajectory.

The same slide also describes escalation, binge patterns, cue effects, and incubation of craving in those who develop problems. “Incubation” emphasizes that craving or relapse vulnerability can increase during abstinence in the discussed models, rather than necessarily fading as acute withdrawal resolves. The route-progression description is a course example, not a universal sequence followed by every individual. A sound explanation considers both factors limiting repeated use and processes that can maintain seeking once learned.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 25. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc21.title: Question 21 — Cocaine produces both tolerance and sensitization
l13-mc21.markdown:
Tolerance and sensitization are **different changes in a specified response**, not mutually exclusive labels for an entire drug. Tolerance means a reduced effect with repeated exposure; sensitization means an enhanced response. Cocaine can produce different patterns depending on the endpoint, exposure schedule, and interval since the last administration.

The lecture contrasts long-access patterns with more sustained exposure and intermittent patterns producing repeated concentration peaks. It associates these with different transporter-related adaptations and behavioral outcomes. Therefore, reduced sensitivity to one effect does not demonstrate reduced sensitivity to every other effect. Always state what was measured and when. This also explains how tolerance to a pleasurable effect can coexist with persistent or increased cue-related motivation.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 27. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc22.title: Question 22 — Cocaine is bad for you
l13-mc22.markdown:
The lecture links cocaine exposure to **multiple possible harms**, including cardiovascular strain, seizures, stroke, and severe psychological disturbances. These consequences follow from actions on both central and peripheral systems, rather than from dopamine-related reinforcement alone.

Some harms also depend on the exposure route, such as damage to nasal tissue associated with repeated local use. That illustrates how pharmacology, tissue contact, and behavior combine to shape risk. The pregnancy slide uses a stigmatizing historical label that should not be adopted as a description of children; developmental outcomes require careful interpretation of exposure and other conditions. A substantive answer explains categories of harm and their mechanisms without treating every adverse outcome as inevitable or every association as a complete causal demonstration.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 28. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc23.title: Question 23 — Potential pharmacotherapies for cocaine use disorder
l13-mc23.markdown:
The slide discusses **candidate treatment mechanisms**, not an established medication recommendation. Replacement-oriented approaches aim to alter the reinforcing or motivational consequences of cocaine use, while immune-based approaches aim to bind cocaine or enhance its breakdown before it reaches relevant brain targets.

These strategies act at different levels: receptor/transmitter systems versus drug availability in the circulation. A plausible mechanism must still be evaluated for efficacy and safety. The statement that no medication had been approved belongs to the supplied course/textbook context and is not independently updated here as a current regulatory claim. The explanation should preserve the difference between a proposed intervention, evidence from a study, and an approved treatment rather than treating the candidate list as instructions for clinical use.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 29. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc24.title: Question 24 — There are many amphetamines to choose from
l13-mc24.markdown:
The lecture groups **amphetamine-related psychostimulants by structural and pharmacological relationships**. It distinguishes amphetamine forms and methamphetamine while also introducing structurally related plant compounds such as cathinone and ephedrine. Similarity to catecholamine structures helps motivate the later discussion of monoamine transport and release.

Being related does not make the compounds interchangeable in potency, distribution, duration, or adverse effects. Nor does a natural plant origin guarantee safety; the lecture explicitly uses plant compounds to challenge that assumption. The keyed answer provides only the beginning of the list. The important explanation is the relation between chemical family and mechanism, not a catalog of brand names or any practical description of how to synthesize or prepare the substances.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 30. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc25.title: Question 25 — Amphetamine pharmacokinetics make facilitate binging
l13-mc25.markdown:
Amphetamine-related drugs have a **longer elimination time course than cocaine in the lecture's comparison**. Continued exposure can therefore accumulate when additional drug is taken before earlier drug has been cleared. Prolonged stimulation, reduced sleep, and disrupted eating can then combine with the drug's direct physiological effects.

The repeated-use schedule in the original key describes a hazardous pattern, not a dosing recommendation or a necessary feature of all use. The approximate half-lives are teaching summaries and vary with conditions. The mechanistic lesson is that onset and elimination are separate dimensions: a drug can enter rapidly and remain active for much longer. Understanding that distinction explains why repeated exposure can extend effects and risks rather than simply produce isolated, independent episodes.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 32. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc26.title: Question 26 — Pharmacodynamics of amphetamine
l13-mc26.markdown:
Amphetamine acts as an **indirect catecholamine agonist** by changing transmitter handling rather than simply replacing dopamine at its receptor. The lecture describes entry through DAT, redistribution of vesicular dopamine, and outward transport that increases extracellular dopamine; norepinephrine handling is also affected.

The slide calls transporter reversal “inverse agonism,” but Chapter 12 of the full textbook distinguishes transporter-mediated release from receptor inverse agonism. An inverse receptor agonist reduces constitutive receptor activity; reversing the direction of a transporter is a different mechanism. The explanation should therefore use the more precise transport language. This also distinguishes amphetamine from cocaine's predominant reuptake-blocking action, even though both can increase monoamine availability and produce stimulant effects.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 33. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc27.title: Question 27 — Subjective effects of amphetamines
l13-mc27.markdown:
The subjective effects reflect **increased arousal and altered perception of fatigue**, including greater alertness, confidence, and feelings of energy. The lecture also describes reduced sleep, particularly REM sleep, during exposure. These observations concern how a person feels and behaves, not proof that the physiological need for recovery has been removed.

The distinction matters because sustained activity without normal sleep can coexist with accumulating impairment and risk. Therapeutic use, nonmedical use, and repeated high exposure cannot be treated as identical situations simply because they involve the same drug family. A strong explanation connects the arousal profile to monoamine actions while avoiding the inference that feeling more capable necessarily means safer or uniformly better cognitive and physical performance.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 34. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc28.title: Question 28 — Therapeutic effects of amphetamines
l13-mc28.markdown:
The lecture identifies **narcolepsy and ADHD as therapeutic contexts** for stimulant pharmacology. In narcolepsy, reducing excessive daytime sleepiness is a different target from producing a recreational high. In ADHD, the intended outcomes concern attention and behavioral regulation, not generalized activation for its own sake.

These examples show that a drug's classification as a stimulant does not determine whether a particular use is therapeutic or harmful. Dose, formulation, route, clinical indication, and monitoring matter. The symptom list in the key describes features discussed under narcolepsy, but does not establish that every patient has every listed feature. This course question concerns the rationale for therapeutic use, not diagnosis or a recommendation that a particular person take amphetamine.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 35. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc29.title: Question 29 — Methamphetamine is worse for you than other amphetamines
l13-mc29.markdown:
The slide emphasizes **psychotic reactions and possible persistent neurobehavioral consequences** associated with substantial methamphetamine exposure. Pre-existing vulnerability is identified as relevant, and the lecture distinguishes symptoms during use from a psychotic state that can continue after abstinence.

Similarity to schizophrenia-like symptoms does not mean that every such episode is identical to schizophrenia or that every exposed person develops a persistent disorder. Likewise, the heading's broad comparison with “other amphetamines” is not a controlled ranking across all doses and routes. A careful explanation reports the particular risks and conditions discussed, distinguishes acute symptoms from longer-lasting outcomes, and avoids treating a general warning as evidence of a universal, inevitable effect.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 37. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc30.title: Question 30 — Crystal meth is unhealthy
l13-mc30.markdown:
The lecture describes **multisystem risks associated with heavy, chronic methamphetamine use**, extending beyond acute alertness or euphoria. Cardiovascular, oral, gastrointestinal, infectious, and neurological outcomes illustrate that a psychoactive drug can affect health through many direct and indirect pathways.

The original wording is stigmatizing; “people with heavy or chronic use” more accurately identifies the exposure pattern without defining a person by it. Reported increased risks are not certainties for every individual, and observational associations can reflect interacting exposure, health, and environmental factors. The key should therefore be understood as a risk profile in the course's evidence base, not a prediction of one person's future or proof that all the listed outcomes have one identical mechanism.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 38. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc31.title: Question 31 — Integration: Origin of The Dopamine = Pleasure Fallacy: James Old’s “Pleasure Centers in The Brain”
l13-mc31.markdown:
This integration item returns to **the difference between an observed reinforcing effect and a proposed hedonic explanation**. Self-stimulation demonstrates that a consequence can sustain repeated responding. Calling that consequence pleasurable adds an interpretation that requires more than the response count itself.

The connection to the rest of the lecture is that cocaine seeking, cue-driven behavior, and dopamine release can likewise be measured without being interchangeable with subjective liking. The historical citation in the answer does not explain this distinction. A useful response identifies the experimental observation first, then asks what additional evidence would be needed to support a claim about pleasure or a particular neurotransmitter. This avoids using the phrase “pleasure center” as its own proof.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-mc32.title: Question 32 — Integration: Renaissance of The Pleasure Fallacy: Roy Wise’s Hedonic Theory of Addiction
l13-mc32.markdown:
The historical hedonic theory links **drug reinforcement to dopamine-mediated pleasure**. The lecture uses that account as a starting point, then contrasts it with evidence and theories emphasizing learned predictions, incentive salience, and compulsive seeking. The integration lies in understanding why an influential explanation was attractive and why it is incomplete.

A rise in dopamine after a drug is consistent with involvement of the system, but does not specify whether the relevant process is liking, wanting, learning, movement, or a combination. The correct answer here identifies the theory being discussed; it should not be read as endorsing every part of its quotation. Distinguish explaining a historical position from accepting that position as the lecture's final scientific conclusion.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — People simply want dopamine. They do not find pleasure in it.
l13-sa01.markdown:
The provocative heading is best interpreted as a **dissociation between wanting and liking**, not a literal claim that people consciously seek the dopamine molecule. The slide combines evidence relating dopamine measures to drug wanting, subjective ratings under receptor blockade, and hedonic reactions in an animal model. These are different measurements that challenge the idea of one simple pleasure scale.

Connect this to addiction by explaining how cue-related motivation or seeking can remain strong even when reported pleasure is unchanged or diminished. That provides a rationale for focusing on craving and difficult-to-control behavior rather than defining the disorder solely by enjoyment. The title is broader than any single experiment establishes: the evidence does not prove that dopamine has no relationship to reward processing under all circumstances. A strong answer separates the specific findings, their common implication, and the limits of the generalization. The original answer's citations and figure labels are not a complete model response without that reasoning.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Drug dependence leads to withdrawal symptoms when abstinence is attempted
l13-sa02.markdown:
Physical dependence involves **adaptation to repeated drug exposure**, with withdrawal when exposure is reduced or stopped. If taking the drug relieves an aversive withdrawal state, that relief can negatively reinforce taking. “Negative” refers to removal of an aversive consequence, not punishment or a morally negative act.

The antireward/neuroadaptation account extends this idea by describing a motivational state in which avoiding distress becomes increasingly important. However, the lecture explicitly notes two limitations: not every addictive drug produces the same severe withdrawal syndrome, and relapse can occur after acute detoxification. A developed answer must therefore connect dependence to continued use without equating the two. Cue learning, stress, and persistent changes in motivation help explain phenomena beyond immediate withdrawal relief. The opioid replacement examples illustrate a treatment rationale within the course, but the question does not provide individual clinical guidance or justify treating all substances with the same approach.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Cocaine
l13-sa03.markdown:
The lecture distinguishes **chemical form, administration route, and the resulting exposure pattern**. Cocaine hydrochloride is a water-soluble salt; other forms differ in physical properties and suitability for different routes. The important pharmacological connection is that the speed with which exposure rises can alter the immediacy and reinforcing character of the effect. No preparation method is needed to explain that principle.

Connect this to cue learning by considering the events consistently paired with taking the drug. Objects, contexts, and internal sensations can become predictors and later evoke motivation or craving even without immediate drug delivery. The acute pharmacokinetic effect and the learned cue effect are therefore complementary, not competing explanations. A strong response distinguishes the drug's physical properties, transporter-blocking action, and learned associations. It should not imply that every route has an identical risk profile or that cue-associated dopamine release directly measures subjective pleasure.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Behavioural effects of cocaine
l13-sa04.markdown:
The lecture describes **dose- and pattern-dependent changes in behavior**, including locomotor activation and more focused repetitive stereotypies. Stereotypy is not simply “more movement”: behavior can become restricted to repetitive acts even when general movement through the environment decreases.

Connect this to peripheral physiology by explaining that the same exposure also affects monoamine signaling outside the relevant motor circuits. Sympathomimetic effects can include increased heart rate, vasoconstriction, blood-pressure elevation, and hyperthermia. Thus, a behavioral observation does not exhaust the drug's effects or indicate that the body is tolerating it safely. The regional manipulation table further distinguishes accumbens-related locomotor effects from dorsal-striatal stereotypy in the studied models. A complete answer specifies the behavioral endpoint, its relation to exposure, and a separate physiological consequence, avoiding the vague claim that cocaine simply “stimulates everything” in one uniform way.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 21. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa05.title: Short Essay 5 — Chronic cocaine exposure changes the brain
l13-sa05.markdown:
The imaging examples associate chronic stimulant use with **altered striatal dopaminergic measures**, which the lecture interprets in relation to down-regulation and tolerance. The important point is that the state of the system after repeated exposure can differ from its response to an initial acute dose.

Connect this to tolerance and sensitization by specifying the endpoint and exposure pattern. Reduced response in one measure can coexist with enhanced response in another, particularly under different schedules or after different abstinence intervals. A single scan or group difference does not, by itself, establish the complete causal history of every participant or prove permanent irreversible damage. A strong answer distinguishes the measured imaging signal, the adaptation proposed to explain it, and the behavioral consequences being inferred. The lecture's contrasting long-access and intermittent-access models show why the phrase “chronic cocaine changes dopamine” needs that additional precision.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 26. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa06.title: Short Essay 6 — Common routes of administration
l13-sa06.markdown:
Route influences **onset**, while metabolism and excretion influence **persistence**. The lecture contrasts slower gastrointestinal absorption with more rapid delivery and notes the relatively long elimination time course of amphetamine-related drugs. These dimensions should be considered separately: rapid entry does not imply rapid clearance.

Connect the distinction to repeated-use patterns. Additional exposure before earlier drug has been eliminated can prolong or accumulate effects, while reduced sleep and food intake add further physiological strain. The source's descriptions of repeated use are examples of hazardous behavior, not instructions or safe schedules. A developed response explains how concentration over time links administration to effects without providing techniques for maximizing intoxication. It should also avoid concluding that route alone determines addiction: reinforcement depends on immediacy, but individual history, context, exposure amount, and the broader learning and adaptation processes discussed in the lecture remain relevant.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 31. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa07.title: Short Essay 7 — Amphetamines are addictive
l13-sa07.markdown:
Dependence and problematic use can develop with **amphetamine-related stimulants even when withdrawal does not resemble severe alcohol or opioid withdrawal**. This is one reason a withdrawal-only theory cannot explain every addictive pattern. Cue-triggered motivation, reinforcement, and changes in control can contribute alongside negative affect during abstinence.

The lecture also describes cognitive impairments and psychotic reactions associated with substantial methamphetamine use. These are different outcomes and should not be treated as interchangeable definitions of dependence. Its comparative phrase “less severe” concerns the course's contrast in withdrawal syndromes; it should not minimize distress, psychiatric risk, or the need for appropriate care. A complete answer links the evidence to the theoretical limitation, distinguishes acute and persistent effects, and avoids claiming that every person follows the same progression. The broad comparison with other amphetamines requires attention to dose, route, and exposure pattern rather than relying on the lecture heading alone.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 36. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l13-sa08.title: Short Essay 8 — Integration: Origin of The Dopamine = Pleasure Fallacy: James Old’s “Pleasure Centers in The Brain” and Renaissance of The Pleasure Fallacy: Roy Wise’s Hedonic Theory of Addiction
l13-sa08.markdown:
The two slides concern **different stages in the development of a pleasure-centered explanation**. Brain self-stimulation established an experimentally observable reinforcing consequence: animals worked to obtain stimulation. The later hedonic theory linked dopamine more explicitly to pleasurable reward and the effects of addictive drugs.

Their connection is the inference from reinforcement or dopamine activation to subjective pleasure. The lecture challenges that inference by separating liking from wanting and by presenting cue-learning and sensitization accounts. A strong comparison should therefore identify what each approach observed or proposed, then explain why neither a high response rate nor a dopamine increase is automatically a direct pleasure measurement. The original answer combines a citation and a quotation but lacks this analytical distinction. The task is not to dismiss the historical work; it is to recognize its contribution while being precise about which conclusions the evidence supports and which require additional measures.

**Source:** Lecture 13 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 9. Stimulant-specific context also draws on Chapter 12 of the supplied full textbook (not an assigned chapter in this folder).

**Review:** [Lecture 13 study guide](../study-guides/lecture13.qmd).

l14-mc01.title: Question 1 — How alcohol is made
l14-mc01.markdown:
Ethanol is the **alcohol in alcoholic beverages**, produced when yeasts ferment sugars, generating ethanol and carbon dioxide. Identifying the chemical matters because other small alcohols have different metabolic products and toxicity profiles; “alcohol” is a chemical category, not a guarantee of interchangeability.

The contrast also does not mean ethanol itself is harmless. The lecture later describes dose-dependent intoxication, toxicity, and chronic injury. Its nutritional point is that alcohol supplies energy without replacing the nutrients needed for normal health. The historical suggestion about accidental first consumption is speculative context rather than a necessary pharmacological fact. The substantive answer should focus on fermentation, chemical identity, and why a source of calories is not necessarily an adequate source of nutrition.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc02.title: Question 2 — Pharmacokinetics - solubility
l14-mc02.markdown:
Ethanol's **small size and ready mixing with water** help explain its absorption and broad distribution through body fluids and tissues. The lecture's ionization statement concerns physiological conditions; it is not a claim about every possible chemical environment. Modest lipid affinity does not prevent this small molecule from reaching the brain.

The relevant behavioral exposure measure is blood alcohol concentration rather than simply the number or volume of drinks consumed. The same amount ingested can yield different concentrations when body-water volume, absorption, or metabolism differs. This connects chemical properties to pharmacokinetics: what enters the body, how it distributes, and the concentration achieved at a given time are related but not identical quantities.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc03.title: Question 3 — Pharmacokinetics - absorption
l14-mc03.markdown:
Most oral alcohol absorption in the lecture's account occurs across the **small intestine**, so the rate of gastric emptying influences how quickly blood concentrations rise. Food can delay movement from the stomach to this large absorptive surface and therefore change the timing of the concentration peak.

Do not confuse slower absorption with complete prevention of intoxication. The ingested alcohol can still be absorbed later, while distribution and metabolism occur at the same time. The lecture also discusses concentration and average physiological differences, but these should not become exact predictions for every individual. A developed explanation follows the route from ingestion to the intestine and blood, rather than assuming that the amount in a glass directly specifies the concentration in the brain.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc04.title: Question 4 — Metabolism of ethanol – gastric and hepatic
l14-mc04.markdown:
Alcohol dehydrogenase converts **ethanol to acetaldehyde**, and aldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde onward to acetate, described in the lecture as acetic acid. Acetaldehyde accumulation helps explain the flushing and other adverse reactions discussed when its metabolism is impaired.

The lecture emphasizes approximately constant-rate elimination under the relevant conditions, contrasting it with first-order removal of a fixed fraction per interval. If intake exceeds elimination, alcohol accumulates. The “ounces per hour” statement is underspecified in the answer because beverage strength and units matter; it must not be used as a personal clearance calculator or a rule for deciding when driving is safe. Learn the enzyme sequence and kinetic principle rather than treating an approximate course number as an individual prediction.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc05.title: Question 5 — Tolerance to ethanol
l14-mc05.markdown:
Tolerance means a **smaller response to comparable exposure after prior use**, but it can arise through several mechanisms. The lecture distinguishes increased metabolism, compensatory changes in neural function, and learned behavioral compensation. These mechanisms need not develop equally for all effects.

Acute tolerance adds an important warning: a person may experience fewer apparent effects on the falling limb of the blood-concentration curve than at the same concentration while it was rising. Feeling less intoxicated therefore does not establish absence of impairment. Cross-tolerance with some sedative–hypnotics reflects overlapping actions or adaptations, not protection from all combined-drug hazards. Specify the response being measured rather than describing an experienced drinker as globally resistant to alcohol's effects.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc06.title: Question 6 — Ethanol dependence
l14-mc06.markdown:
Physical dependence reflects **adaptation to repeated alcohol exposure**, so removing alcohol can leave compensatory activity temporarily unopposed. The lecture lists tremor, anxiety, autonomic activation, and potentially severe withdrawal states, connecting those symptoms to a system no longer functioning under its adapted drug condition.

Severity depends on exposure history and individual circumstances; a hangover should not automatically be equated with the same withdrawal syndrome. Cross-dependence means another drug with overlapping actions may affect withdrawal expression, not that combining sedatives is a safe self-management strategy. This is a mechanism question, not a detoxification plan. Distinguish dependence from addiction and distinguish the pharmacological explanation of withdrawal from the clinical assessment needed for someone at risk of severe symptoms.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc07.title: Question 7 — Effects of alcohol
l14-mc07.markdown:
Alcohol's central effects vary with **dose, exposure, and context**. Early relaxation or reduced anxiety can coexist with declining judgment and coordination, while greater exposure can impair memory, produce blackouts or sleep, and at high levels cause dangerous depression of vital functions.

A blackout refers to impaired memory formation for events during intoxication, not necessarily loss of consciousness throughout those events. The behavioral risks on the slide also depend on setting and expectations, as Chapter 10 discusses. Thus, the same pharmacological exposure does not make every person behave identically. The explanation should connect increasing CNS effects to impaired functioning rather than assume that a positive subjective feeling accurately measures safety or cognitive performance.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc08.title: Question 8 — Alcohol is poison
l14-mc08.markdown:
The lecture describes **multiple pathways of alcohol-related brain injury**, including thiamine deficiency and excitotoxic processes. Thiamine-related disorders involve damage to brain systems important for memory and other functions; this is different from the temporary memory impairment that occurs during an acute episode of intoxication.

Heavy long-term use can contribute to deficiency and other injury, but the key's wording should not be read as saying every exposed individual inevitably develops Wernicke's encephalopathy. Likewise, all observed tissue loss cannot be attributed to nutrition alone. A strong explanation distinguishes nutritional deficiency, direct or indirect neural injury, and withdrawal-related hyperexcitability, instead of using the heading “poison” as a substitute for specifying the mechanism and time course.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 11. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc09.title: Question 9 — Psychopharmacology of Alcohol (13 of 16)
l14-mc09.markdown:
Alcohol's effects are **not limited to the brain**. Reduced antidiuretic-hormone signaling can increase water loss through urine, while chronic exposure can be associated with different forms of liver injury, including fatty change, hepatitis, and cirrhosis. These examples involve different organs and time courses.

The lecture also distinguishes subjective sexual arousal from performance, which is developed in the following figure. Feeling more aroused does not demonstrate improved physiological function. The common lesson is that one drug can have multiple effects because it acts through several systems. Do not treat diuresis as evidence that alcohol has been rapidly cleared, or assume that a short-term effect and a chronic organ disorder are simply the same process at different intensities.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc10.title: Question 10 — Effect of alcohol on male sexual function
l14-mc10.markdown:
The figure distinguishes **physiological performance measures from subjective arousal**. Across the illustrated blood-alcohol concentrations, the rate of tumescence decreases and orgasmic latency increases. Maximum tumescence shows a less uniform low-dose pattern before declining at the higher concentrations shown.

These outcomes explain why the preceding slide can describe increased arousal together with poorer performance. The graph is evidence about the measurements and conditions depicted, not proof that every individual responds identically. The original keyed option is merely a placeholder and does not state any of these results. A substantive answer should identify the axes, describe each trend accurately, and avoid converting a nuanced graph into the blanket claim that every sexual response changes monotonically in the same direction.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc11.title: Question 11 — The pharmacodynamic profile of ethanol is diverse
l14-mc11.markdown:
The lecture contrasts **broad membrane effects with actions on particular signaling proteins**. Ethanol can alter membrane properties and also influence ligand-gated channels and intracellular signaling. This helps explain why no single receptor mechanism accounts for its full behavioral and physiological profile.

The small molecule's ability to distribute readily supports widespread access, but access is not the same as a specific action at every target. The following GABA, glutamate, dopamine, and opioid examples provide distinct mechanisms and circuit consequences. A good explanation therefore separates pharmacokinetics—reaching tissues—from pharmacodynamics—changing their function. Calling alcohol a CNS depressant summarizes an important overall effect without implying that every neuron or transmitter pathway is directly inhibited in the same way.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc12.title: Question 12 — Ethanol at GABA receptors
l14-mc12.markdown:
In the lecture's account, acute alcohol exposure can **enhance GABAA-mediated inhibition**, increasing the effect of GABA on chloride conductance. This is described as positive allosteric modulation, rather than alcohol substituting for GABA at its usual transmitter-binding site.

Repeated exposure can be associated with compensatory reductions in this inhibitory response. That provides one contribution to tolerance while alcohol is present and hyperexcitability when it is removed. The mechanism must be combined with the glutamate and other examples, because alcohol's actions are diverse and receptor populations differ. A stronger GABA-related inhibitory effect at one point in the system does not automatically specify the net activity of every connected neuron or explain all alcohol-related behavior.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 16. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc13.title: Question 13 — Why might alcohol be addictive?
l14-mc13.markdown:
The lecture links alcohol reinforcement to **increased activity in mesolimbic dopamine pathways**, including VTA projections to the nucleus accumbens. It also notes reduced dopaminergic activity during withdrawal in the rodent examples, illustrating that acute and adapted states can differ.

The slide's “core = reinforcement, shell = reward” labels are simplified teaching cues, not exclusive one-function maps. As the preceding lecture emphasized, dopamine release, reinforcing behavior, and subjective liking are related but nonidentical measurements. A complete explanation therefore connects alcohol's circuit effects to motivated behavior without reducing addiction to a single pleasure signal. It also leaves room for opioid, glutamate, GABA, and learned-cue contributions rather than treating dopamine as the only relevant system.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 18. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc14.title: Question 14 — Ethanol causes endogenous opioid release
l14-mc14.markdown:
Endogenous opioid signaling is presented as **one contributor to alcohol's rewarding and reinforcing effects**. The lecture links alcohol exposure to opioid release and reports that opioid-receptor blockade or μ-receptor knockout reduces the relevant self-administration outcome in the studied models.

These comparisons motivate a receptor-level treatment rationale: blocking part of the opioid contribution can reduce alcohol's reinforcing effects without directly changing the molecule into another substance. However, release from the pituitary should not automatically be equated with identical signaling at every brain synapse; anatomical location matters. The chronic gene-expression statement also concerns adaptation over time, not the same process as acute peptide release. Keep acute action, repeated-exposure changes, and experimental manipulation distinct.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 19. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc15.title: Question 15 — Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder
l14-mc15.markdown:
The two strategies change **different consequences of drinking**. Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so alcohol exposure can lead to acetaldehyde accumulation and an aversive reaction. Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors, aiming to reduce the reinforcing contribution of alcohol-associated endogenous opioid signaling.

The lecture uses behavioral terminology to contrast adding an unpleasant consequence with weakening a reinforcing consequence. Neither mechanism is simply “removing alcohol from the blood,” and neither is established by the fact that it sounds plausible. These are course explanations of supervised treatment approaches, not instructions to combine a medication with alcohol or test a reaction. The small amount mentioned in the original key is a toxicity warning, not a threshold below which the combination is safe.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 20. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-mc16.title: Question 16 — Integration: How alcohol is made
l14-mc16.markdown:
This integration item connects **the identity and production of ethanol to its later biological effects**. Fermentation explains how ethanol can arise from sugars, but the resulting molecule's absorption, metabolism, and receptor-related actions explain intoxication and toxicity after consumption.

The word “alcohol” therefore needs chemical precision: different alcohols can be metabolized differently, while ethanol itself can still be harmful. Its energy content also does not make it a substitute for nutritional intake. The original historical suggestion about accidental first use is not the mechanism being tested. A useful synthesis follows chemical product → exposure → metabolism and effects, rather than treating familiarity, natural production, or beverage status as evidence of safety.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-sa01.title: Short Essay 1 — Metabolism of ethanol – hepatic
l14-sa01.markdown:
Hepatic metabolism can change through **competition and enzyme induction**, with different consequences. When substrates compete for a metabolic pathway, clearance of one or more substances can be reduced. With repeated exposure, increased abundance or activity of relevant enzymes can instead increase metabolic capacity. The lecture uses alcohol and CYP enzymes to illustrate these two situations.

Connect induction to metabolic tolerance: less drug may reach or remain at the target for a given exposure. This differs from pharmacodynamic tolerance, in which cells respond less despite comparable exposure, and behavioral tolerance, in which learned compensation changes observed performance. A strong response also avoids assuming that every alcohol–drug interaction is explained by enzyme competition; overlapping sedative effects can create another kind of interaction. The course example teaches why acute co-exposure and a history of repeated exposure can produce different outcomes, not that a person can safely “train the liver” or predict a combination's safety from one mechanism alone.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 6. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-sa02.title: Short Essay 2 — Some positive effects
l14-sa02.markdown:
This item requires **critical interpretation of claims presented as possible benefits**, not an endorsement of drinking for health. The lecture mentions vasodilation, lipid-related changes, and possible associations with some outcomes, but also notes increased hypertension, stroke, and cardiac risks with problematic use. An effect on one physiological variable is not equivalent to an overall clinical benefit.

The supplied slide does not establish that the associations are causal, apply to every population, or outweigh other harms. Connect this to the following systemic-effects slide by showing that the same substance affects water balance, liver function, and other processes. A developed answer should distinguish a proposed mechanism, an observed association, and a recommendation, which would require a much broader evidence assessment. The original key should therefore not be used as current medical advice or as a reason to begin drinking. Its role here is to examine the course's historical claims and their evidential limits.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-sa03.title: Short Essay 3 — Ethanol at glutamate receptors
l14-sa03.markdown:
The lecture contrasts **acute suppression of glutamatergic signaling with compensatory changes after repeated exposure**. Acute alcohol can reduce NMDA-related responses and glutamate release in the described regions. Repeated exposure can lead to adaptations that offset that suppression, including increased receptor-related responsiveness or availability.

During withdrawal, alcohol's acute suppressive action is removed while adaptations may persist. The resulting imbalance can contribute to hyperexcitability, seizures, and potentially injurious calcium signaling. This is an opponent-process explanation, not a claim that all withdrawal effects arise from NMDA receptors alone. Connect it to addiction by explaining how an aversive withdrawal state can motivate renewed use through negative reinforcement, alongside dopamine- and opioid-related reinforcement and learned cue effects. Also distinguish acute blackouts from chronic injury: both involve impaired neural function, but they are not identical outcomes or proof of the same duration of damage.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l14-sa04.title: Short Essay 4 — Integration: How alcohol is made and Pharmacokinetics - solubility
l14-sa04.markdown:
The production question asks **where the molecule comes from**, while the solubility question asks **how that molecule behaves in the body**. Fermentation of sugars by yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Ethanol's small size, lack of appreciable ionization under physiological conditions, and ready mixing with water help explain its absorption and widespread distribution.

The connection is that the same chemical product can reach the brain and other tissues after consumption, regardless of the cultural setting in which the beverage was made. Amount ingested still does not directly determine blood concentration: body-water distribution, absorption rate, and elimination also matter. A strong comparison therefore moves from production to molecular properties to exposure, without providing production procedures or treating fermentation as evidence of harmlessness. The historical comment about accidental first consumption is incidental; the pharmacological explanation rests on chemical identity and the processes governing concentration over time.

**Source:** Lecture 14 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 10.

**Review:** [Lecture 14 study guide](../study-guides/lecture14.qmd).

l15-mc01.title: Question 1 — Opioids are narcotic analgesics
l15-mc01.markdown:
Analgesia means **reduction of pain**, not necessarily loss of consciousness. The lecture contrasts this therapeutic effect with general anesthesia, while also noting that increasing opioid exposure can produce sedation, coma, and life-threatening respiratory effects.

The phrase “without producing unconsciousness” therefore describes the intended distinction, not an absolute guarantee at every dose. The same drug can affect pain processing, alertness, mood, and autonomic function through receptors in different locations. A strong explanation separates desired analgesia from unwanted sedation and toxicity. It also avoids assuming that powerful pain relief automatically means addiction: repeated exposure can produce tolerance or physical dependence, but those adaptations are not, by themselves, the complete behavioral pattern of addiction.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 2. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc02.title: Question 2 — Opium has been around for a long time
l15-mc02.markdown:
Opium is a **plant-derived mixture**, and compounds such as morphine and codeine connect its historical use to the pharmacology of opiates. The lecture uses laudanum and older remedies to illustrate that medical and nonmedical opioid use long predate modern receptor science.

Historical familiarity does not establish safety, and not every opioid is extracted directly from the plant. The later taxonomy includes semisynthetic substances, fully synthetic compounds, and endogenous peptides. Thus, “opioid” is a broader functional category than a particular botanical preparation. The relevant explanation connects source history to the emergence of chemically characterized agents, while distinguishing the historical claim from a mechanism of receptor activation or an assessment of modern treatment practices.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 3. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc03.title: Question 3 — The structure of opioids determines their pharmacokinetics
l15-mc03.markdown:
Changing molecular structure can change **lipid solubility, brain entry, metabolism, and duration**, even when related compounds ultimately affect similar receptor systems. The lecture uses heroin's greater lipid solubility and metabolic conversion to illustrate how access to the brain contributes to its different time course from morphine.

These are pharmacokinetic explanations: they concern the amount and timing of active substance reaching targets. They should be distinguished from pharmacodynamic differences in affinity or efficacy at a receptor. Nor should the diagram be taken as saying that one simple chemical modification predicts every aspect of safety or dependence risk. Follow the causal chain from structure to distribution and metabolism, rather than treating milligram potency as a complete measure of clinical usefulness or danger.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 4. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc04.title: Question 4 — The structure of opioids determines their pharmacodynamics
l15-mc04.markdown:
Molecular changes can also alter **what a ligand does after binding a receptor**. A full agonist can produce greater intrinsic activation than a partial agonist in the same system; a neutral antagonist binds without producing that agonist response and can block an agonist's action. Naloxone illustrates antagonism in the lecture.

This distinction is pharmacodynamic, unlike a change in how quickly a compound crosses the blood–brain barrier. The key's claim about partial agonists should not be generalized into “no dependence” or guaranteed safety: receptor efficacy is only one determinant of the whole-drug effect. Receptor subtype and experimental context also matter. A complete answer identifies binding versus activation and separates intrinsic efficacy from dose, delivery rate, and the eventual behavioral response.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 5. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc05.title: Question 5 — A taxonomy of opioids Opiates
l15-mc05.markdown:
The taxonomy distinguishes **natural opiates, semisynthetic drugs, fully synthetic drugs, and endogenous opioid peptides**. Morphine and codeine appear under natural opiates; chemically modified derivatives form another category; fentanyl and methadone illustrate synthetic compounds; enkephalins, endorphins, and dynorphins are produced by the body.

The broad term “opioid” links these categories through their pharmacological relationships, not through identical origin or molecular shape. The answer panel's words “Opiates Opioids” do not state that distinction and are not a complete answer. Read the hierarchy in the source figure rather than assuming every opioid is a poppy extract. The taxonomy is descriptive: placement in a natural or synthetic category does not by itself determine potency, safety, or dependence potential.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 7. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc06.title: Question 6 — Physiological and psychological effects of opioids
l15-mc06.markdown:
The lecture emphasizes **dose and rate of absorption** as influences on opioid effects. Analgesia, constricted pupils, drowsiness, reduced concentration, and changes in subjective experience can occur together because receptors operate in multiple systems.

Euphoria can contribute to reinforcement, but it is not the defining mechanism of every therapeutic effect. Likewise, drowsiness is not identical to pain relief, and relief of distress does not establish that an opioid is appropriate for every cause of anxiety. The question's keyed list identifies effects; the explanation links their variability to exposure and receptor distribution. Increasing exposure can move beyond intended analgesia toward severe CNS and respiratory depression, so apparent familiarity with an effect is not a complete indicator of safety.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 8. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc07.title: Question 7 — Mechanisms of opioid overdose
l15-mc07.markdown:
The central overdose mechanism highlighted by the lecture is **depression of brainstem respiratory function**. At sufficiently high exposure, opioid effects can impair breathing and lead to respiratory failure. Profound sedation, constricted pupils, and reductions in blood pressure or temperature are associated observations, but naming them does not replace explaining the respiratory mechanism.

Nausea and vomiting involve another brainstem site, the area postrema, demonstrating that different adverse effects need not share one immediate pathway. The original answer excerpt omits the slide's key respiratory-failure statement, so the full slide is needed for a complete response. This explanation concerns the biological mechanism; it is not an estimate of a safe dose, a diagnostic checklist, or instructions for managing an overdose independently.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 9. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc08.title: Question 8 — Opioids are very important in the GI tract
l15-mc08.markdown:
Opioid receptors in the gastrointestinal system can **slow intestinal function**, helping explain both antidiarrheal action and constipation during analgesic treatment. The same physiological effect can be desired in one context and unwanted in another.

The loperamide example adds a pharmacokinetic distinction: Chapter 11 describes restricted CNS effects at recommended doses, allowing a predominantly peripheral action. That restriction is not an assurance of safety at very high exposure. The lecture specifically warns about cardiac toxicity associated with misuse; no high-dose amount should be interpreted as a strategy for treating withdrawal. The historical claim about diarrheal illnesses illustrates an effect on symptoms, not a general recommendation to suppress every episode of infectious diarrhea or a treatment of its underlying cause.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 10. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc09.title: Question 9 — Structure and function of the opioid receptors (Brigitte Kieffer; 1992; delta first)
l15-mc09.markdown:
The opioid receptors discussed are **inhibitory G-protein-coupled receptors**, rather than ligand-gated chloride channels. The source figure links receptor activation to opening potassium channels postsynaptically, reducing excitability, and closing calcium channels at terminals, reducing transmitter release.

These are cellular mechanisms, not a guarantee that every connected neuron becomes less active. If an opioid inhibits an inhibitory interneuron, the next neuron can be disinhibited, as in the VTA example from the GABA lecture. The same receptor class can therefore contribute to analgesia in one pathway and enhanced downstream activity in another. Identify the receptor's location and the sign of the intervening synapses before predicting the circuit-level effect.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 12. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc10.title: Question 10 — Where are endogenous opioids produced and released?
l15-mc10.markdown:
Endogenous opioids are **peptides produced by the body**, not small monoamines such as dopamine. Their precursors and products can be investigated with methods that identify gene expression or peptide distribution. In situ hybridization detects relevant RNA, while immunohistochemistry detects the antigen recognized by an antibody.

The lecture's brain and pituitary figures also distinguish local neural signaling from release into the circulation. Detecting a peptide in blood does not automatically establish its concentration at a particular brain synapse. The short key “small proteins” identifies chemical class but does not answer the anatomical question fully. A developed explanation connects peptide synthesis, the cells or tissues producing it, and the location where release can influence receptors.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 13. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc11.title: Question 11 — An opioidergic projection for food reward
l15-mc11.markdown:
The source illustration **depicts an enkephalin-containing projection from the nucleus tractus solitarius to the nucleus accumbens shell**, linking gustatory input to opioid-related reward modulation. Within the drawing, opioid release acts at receptors on shell neurons and changes their excitability and motivational processing.

This is what the diagram proposes, not a result established by the question's answer choices. The slide provides no primary-study citation or experimental comparison sufficient to verify the pathway and all of its claimed functions independently. The original key is only a placeholder. Use the illustration to trace the proposed sensory → projection → receptor → behavioral chain, but retain its source limitation rather than presenting every label as conclusively demonstrated evidence.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 14. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc12.title: Question 12 — The ascending pain pathway (anterolateral system)
l15-mc12.markdown:
The lecture contrasts **faster myelinated Aδ input with slower unmyelinated C-fiber input**. Their different conduction properties help explain distinguishable early and later aspects of pain. Ascending pathways relay information through the spinal cord and thalamic targets toward cortical and other brain systems.

The sensory-discriminative component concerns features such as location and intensity, while affective processing concerns unpleasantness and motivational significance. These are interacting dimensions, not two completely independent experiences or an absolute rule that a fiber type carries only one psychological category. The key's “PVL” label should be checked against the source anatomy rather than treated as a self-explanatory nucleus name. The primary learning task is to link conduction, pathway organization, and multiple dimensions of pain.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 15. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.

**Review:** [Lecture 15 study guide](../study-guides/lecture15.qmd).

l15-mc13.title: Question 13 — Supraspinal modulation of pain by opioids
l15-mc13.markdown:
Supraspinal opioid modulation concerns **processing above the spinal cord**, including sensory and affective components of pain. The lecture's PET example uses a μ-receptor radioligand and relates changes in its binding to reported pain scores in particular brain regions.

Greater endogenous opioid engagement can compete with the tracer, so tracer displacement is an indirect measure requiring a binding model; it is not a direct photograph of pain or peptide concentration. The reported negative association with sensory pain scores is consistent with a role in pain modulation, but correlation alone does not identify every causal link. A complete answer distinguishes the molecular measurement, its anatomical location, and the subjective outcome instead of treating them as interchangeable quantities.

**Source:** Lecture 15 presentation, original topic anchor at PDF p. 17. Supporting reading: Meyer et al. (2023), Chapter 11.
